definition: A code used over the walkie-talkie to indicate someone needs a bathroom break. This quick shorthand helps maintain clear communication on set without interrupting workflow.
extra: Commonly used in film and TV productions to discreetly signal a short pause. Helps crew stay efficient and informed without drawing attention.

definition: A fundamental guideline that keeps the camera on one side of an imaginary axis between two characters or objects, ensuring consistent spatial relationships on screen. This keeps one character always appearing on the right side of the other. Crossing this imaginary line is called 'jumping the line' and can confuse viewers. Breaking it entirely by shooting on all sides is known as 'shooting in the round.'
extra: Maintaining the 180 degree rule helps preserve orientation and continuity, making scenes easier to follow. Directors use this rule to avoid disorienting audiences during conversations or action.

definition: The standard frame rate for movies shot on film, referring to projecting 24 individual frames every second. This frame rate creates smooth motion and the classic 'film look' most audiences recognize.
extra: While older films used 16 or 18 fps, 24 fps became the norm in the sound era. Modern digital filmmaking often sticks to this rate for cinematic feel, though some genres experiment with different speeds.

definition: A basic editing guideline stating the camera should move at least 30 degrees relative to a subject between successive shots to avoid a jarring jump cut effect.
extra: Following this rule helps maintain visual continuity and smooth transitions, keeping the audience engaged in the story rather than distracted by abrupt camera changes.

definition: Movies designed to create an illusion of depth by delivering two slightly different images—one to each eye—usually viewed with special glasses. This gives the impression of three-dimensional solidity on a flat screen.
extra: 3D filming uses twin-lensed cameras to capture these images. When projected separately and viewed correctly, the brain combines them into a realistic perception of depth, enhancing immersion.

definition: Special glasses worn to view 3D films, designed to filter or separate images so each eye sees a different perspective, enabling the 3D effect.
extra: There are three main types: anaglyph (red/blue or red/cyan lenses), polarized, and active shutter glasses. Each corresponds to a different method of delivering separate images to each eye.

definition: A term used in film production referring to the second-to-last shot of the day, named after assistant director Abby Singer who popularized calling it out.
extra: Knowing when the 'Abby' shot is coming helps cast and crew prepare to wrap up efficiently, improving overall shoot day management.

definition: A budgeting term describing the key creative professionals who shape the artistic direction of a film or TV show, including the screenwriter, producer, director, and main actors.
extra: Expenses for above-the-line personnel are usually fixed early in production and can significantly impact the overall budget.

definition: Major upfront costs before production begins, such as story rights, salaries for producers, directors, and principal cast, travel, and production fees for purchased projects.
extra: Everything else, like crew wages and equipment rentals, falls under below-the-line expenses, which cover the physical production costs.

definition: Non-narrative films that do not feature acting or reference reality, relying instead on motion, rhythm, light, and composition to evoke emotional responses.
extra: These films explore cinema’s unique visual and auditory qualities and often challenge traditional storytelling conventions.

definition: A philosophical and artistic focus on characters facing meaningless or purposeless situations, often highlighting the irrationality and futility of human existence.
extra: In film and theater, absurdism challenges accepted truths and explores existential themes through seemingly pointless or repetitive actions.

term: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS)
definition: A professional honorary organization dedicated to advancing the arts and sciences of motion pictures, managed by a board representing various film crafts.
extra: AMPAS organizes the annual Academy Awards and supports film preservation, research, and education.

definition: Annual awards presented by AMPAS recognizing outstanding achievements in film across numerous categories, symbolized by the Oscar statuette.
extra: Winning or being nominated for an Academy Award often significantly boosts a film’s prestige and commercial success.

definition: An editing technique that speeds up footage or shortens duration to convey excitement, rhythm, or the passage of time efficiently.
extra: Commonly used in action sequences or to compress lengthy events while maintaining viewer engagement.

definition: A focused light used to highlight a specific area, object, or detail within a scene, often to draw viewer attention or add depth.
extra: Types include wall sconces, floodlights, recessed lighting, torchière lamps, and track lighting, each offering different intensity and coverage.

definition: Sound heard without an identifiable visible source, often used to create mystery or tension in a scene.
extra: Common in horror or suspense genres where off-screen sounds heighten atmosphere.

definition: The science and study of sound wave behavior and transmission in different environments.
extra: Good acoustic design is vital for clear dialogue and sound quality in film and theater productions.

definition: A primary division within a film’s narrative structure, usually marking major plot points or shifts.
extra: Most films follow a three-act structure: setup, confrontation, and resolution, guiding story progression.

definition: A person who portrays a character in a film, television, theater, or other performance mediums, using voice, expression, and movement to tell a story.
extra: Actors often undergo training and use various techniques to embody their roles convincingly.

definition: The cue given by the director at the start of a take, signaling cast and crew to begin performing and recording.
extra: This command initiates filming and helps synchronize everyone on set.

definition: A cut that uses on-screen motion to cover the transition, making the action appear continuous and uninterrupted.
extra: Commonly used in action sequences to maintain flow and avoid jarring the audience.

definition: A film genre where the protagonist faces a series of violent or physically challenging events, usually culminating in the hero's victory over adversity.
extra: Features high energy, stunts, chases, and battles with a resourceful hero fighting against dangerous odds.

definition: The process of transferring a creative work, either fiction or nonfiction, into a motion picture format, often involving rewriting or reimagining.
extra: Includes adaptations of novels, plays, true stories, or previous films.

definition: An extra camera used during filming, often employed for complex action scenes or to speed up coverage.
extra: Allows simultaneous shooting of multiple angles to enhance editing options.

definition: Additional filming conducted after principal photography to replace, add, or improve scenes based on feedback or creative decisions.
extra: May involve recalling actors and altering parts of the film to improve the final product.

term: Adjusted Gross Deal/ Adjusted Gross Participation/ Gross Deal
definition: A distribution agreement where producers receive an advance payment plus a share of the net profits from the film.
extra: Often structured to incentivize filmmakers while managing financial risk.

definition: Improvised dialogue spoken by an actor during a performance, either spontaneously or deliberately unscripted.
extra: Can add realism or humor when used appropriately in scenes.

definition: The process of re-recording dialogue in a studio after filming to improve audio quality or alter lines.
extra: Used to fix background noise issues or change scripted content without reshooting.

definition: The time difference between a point on the soundtrack and the corresponding image on screen.
extra: Important in synchronizing audio and visual elements in post-production.

definition: An upfront payment made before services are rendered or expenses incurred.
extra: Common in production to cover initial costs and secure talent or resources.

definition: A pre-release copy of a film or TV show sent to critics and awards voters for early viewing.
extra: Helps generate buzz and gather feedback before official release.

definition: The effect the atmosphere has on an object's appearance from a distance, reducing contrast and detail clarity.
extra: Used in cinematography and art to convey depth and realism.

definition: A bird’s eye view shot taken from high above using helicopters, drones, planes, or other airborne devices.
extra: Provides expansive views and dramatic perspectives, often establishing location.

definition: Casting an actor in a role that is the opposite of their usual character type, challenging audience expectations.
extra: Can showcase an actor’s range and bring fresh dynamics to a film.

definition: Companies specializing in representing clients such as actors, writers, and musicians to find them work and negotiate contracts.
extra: Often divided into departments focusing on specific industries like film, television, or modeling.

definition: A professional who represents and promotes clients, negotiates deals, and manages career opportunities on their behalf.
extra: Acts as a liaison between clients and production companies to secure roles and contracts.

definition: A pseudonym used by directors who wish to disassociate themselves from a film due to creative differences or dissatisfaction.
extra: Historically the only approved alias for such cases in the industry.

definition: Refers to top-tier actors, producers, directors, or writers who command high salaries and have significant influence on film projects.
extra: Their involvement often guarantees financing and distribution opportunities.

definition: An extended metaphor; in film, it means a suggestive resemblance between a visible event or character and more significant or abstract meanings outside the film.
extra: Often used to convey deeper messages or social commentary.

definition: The repetition of the same letter or sound at the beginning of closely connected words. Example: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.
extra: Commonly used in dialogue or titles for stylistic effect.

definition: An implied direct or indirect reference to something or someone else, through image or dialogue.
extra: Can enrich storytelling by invoking external meanings or cultural references.

definition: An ending that was considered, written, or produced but ultimately discarded in favor of another resolution.
extra: Sometimes included in DVD extras or director’s cuts.

definition: The feeling or mood evoked by a particular scene or setting.
extra: Created through lighting, sound, set design, and music.

definition: Natural or surrounding light around a subject; usually soft and diffused.
extra: Provides general illumination and sets the tone of a scene.

definition: When a phrase, statement, or resolution is not explicitly defined, allowing multiple interpretations.
extra: Used to provoke thought or create mystery.

definition: A space lacking clear depth cues, making it difficult for the viewer to understand what they are seeing.
extra: Can be used to create surreal or disorienting effects.

definition: An honorary society of film editors recognized for professional achievement, education, and dedication to editing. Members use the post-nominal letters ACE.
extra: Promotes excellence in film editing.

definition: A professional organization advancing the art and science of cinematography and advocating motion pictures as an art form.
extra: Not a labor union or guild, but a cultural and educational society.

term: American Society of Composers, Authors, and Publishers (ASCAP)
definition: An organization protecting music creators’ rights by collecting and distributing royalties for public performances.
extra: Ensures composers and songwriters are compensated when their music is used in media.

definition: The original organization that created the ASA speed rating system for photographic film sensitivity to light, precursor to modern ISO ratings.
extra: Important in measuring camera sensor sensitivity and film speed.

definition: An element in a film that belongs to a different time or place, often considered a mistake or inconsistency.
extra: Can be used intentionally for stylistic or comedic effect.

definition: A method of creating widescreen images by distorting the picture using special lenses during filming and projection.
extra: Produces unique horizontal and vertical magnifications for cinematic effect.

definition: Additional film-related rights such as soundtrack, publishing, novelization, stageplay, and merchandising rights.
extra: Merchandising often includes interactive games based on the film.

definition: The perspective from which the camera depicts its subject.
extra: Can influence how the audience perceives the subject.

definition: To direct or move the camera to focus on a particular subject.
extra: Used to emphasize or isolate a character or object.

definition: The process of animating a storyboard into a moving sequence to preview scenes before full production.
extra: Helps visualize timing and flow of a film.

definition: The photographing and manipulation of successive drawings or models to create the illusion of movement when projected as a sequence.
extra: Includes hand-drawn, stop-motion, and computer-generated techniques.

definition: Mechatronic puppets used in films and theme parks to portray characters with realistic movement.
extra: A modern evolution of automatons used for lifelike effects.

definition: A hand-drawn and computer-generated animation originating from Japan. Outside of Japan and in English, anime refers specifically to animation produced in Japan. However, in Japan and in Japanese, anime describes all animated works, regardless of style or origin.
extra: A distinct style often characterized by colorful graphics, vibrant characters, and fantastical themes.

definition: The first version of a motion picture printed to film after color correction on an interpositive. It is also the first version of the movie printed to film with the sound properly synced to the picture.
extra: Used for final review before mass duplication.

definition: The main character, person, group, society, nature, force, spirit world, bad guy, or villain of a film or script who is in adversarial conflict with the film’s hero, lead character, or protagonist. Sometimes termed ‘the heavy’.
extra: Essential to creating conflict and driving the story.

definition: A single film consisting of several shorter films, each complete in itself and distinguished from the others, though frequently tied together by a single theme, premise, or author.
extra: Often used to explore multiple perspectives or stories.

definition: The tendency in animated films to give creatures or objects human qualities, abilities, and characteristics.
extra: Used to create relatable characters out of non-human entities.

definition: Anything in a film, usually following the film’s high point, zenith, apex, crescendo, or climax, in which there is an unsatisfying and disappointing let-down of emotion, or what is expected doesn’t occur.
extra: Can be used intentionally to subvert audience expectations.

definition: The principal protagonist of a film who lacks the attributes or characteristics of a typical hero archetype, but with whom the audience identifies.
extra: Often flawed or morally ambiguous characters.

definition: The size of a camera lens opening through which light passes. It is calibrated in f/stops and is generally written as numbers such as 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 5.6, 8, 11, and 16.
extra: Controls exposure and depth of field in photography and cinematography.

definition: Wooden boxes or crates of varying sizes with holes on each end used chiefly in film production. These boxes are specialized pieces of equipment belonging to the grip department, and should not be confused with simple crates, other boxes, or boxes for apples. There are 4 sizes: full, half, quarter, and pancake.
extra: Used for elevating actors, equipment, or props on set.

definition: A shot in which the subject or subjects are photographed by an encircling or moving camera.
extra: Creates a dynamic sense of movement around the subject.

definition: A character, place, or thing, that is repeatedly presented in films with a particular style or characterization; an archetype usually applies to a specific genre or type classification.
extra: Common examples include the hero, the mentor, and the villain.

definition: A metal rod attached to a C-Stand.
extra: Used to hold flags, scrims, lights, or other grip equipment.

definition: A member of the shooting crew who handles, maintains, and is responsible for real and prop weapon safety on set, including firearms, knives, swords, bows, and staff weapons.
extra: Ensures all weapons are used safely and correctly during production.

definition: Includes all types of footage that feature key plot actions, talking characters, or interview subjects. A-roll footage is more often known in the industry these days as main footage, primary footage, hero footage, or principal shots.
extra: Forms the backbone of the film's narrative.

definition: A French word meaning halt or stop, which refers to the in-camera trick of stopping the camera, then removing or inserting an object, then restarting the camera to have an object magically disappear or appear. This is one of the earliest techniques of silent film.
extra: A primitive special effect technique.

definition: The section of a production’s crew concerned with visual artistry. Working under the supervision of the production designer and/or art director, the art department is responsible for arranging the overall look of the film.
extra: Includes set design, props, and visual elements.

definition: A labour union and local of the International Alliance of Theatrical and Stage Employees (IATSE) representing over 3,000 motion picture and television professionals working in the United States. Members include production designers, art directors, set designers and modelmakers, illustrators and matte artists, scenic artists, and title and graphic artists.
extra: Advocates for the rights and standards of art department professionals.

definition: A movie theatre that shows independent films, documentaries, experimental films, foreign films, low-budget films, local films, and/or any film considered “high brow” or an “art film”.
extra: Often targets niche or cinephile audiences.

definition: Typically an independent film, aimed at a niche market rather than a mass market audience.
extra: Usually characterized by artistic or experimental content.

definition: A person who takes an artist’s designs and builds them in a computer, so that animators can manipulate the figures to tell the story of the film.
extra: Works primarily in 3D animation and rigging.

definition: A visual defect on a film image caused by limitations or the malfunction of imaging equipment. An artifact is a distortion or imperfection, such as compression artifacts, digital noise, or aliasing, resulting from limitations or errors in the digital processing, encoding, or transmission of signals.
extra: Can degrade image quality and distract viewers.

definition: The two main categories of filmmaking light sources include artificial and natural light. Artificial lights can be either on-camera or off-camera, while natural light nearly always comes from an outside source such as the sun or a window.
extra: Artificial lights include tungsten, LED, fluorescent, and HMI lights used to control and shape the lighting environment on set.

definition: ASA Speed was a numerical scale developed by the American Standards Association to indicate the sensitivity of photographic film to light, with higher numbers representing greater sensitivity. This scale was a precursor to the ISO standard used today in photography to measure the sensitivity of both film and digital sensors.
extra: Higher ASA/ISO values allow shooting in lower light but may introduce more grain or noise.

definition: Occurs when a character in a film breaks the ‘fourth wall’ and directly addresses the audience with a comment.
extra: Used to reveal inner thoughts or provide commentary, often creating intimacy or humor.

definition: A dimensionless ratio that defines the proportional relationship between the width and height of an image or screen, calculated by dividing the width by the height. Common aspect ratios include 16:9 (widescreen HD), 4:3 (standard definition), 21:9 (ultrawide cinema), and 1:1 (square), each impacting the shape and composition of visual content across different media formats.
extra: Aspect ratio influences storytelling by shaping the viewer's focus and framing.

definition: A lens designed with a non-spherical surface to reduce optical aberrations and distortions (like barrel distortion), improving image quality and focusing. This design allows for more precise and compact lens systems compared to traditional spherical lenses.
extra: Commonly used in high-end camera lenses and corrective eyewear.

definition: The assembly edit is when the editor looks through all of the footage and creates a story outline. The first stage of editing, is when the editor looks through all of the footage and arranges the shots in script order.
extra: Provides a raw chronological sequence of scenes to aid in storytelling refinement.

definition: An assistant to the art director working in the art department. Assistant art director’s responsibilities differ widely depending on what they are hired for based on their skills and what is needed on a project.
extra: May handle scheduling, coordinating with other departments, and supervising art department tasks.

definition: A member of the camera crew who assists the camera operator. This person is responsible for the maintenance and care of the camera, as well as preparing dope sheets. In smaller camera crews, they may also perform the duties of clapper-loader and/or a focus puller.
extra: Crucial for smooth camera operations and technical support during shoots.

definition: The role includes tracking daily progress against the filming production schedule, arranging logistics, preparing daily call sheets, checking cast and crew, and maintaining order on the set.
extra: Often the primary organizer and troubleshooter during production.

definition: Aid the editor and director in collecting and organizing all the elements needed to edit the film. When editing is finished, they oversee the various lists and instructions necessary to put the film into its final form.
extra: Handles syncing, labeling footage, and preparing materials for final post-production.

definition: An assistant to the production manager in the production department.
extra: Helps with budget management, scheduling, and coordinating resources.

definition: Someone who works closely with the producer and assists him or her in putting a TV show or film together. They serve as a producer’s right-hand and are therefore entrusted to complete a wide range of tasks.
extra: May manage specific production aspects, communications, or logistics.

definition: When sound doesn’t match a film’s visuals. Filmmakers use asynchronous sound to manipulate emotion and narrative.
extra: Often used to create irony, tension, or a dreamlike atmosphere.

definition: Refers to any concrete or nebulous feeling that contributes a dimensional tone to a film’s action.
extra: Created through visuals, sound, lighting, and performance.

definition: All sound in a film including diegetic and non-diegetic sound. A strip of film carrying sound records in addition to the pictures.
extra: Essential for storytelling, mood, and realism.

definition: When audio is carried over the visual transition to tie together two scenes.
extra: Helps smooth transitions and maintain narrative flow.

definition: A sample or test of a performance by an actor, singer, musician, dancer or other performer.
extra: Used by casting directors to evaluate talent.

definition: A critical theory that ascribes overall responsibility for the creation of a film and its personal vision, identifiable style, thematic aspects and techniques to its film director, rather than to the collaborative efforts of all involved; an auteur can refer to a director with a recognizable or signature style.
extra: Highlights the director as the primary creative force.

definition: The feature of a camera that tries to ensure that your chosen subject is sharp within the photo. Sensors detect how far away the subject is from the camera, and this information is relayed to the lens, which then uses an electronic motor to adjusts the focal distance of the lens.
extra: Widely used in modern digital cameras for convenience and speed.

definition: A production may ask actors, filmmakers, crew, or agents for their clients avails while casting or crewing. They are asking whether one is simply available during the dates specified for production before getting into any further conversation or consideration for the position. Actors often give their avail to a production as a courtesy. Avails hold no legal or contractual status in the hiring process.
extra: Important early step in scheduling and casting decisions.

definition: The use of naturally-existing light on location rather than creating artificial light.
extra: Often used for a naturalistic look and to save time or equipment.

definition: Experimental films or avant-garde cinema is a mode of filmmaking that rigorously re-evaluates cinematic conventions and explores non-narrative forms or alternatives to traditional narratives or methods of working.
extra: Often challenges viewers with abstract or unconventional content.

definition: A film and video editing software application or non-linear editing system (NLE) developed by Avid Technology.
extra: Industry-standard software used in professional post-production.

definition: An axial cut is a type of jump cut, where the camera suddenly moves closer to or further away from its subject, along an invisible line drawn straight between the camera and the subject. While a plain jump cut typically involves a temporal discontinuity (an apparent jump in time), an axial cut is a way of maintaining the illusion of continuity. Axial cuts were fairly common in the cinema of the 1910s and 1920s.
extra: Used to create emphasis or disorientation without breaking spatial logic.

definition: An imaginary or invisible line (or axis) that passes through two main subjects being filmed in a scene, who face each other (one is left, the other is right). Conventionally, the camera must not cross the axis of action and maintains that left-right relationship or orientation in order to avoid disorienting or distracting the viewer with a reverse angle shot. See also 180-Degree Rule.
extra: Helps maintain spatial consistency in scenes.

definition: Refers to a large photographic backing or painting for the background of a scene. These large scale photos/paintings are printed/painted, hung, and lit to give the illusion of the outdoors on set or an extension to the set.
extra: Common in studio productions for seamless environments.

definition: Profit participation in a film after distribution and/or production costs have been recouped.
extra: Often a way to incentivize talent and investors.

definition: The area behind the middle ground and foreground in a shot that can often extend far into the distance.
extra: Contributes to depth and context in composition.

definition: The Background actors start their action when this phrase is called.
extra: Ensures timing and coordination of extras during filming.

definition: Also known as a film score, this music plays during a scene to set the mood or tone without being part of the on-screen action or dialogue.
extra: Helps guide the audience’s emotional response.

definition: An actor who appears in non-speaking or silent roles in the background of scenes, such as crowds or passersby.
extra: Also called extras; essential for realistic environments.

definition: Lighting placed behind the subject to create separation from the background and highlight outlines.
extra: Often used for dramatic or halo effects.

definition: An outdoor area on studio property used for shooting exterior scenes with pre-built sets or natural backdrops.
extra: Allows for flexible filming without leaving the studio.

definition: A technique where live actors perform in front of a screen showing a pre-recorded background.
extra: Commonly used in driving scenes.

definition: A fictional or real history developed for a character or event that occurred before the story begins.
extra: Gives depth and motivation to characters.

term: Back to One/ Back to First Marks
definition: A direction given to reset actors and elements to their starting positions after a take.
extra: Often called out by the assistant director.

definition: The arrangement of elements like light, color, and composition to create visual harmony in a scene.
extra: Affects mood and viewer focus.

definition: A film prohibited from distribution or screening due to legal, political, or moral reasons.
extra: Censorship varies by region and time period.

definition: Metal flaps attached to lights that control the direction and spread of light.
extra: Used to prevent spill and shape lighting.

definition: A sound-absorbing cover placed over a camera to muffle its operational noise.
extra: Useful during scenes with sensitive audio.

definition: Indicates that a film’s plot is inspired by real events, though often with fictionalized elements.
extra: Allows for creative freedom while honoring facts.

definition: A short pause or small action used to create rhythm in dialogue or indicate a shift in emotion.
extra: Essential in timing both performance and editing.

definition: A breakdown of a film’s major events or moments, organized scene-by-scene or act-by-act.
extra: Used by writers to plan structure before scripting.

definition: Activities and people involved in the production process but not seen in the final film.
extra: Often featured in promotional content or documentaries.

definition: Refers to crew and costs not involved in the creative development of a film, like lighting or catering.
extra: Distinguished from above-the-line roles like directors.

definition: Costs associated with production operations, including labor, equipment, and set construction.
extra: Tracked separately from creative personnel costs.

definition: The chief assistant to the gaffer (Best Boy Electric) or key grip (Best Boy Grip).
extra: Handles daily operations and logistics of their department.

definition: The order and manner in which cast and crew names are presented in a film’s credits or advertising.
extra: Often negotiated in contracts, especially for lead roles.

definition: A short written biography of someone involved in a film, used for press and promotional materials.
extra: Often written by publicists or provided by the artist.

definition: A film that dramatizes the life of a real person, often based on historical records or biographies.
extra: Differs from documentaries by using actors and dramatization.

term: Bird’s Eye View Shot/ Overhead Shot/Elevated Shot
definition: A shot taken from directly above the subject, providing a top-down perspective like a bird in flight.
extra: Often used to show scale, isolation, or geography.

definition: A small acting role with limited lines, usually fewer than five, but with interaction with main characters.
extra: Also known as a five-or-less or under-five role.

term: Black and White/ B&W/ BW/ Monochrome
definition: A film shot and presented without color, using only shades of gray from black to white.
extra: Still used today for stylistic or thematic reasons.

definition: A form of humor that treats serious, taboo, or grim subjects with irony or satire.
extra: Often explores death, war, or existential themes.

definition: Banning or excluding individuals from work in the industry, often due to political or social views.
extra: Notable during the Hollywood Red Scare era.

definition: A 1970s film genre targeting Black audiences with urban stories, style, and music.
extra: Popularized new stars and cultural trends.

definition: A film processing technique that skips bleaching to retain silver in the film, creating a high-contrast, desaturated look.
extra: Used to create a gritty, stylized effect.

definition: A soundproof cover for a camera to muffle mechanical noises during filming.
extra: Essential during dialogue scenes with quiet audio.

definition: A major studio film with a large budget, high production values, and mass appeal.
extra: Often associated with summer releases and big profits.

definition: The planned movement and positioning of actors and cameras within a scene.
extra: Determined during rehearsals to guide filming.

definition: Filming multiple episodes or scenes in a single session to optimize time and resources.
extra: Common in television production.

definition: Shooting all scenes from one angle or lighting setup before moving to the next.
extra: Speeds up production and minimizes resets.

definition: A mistake or error made during filming, often humorous and kept for outtake reels.
extra: Popular in blooper reels and end credits.

definition: The process of enlarging film to a higher format, like from 35mm to 70mm.
extra: Used to improve image quality for larger screens.

definition: Humor that includes risqué, sexual, or profane content.
extra: Often meant for mature audiences only.

definition: A chroma key technique using a blue (or green) screen to composite subjects onto different backgrounds.
extra: Standard in visual effects before CGI backgrounds are added.

definition: A low-budget film, often in a genre like horror or sci-fi, sometimes released as a secondary feature.
extra: Many cult classics come from B-movie origins.

definition: A performer who substitutes for an actor in specific scenes, like stunts or nudity.
extra: Used to protect the actor or meet performance needs.

definition: Cosmetic makeup applied to parts of the body other than the face, usually for continuity or effect.
extra: Used to conceal blemishes or match costumes.

definition: The Hindi-language film industry based in Mumbai, India, known for musicals and colorful storytelling.
extra: One of the largest film industries in the world.

definition: A film that fails to make back its production costs, resulting in financial loss.
extra: Opposite of a blockbuster; often critically panned.

definition: Scenes at the beginning and end of a film that frame or tie the story together.
extra: Provides closure or narrative symmetry.

definition: A microphone mounted on a pole used to capture audio while staying out of the camera frame.
extra: Operated by a boom operator during takes.

definition: A sound crew member responsible for holding and positioning the boom microphone.
extra: Works closely with the sound mixer to ensure clean audio.

term: Boom Shot/ Jib Shot/ Crane Shot
definition: A high-angle moving shot captured using a mechanical arm like a jib or crane.
extra: Adds cinematic motion and vertical perspective.

definition: An unauthorized copy of a film, often distributed illegally without copyright permission.
extra: Damages revenue and violates copyright laws.

definition: A TV episode using limited sets, characters, and effects to reduce cost or focus on dialogue.
extra: Often character-driven and intense in tone.

definition: A large reflective surface used to redirect light onto a subject, often made of foam or poster board.
extra: Softens shadows and fills in light during filming.

definition: The total revenue earned by a film during its theatrical run, often measured by domestic and worldwide earnings.
extra: Opening weekend gross is crucial for a film’s success.

definition: Shooting multiple takes of a scene with varied camera settings, especially exposure, to ensure the best result.
extra: Commonly done when lighting or conditions are uncertain.

definition: A document listing all elements required for production on a scene-by-scene basis, such as cast, props, and wardrobe.
extra: Used to schedule and organize production efficiently.

definition: The process of aging or distressing props, costumes, and sets to make them look used or worn.
extra: Enhances realism and visual storytelling.

definition: A shot that visually indicates a passage of time between scenes.
extra: Examples include time-lapse or changing seasons.

term: British Academy of Film and Television Arts/ BAFTA
definition: A UK-based organization supporting film, TV, and games, known for hosting the annual BAFTA Awards.
extra: Considered the British equivalent of the Oscars.

definition: A charitable organization promoting UK film culture and preservation.
extra: Manages archives and hosts the BFI London Film Festival.

definition: A UK-based professional association for advancing the craft of cinematography.
extra: Members include top British directors of photography.

definition: Supplementary footage used to enrich a story or cover edits in the main footage.
extra: Often includes cutaways, establishing shots, or action inserts.

definition: A genre where two mismatched characters are paired together on a journey or mission.
extra: Focuses on their evolving relationship and chemistry.

term: Building/ Building a Scene/ Building to Climax
definition: A technique of increasing intensity and energy within a scene to reach a dramatic high point.
extra: Involves pacing, acting, sound, and editing.

term: BVK/Berufsverband Kinematografie/ German Society of Cinematographers
definition: A German association representing freelance cinematographers and advancing professional standards.
extra: Promotes cinematographic education and networking.

definition: A raise in pay, typically granted for taking on additional duties or stepping into a higher-level position.
extra: Common when responsibilities shift mid-production.

definition: Short audio or visual segments used to transition or introduce content, such as a studio logo.
extra: Often used at the beginning or end of programming.

definition: A large overhead frame with fabric to diffuse or control light on set.
extra: Standard sizes include 6×6, 8×8, 12×12, and 20×20.

definition: A knot used in rigging that allows a secure loop in the middle of a rope.
extra: Preferred for its strength and ease of untying.

definition: Industry or audience excitement generated about a film or show.
extra: Buzz can influence marketing and box office success.

definition: A low background noise track added to scenes to prevent unnatural silence.
extra: Now more commonly called ambient sound or room tone.

definition: A clothespin used on set, primarily to attach gels or materials to lighting gear.
extra: Despite its simplicity, it's a must-have grip tool.

definition: A clothespin with the spring removed, used on set for specific tasks requiring less tension than a standard C-47.
extra: Used informally; not as common or standardized as the C-47.

definition: Insulated wires used to deliver electrical power to film set equipment such as lights and cameras.
extra: Available in various lengths and gauges depending on usage.

definition: A subscription-based service delivering TV content through coaxial or fiber-optic cables instead of over-the-air signals.
extra: Offers premium channels, HD content, and on-demand access.

definition: A daily production document listing call times, scene details, cast and crew schedules, weather, and other logistics.
extra: Usually distributed by the 2nd Assistant Director.

definition: The exact time each crew member or actor is expected to arrive and be ready for work on set.
extra: Listed on the call sheet and strictly followed.

definition: A brief appearance in a film by a notable or famous person, often playing themselves or a minor role.
extra: Usually non-speaking and uncredited.

definition: A device used for capturing visual images, either as still photographs or motion pictures.
extra: Essential to every film and video production.

definition: The position and direction from which a camera films a subject, affecting perspective and viewer interpretation.
extra: Can convey emotion, power, or scale.

definition: The planning and movement of the camera within a scene for optimal visual storytelling.
extra: Coordinated with actor blocking and lighting.

definition: A team of professionals responsible for operating and supporting camera functions during a shoot.
extra: Includes roles like camera operator, 1st AC, and 2nd AC.

definition: The motion of the camera to follow action, reveal information, or shift viewer perspective.
extra: Examples include dolly, pan, tilt, and crane movements.

definition: The person physically operating the camera during filming, under the guidance of the Director of Photography.
extra: May be responsible for framing, focus, and movement.

definition: Directional terms indicating the right or left side from the perspective of the camera.
extra: Often opposite from the actor or crew's visual left/right.

definition: A style that is deliberately exaggerated and theatrical, often for comedic or ironic effect.
extra: Often overlaps with kitsch or parody; embraced in cult cinema.

definition: An old film industry term meaning that a scene or project has been completed and safely recorded.
extra: Derived from storing film reels in metal canisters.

definition: A nonprofit trade organization supporting production designers and art department professionals in Canada.
extra: Promotes excellence and advocacy within the field.

definition: A nonprofit association promoting the creative and technical craft of cinematography in Canada.
extra: Offers networking, education, and professional recognition.

definition: The use of actual or simulated candlelight to create a warm, intimate, and atmospheric lighting effect.
extra: Common in romantic or period films.

definition: A brief critical review of a film or show, typically summarizing key strengths or weaknesses.
extra: Used in publications where space is limited.

definition: An exaggerated portrayal of a character, emphasizing distinctive traits to the point of distortion.
extra: Often used for satire or comedic effect.

definition: An animated film or TV program made by photographing drawings or using computer-generated imagery.
extra: May be aimed at children or adults depending on style and content.

definition: A film or franchise that consistently earns high profits over time, often through both ticket sales and merchandise.
extra: Examples include Star Wars and Marvel franchises.

definition: The group of performers who portray characters in a film, show, or play.
extra: Includes leads, supporting roles, and extras.

definition: The process of selecting actors for roles in a film or production.
extra: May involve auditions, screen tests, and callbacks.

definition: A term referring to coercive or exploitative sexual practices in casting, now widely condemned and illegal.
extra: Symbolic of historic abuses in the entertainment industry.

definition: A professional who selects and auditions talent for roles, often collaborating closely with the director and producers.
extra: Plays a crucial role in shaping the cast and tone of a project.

definition: A professional association of casting directors across the globe, now known simply as Casting Society.
extra: Members use 'CSA' in their credits as a designation of membership.

definition: A memorable or repeated line often associated with a specific character or personality.
extra: Can become iconic and influence pop culture.

definition: An individual or company responsible for providing food and meals for cast and crew on set.
extra: Different from craft services, which provides snacks and drinks.

definition: During a film’s climax, the audience may experience a purging or cleansing of emotional tension, providing relief or therapeutic restoration.
extra: A key concept in drama and storytelling, originally from Greek tragedy.

definition: A literary term referring to a narrative that follows the same structure as tales told in folklore to warn its listener of a danger. There are three essential parts to a cautionary tale, though they can be introduced in a large variety of ways. First, a taboo or prohibition is stated: some act, location, or thing is said to be dangerous. Then, the narrative itself is told: someone disregarded the warning and performed the forbidden act. Finally, the violator comes to an unpleasant fate, which is frequently related in expansive and grisly detail.
extra: Often used to teach moral lessons through storytelling.

definition: Cel Animation:A transparent sheet on which objects are drawn or painted for traditional, hand-drawn animation. Actual celluloid (consisting of cellulose nitrate and camphor) was used during the first half of the 20th century, but since it was flammable and dimensionally unstable it was largely replaced by cellulose acetate. With the advent of computer-assisted animation production, the use of cels has been all but abandoned in major productions. Disney studios stopped using cels in 1990 when Computer Animation Production System (CAPS) replaced this element in their animation process,and in the next decade and a half, the other major animation studios phased cels out as well.
extra: Named after the original celluloid material; replaced by digital animation techniques.

definition: A class of materials produced by mixing nitrocellulose and camphor, often with added dyes and other agents. Once much more common for its use as photographic film in filmmaking before the advent of safer methods came to be.
extra: Highly flammable, it was largely replaced due to safety concerns.

definition: The process of determining what can or can not be viewed by the public. Film censorship is carried out by various countries to differing degrees, often by a ratings board, sometimes as a result of powerful or relentless lobbying by organizations or individuals. Films that are banned in a particular country change over time.
extra: Varies widely depending on cultural and political contexts.

definition: Various countries or regions have film classification boards for reviewing movies and rating their content in terms of its suitability for particular audiences. For many countries, movies are required to be advertised as having a particular certificate or rating, forewarning audiences of possible objectionable content.
extra: Helps audiences make informed viewing choices.

definition: Computer Generated Imagery or Images; a term referring to the use of 3D computer graphics and technology to create filmed images, special effects and the illusion of motion.
extra: Widely used in modern films for effects and animation.

definition: A person or other being in a narrative. The character may be entirely fictional or based on a real-life person, in which case the distinction of afictionalversusrealcharacter may be made.
extra: Central to driving the plot and engaging the audience.

definition: Largely a supporting actor who plays unusual, interesting, or eccentric characters. The term, often contrasted with that of leading actor, is somewhat abstract and open to interpretation. In a literal sense, all actors can be considered character actors since they all play characters,but the term more commonly refers to an actor who frequently plays a distinctive and important supporting role. Character actors are generally well-known and recognizable by the audience, by appearance if not by name.
extra: Known for memorable supporting roles rather than leads.

definition: When a creator of a work introduces a large number of characters at once, such as at the beginning of a work, they have to find a way to distinguish them and make them memorable in the audience’s mind. Sometimes by giving each character a specific color motif, the audience can quickly associate one color with a character and tell the characters apart with only a glance.
extra: Common technique in animation and comics.

definition: The analysis or portrayal of the traits of a character or an individual in a creative work where the plot and narrative come secondary to the character. Also referred to as a brief narrative or sketch devoted primarily to the underlying study of a character.
extra: Focuses deeply on character development and psychology.

definition: Checking the playback to confirm the image was recorded.
extra: A routine procedure to avoid lost footage.

definition: Taking off the camera lens and examining the film plan for scratches; this happens after every camera set up and is usually done by the 1stAC.
extra: Helps prevent damage and ensure clean film exposure.

definition: A way of saying two actors show sparks of apparent attraction, or are perceived to be well paired by the audience. There is a certain extra thrill from watching such pairings on screen. For example, Bradley Cooper and Lady Gaga were said to have great chemistry in the 2018 filmA Star Is Born.
extra: Can significantly impact audience engagement.

definition: the combination of the two Italian words for “clear/bright” and “dark”; refers to a notable, contrasting use of light and shade in scenes; often achieved by using a spotlight; this lighting technique had its roots in German Expressionistic cinematography.
extra: Creates dramatic visual effects and mood.

definition: A slang term, sometimes used pejoratively, for the film genre catered specifically to women’s interests, and is marketed toward women demographics. They generally tend to appeal more to a younger female audience and deal mainly with love and romance.Although many types of films may be directed toward a female audience, the term “chick flick” is typically used only in reference to films that contain personal drama and emotion or themes that are relationship-based (although not necessarily romantic, as films may focus on parent-child or friend relationships). This term is often considered derogatory and is now used sparingly.
extra: Term reflects cultural attitudes and is controversial.

definition: Generally applied to a child acting on stage or on-screen. An adult who began their acting career as a child may also be called a child actor, or aformer child actor.
extra: Child actors may face unique career challenges.

definition: The Chimera Softbox are designed to handle such large-scale lighting jobs as commercials and motion pictures. Their increased depth allows the full-flood beam of a large Fresnel fixture to fill the front diffusion screen of the Lightbank and deliver a beautiful, translucent quality of light.
extra: Popular for producing soft, flattering light.

definition: A choreographer conceives, creates, and directs dance and movement in a wide range of performance contexts, including dance, theater, film, television, opera, and live events. The choreographic process may employ improvisation for the purpose of developing innovative movement ideas.
extra: Works across many entertainment fields.

definition: The art or practice of designing sequences of movements of physical bodies (or their depictions) in which motion or form or both are specified. Aspects of dance choreography include the compositional use of organic unity, rhythmic or non-rhythmic articulation, theme and variation, and repetition. In general, choreography is used to design dances that are intended to be performed.
extra: Fundamental to dance and movement arts.

definition: A visual effects and post-production technique for compositing (layering) two images or video streams together based on colour hues (chroma range). The technique has been used in many fields to remove a background from the subject of a photo or video, particularly in the newscasting, motion picture, and video game industries. A colour range in the foreground footage is made transparent, allowing separately filmed background footage or a static image to be inserted into the scene.
extra: Widely known as green screen technology.

definition: A text-based graphic that overlays video content, such as broadcast news, television shows, and movies. Chyron is the general name for any graphic that is superimposed over a video or live broadcast. While a chyron is usually placed at the bottom of a frame, it can appear anywhere within the frame.
extra: Chyrons are those on-screen graphics you often see during news or TV shows that help convey additional info to the viewer. Though mostly found at the bottom of the screen, they can show up anywhere to catch your attention.

definition: Refers to a film/movie enthusiast or devotee.
extra: If you're someone who lives and breathes movies, analyzing every frame and loving the craft, you might be called a cineaste — basically a true film buff.

definition: A place where screenings occur. Also refers to film itself as an art form.
extra: Cinema is both the physical space where movies are watched and the artistic world of filmmaking as a whole.

definition: The Cinema Audio Society was formed in 1964 for the purpose of fostering community among mixers, educating and informing the general public and the motion picture and television industry about good and effective sound usage, and achieving deserved recognition for sound mixers as major contributors to the field of entertainment.
extra: This society celebrates and supports the people behind the scenes who craft the soundscapes we hear in movies and TV, making sure their work gets the respect it deserves.

definition: A cinematographic process in which special lenses are used to compress a wide image into a standard frame and then expand it again during projection. It results in an image that is almost two and a half times as wide as it is high.
extra: CinemaScope was a game changer in filmmaking, allowing directors to present much wider, more immersive images that filled the viewer’s field of vision in a dramatic way.

definition: The person responsible for the photographing or recording of a film, television production, music video or other live-action piece. The cinematographer is the head of the camera and lighting crew and would normally be responsible for making artistic and technical decisions related to the image and for selecting the camera, film stock, lenses, and filters. The study and practice of this field is referred to as cinematography.
extra: Think of the cinematographer as the visual storyteller behind a film’s look — they decide how scenes are lit, shot, and framed to bring the director’s vision to life.

definition: The art of motion picture and television photography.
extra: Cinematography is the craft that shapes the visual language of a film, blending lighting, camera work, and composition to tell a story through images.

definition: Relating to, suggestive of, or suitable for motion pictures or the filming of motion pictures.
extra: When something is described as cinematic, it means it has qualities that remind you of a movie — often grand, visually striking, or emotionally impactful.

definition: A method or style of documentary and narrative filmmaking with long takes, no narration, and little or no directorial or editing control exerted over the finished product; used to refer to a documentary-style film or minimalist cinema loosely; popularized in the 1950s French New Wave movement; now widely used (often inappropriately) to refer to the popular, artsy trend of using hand-held camera techniques.
extra: Cinema Verité aims to capture reality as honestly as possible, avoiding fancy effects or narration, though nowadays the term is sometimes used more loosely for any raw, hand-held style of filming.

definition: A process in which three synchronized movie projectors each project one-third of the picture on a wide, curving screen. Many viewers believe that the screen, which thus annexes their entire field of vision, gives a sense of reality unmatched by the flat screen.
extra: Cinerama was an immersive widescreen experience that literally wrapped the picture around you, making movie watching feel larger-than-life.

definition: A grip tool. A clamp is a brace, band, or clasp used for strengthening or holding things together. These are often called spring clips. They come in 4 sizes, #.5, #1, #2 and #3. They are an essential tool for everything a grip has to do.
extra: Clamps are the unsung heroes on set, helping grips hold equipment steady and secure in various sizes to fit different jobs.

definition: A device used in filmmaking and video production to assist in synchronizing picture and sound.
extra: That iconic board with the clapping stick used at the start of takes isn’t just for show — it helps editors sync audio and video perfectly.

definition: An animation technique using movable clay characters and stop-motion recording. It’s a film style often seen in children’s films and cartoons. It’s a meticulous process, with some feature-length films taking months – or even years – to shoot.
extra: Claymation brings clay figures to life frame by frame, a painstaking art that makes each movement feel magical on screen.

definition: Audio without noise or imperfections.
extra: Clean audio means you hear the dialogue or sounds clearly, without any distracting background noise or glitches.

definition: Dialogue without noise and background imperfections.
extra: Clean dialogue ensures the characters’ words come through crisp and clear, free from any unwanted sounds that might pull you out of the story.

definition: Said usually by the 1st AD to keep the actor’s eyeline/line-of-sight clear of anything distracting.
extra: When the 1st Assistant Director calls to 'clear the eyeline,' they want to make sure nothing interferes with where the actor is supposed to be looking.

definition: A cliffhanger or cliffhanger ending is a plot device in fiction characterized by scenes of great tension, danger, adventure, suspense, or high drama, often climaxing at the end of a film or at the end of a multi-part serial episode, where the plot ending and the fate of the protagonist(s) are left unresolved. A cliffhanger is hoped to incentivize the audience to return to see how the characters resolve the dilemma. Some serials end with the caveat, “To Be Continued” or “The End?” In serial films and television series, the following episode sometimes begins with a recap sequence.
extra: Cliffhangers leave you hanging at the most intense moment, making you eager to find out what happens next — a classic way to keep audiences hooked.

definition: The highest point of anxiety or tension in a story or film in which the central character or protagonist faces, confronts, and deals with the consequence(s) of all their actions or faces the antagonist in a climactic battle or final engagement; a crisis often leads to a climax; also called the film’s high point, zenith, apex, or crescendo; an anti-climax or denouement may follow a climax.
extra: The climax is the story’s peak moment — where everything comes to a head, the tension is at its highest, and the big showdown happens.

definition: A short section of film removed from a movie and often exhibited; a part of a film, and sometimes a complete scene or sequence, taken from a film, similar to an excerpt.
extra: Film clips are bite-sized parts of a movie, often used for trailers, highlights, or sharing memorable moments.

definition: Closed captions are a text version of the spoken part of a television, movie or computer presentation. Closed captioning was developed to aid deaf and hard of hearing people, but it’s useful for various situations.
extra: Closed captions display the dialogue as text on the screen, making content accessible to people who are deaf or hard of hearing, and helpful in noisy environments.

definition: A shot taken from a close distance in which the object’s scale is magnified, appears relatively large and fills the entire frame to focus attention and emphasize its importance. For example, a person’s head from the shoulders or neck up is a commonly filmed close-up.
extra: Close-ups zoom in on details like a character’s face or an important object, drawing the audience’s focus and emphasizing emotions or significance.

definition: Coda means “tail” in Italian and usually refers to musical selections; in film, it refers to the epilogue, ending or last section of a film (often wordless) that provides closure, a conclusion, or a summary of the preceding storyline.
extra: A coda is the quiet closing part of a film that wraps things up, often without words, leaving you with a final emotional or thematic impression.

definition: A cold open (also called a teaser sequence) is a narrative technique used in television and films. It is the practice of jumping directly into a story at the show’s beginning before the title sequence or opening credits are shown.
extra: Cold opens throw you right into the action before any titles or credits, grabbing your attention from the very start.

definition: A film credit from yesteryear. At the beginning of filmmaking in colour, Technicolor had to maintain high standards through all stages of production and printing to offer a consistent and quality product. In addition to cameras, cameramen, and on-set technicians, the “Technicolor package” included a colour consultant to advise on appropriate colours for makeup, costumes, and set design.
extra: Back in the early days of color film, colour consultants played a key role in making sure everything from costumes to makeup looked perfect on screen.

definition: Colour film is a type of photographic film that can capture images in colour. It’s made of a plastic base coated with layers of chemicals. These chemicals react when they’re exposed to light, recording the image you see through your camera lens.
extra: Colour film lets cameras capture the world as we see it — in vibrant color — by using special chemical layers sensitive to light.

definition: Colour temperature is a system that uses numerical values to measure the colour characteristics of a light source on a spectrum ranging from warm colours to cool colours. The numerical values are referred to as degrees Kelvin (K). The two common standard colour temperatures for film and video lighting are “Tungsten” at 3200K and “Daylight” at 5600K.
extra: Colour temperature helps filmmakers balance lighting, from warm orange tones of tungsten to cool blues of daylight, measured in degrees Kelvin.

definition: The person responsible for checking all the elements of continuity during filming and editing, ensuring scenes flow smoothly.
extra: This editor acts like a detective during production, making sure all the little details match from shot to shot so the story feels seamless.

definition: A script used to maintain continuity, documenting details like actors’ movements, props, costumes, and camera angles for each scene.
extra: Think of it as a detailed blueprint that helps everyone keep track of how scenes should look to avoid mistakes.

definition: Also known as script supervisor, responsible for maintaining continuity on set and reporting any discrepancies.
extra: This person watches every detail on set, from costumes to props, making sure nothing breaks the illusion of the story.

definition: A legal agreement between parties that outlines the rights and responsibilities of each involved in the production.
extra: Contracts make sure everyone involved in the film production knows their duties, schedules, pay, and other important details.

definition: A term used to describe mainstream filmmaking that follows traditional narrative structures and stylistic norms.
extra: Conventional cinema is what most audiences are used to—stories told in familiar ways, with clear beginnings, middles, and ends.

definition: Sound that follows traditional practices, including clear dialogue, music, and effects that support the story naturally.
extra: Conventional sound aims to immerse the audience without drawing attention to itself, supporting the story with familiar audio cues.

definition: A shot filmed to cover the editing of a scene, often used to fix continuity or provide additional angles.
extra: Cover shots give editors extra footage to smooth out transitions or fix mistakes during post-production.

definition: Colour timing is an analog laboratory process for manipulating colour in photochemical film workflows. This process changes the amounts of red, green, and blue light used to create a film positive (or print) from a film negative.
extra: Before digital colour grading became standard, colour timing was how filmmakers controlled the visual mood of a scene. It required great skill and precision from lab technicians to maintain consistency across reels.

definition: The film-altering process whereby a black and white film is digitally changed to include colour; popularized but controversial in the 1980s.
extra: While colourization was initially met with excitement, it also sparked debates over artistic integrity. Critics argued that it tampered with the filmmaker’s original vision, while proponents viewed it as a way to modernize classics for new audiences.

definition: Colourists are involved in the very final phases of post-production. After a film’s edit is locked, the final cut is sent to the Colorist. A colourist usually starts work on a scene by correcting the issues with exposure and colour on a wide shot. They will then adjust the other clips within the scene to match the look of the first shot. At the end of this process, all of the shots within the scene will be correctly exposed with a neutral colour balance.
extra: The colourist’s job is a blend of technical precision and artistic touch. Their work ensures not only visual consistency but also helps convey emotion and tone through colour contrast, saturation, and lighting balance.

definition: An actor who sometimes specializes in genre films that are designed to elicit laughter from audiences; also known as a comic.
extra: Comedians may work across film, television, or stand-up, often bringing improvisational flair and timing that elevates the humor in a scene. Some transition into dramatic roles, showcasing unexpected range.

definition: A film which elicits laughter or humour by celebrating or showing the eternal ironies of human existence; types include screwball, dark/black comedies, farce, slapstick, deadpan, parody, and romantic comedy.
extra: Comedy films vary widely in tone and style but all share the goal of entertaining through wit, absurdity, or relatable situations. They often serve as cultural time capsules, reflecting societal norms and humor of their era.

definition: A humorous or farcical interlude in a dramatic film, usually provided by a buffoonish character, intended to relieve the dramatic, built-up tension or heighten the emotional impact by means of contrast.
extra: Comic relief provides breathing space in emotionally intense films. When well-placed, it can make dramatic moments even more powerful by contrast, keeping audiences engaged without overwhelming them.

definition: A subgenre of film associated with difficult teen rites of passage (from adolescence to adulthood), the onset of puberty, the loss of naive innocence and childhood dreams, the experience of growing up, and achieving sexual identity.
extra: These films often resonate across generations, portraying universal struggles of identity, family, friendship, and the bittersweet nature of growing up. They're staples in independent cinema and mainstream Hollywood alike.

definition: A commanding performance generally refers to an amazing performance given by an actor. Most of the time, this performance has come right before the actor’s death.
extra: The term also evokes a sense of legacy — when an actor leaves behind a lasting impression with a final role, their performance often takes on extra emotional weight for audiences and critics alike.

definition: A Completion Bond is a Film Investor Insurance. Some call it a “Completion Guarantee” or “Bond”. In the Entertainment Industry, it protects a Film. The Insurance Product acts as a financial guarantee. This security benefits the providers of a film’s finances.
extra: Investors feel more secure with a completion bond in place because it ensures the film will be completed on time and within budget — or the bond company will step in to finish it or cover losses.

definition: A Composer is the musician who creates a movie’s score. This is in contrast to a conductor, who directs the orchestra playing the score, and a lyricist, who writes the lyrics to a song.
extra: Composers often work closely with directors to craft a film’s emotional tone. From sweeping orchestral pieces to subtle atmospheric textures, their work is integral to the storytelling experience.

definition: A composite print is a viewing print with sound and image. It is a positive film with both picture and corresponding sound on the same film, which may be in editorial or projection synchronism. A composite release print contains picture and sound records in projection synchronism on the same film.
extra: This format was the standard before digital distribution. Creating a synchronized print was essential for seamless playback in theaters, especially before digital projectors took over.

definition: Compositing is the process or technique of combining visual elements from separate sources into single images, often to create the illusion that all those elements are parts of the same scene. Live-action shooting for compositing is variously called “chroma key”, “blue screen”, “green screen” and other names.
extra: Used heavily in VFX-heavy productions, compositing allows filmmakers to create entire worlds — blending live-action with CGI, matte paintings, or miniatures to produce a believable final shot.

definition: Refers to the arrangement of different elements (for example, colours, shapes, figures, lines, movement, and lighting) within a frame and in a scene.
extra: Composition can subtly guide viewer focus and evoke emotion. Whether through symmetry, leading lines, or contrast, a well-composed shot adds depth and meaning to a scene.

definition: Compositors create the final image of a frame, shot or VFX sequence. They combine all the digital materials used (assets), such as computer-generated (CG) images, live-action footage and matte paintings, and combine them to appear as one cohesive image and shot. Compositors consider the visual aspects of a scene.
extra: They’re often the last touchpoint in the VFX pipeline, ensuring lighting, shadows, color, and effects match flawlessly. Their work can make or break the realism of a scene.

definition: A proprietary collection of software, scanning camera systems, servers, networked computer workstations, and custom desks developed by Disney and Pixar in the late 1980s. Although outmoded by the mid-2000s, it succeeded in reducing labour costs for ink and paint and post-production processes of traditionally animated feature films. It also provided an entirely new palette of digital tools to the filmmakers. Today, most animations are made with computer-generated imagery (CGI).
extra: CAPS revolutionized traditional animation workflows and helped bridge the gap between hand-drawn and digital animation. Disney’s 'The Rescuers Down Under' (1990) was the first feature fully produced using CAPS.

definition: A concert film is a movie that records a live musical performance of a band, singer, or stand-up comedian. It can take footage from a single performance or stitch together footage from multiple concerts.
extra: These films offer fans the chance to relive iconic performances, often enhanced with behind-the-scenes footage or interviews. Famous examples include 'Stop Making Sense' and Beyoncé's 'Homecoming.'

definition: Construction Coordinators supervise the construction of sets and stages for film productions. They coordinate the entire process of set building, from initial planning through to the final coat of paint on the finished sets.
extra: They work closely with the production designer and art department, ensuring sets are not only visually accurate but also structurally sound and completed on schedule.

definition: Contemporary films are modern and relate to the present time.
extra: When people talk about contemporary film, they’re often referring to movies that reflect the themes, aesthetics, and social issues of our present era. They may age quickly as culture shifts, but they also capture the zeitgeist of their time.

definition: Continuity is one of the responsibilities of the Script Supervisor to make sure elements are consistent from shot to shot and scene to scene. When there is a mistake, such as an actor wearing different clothing within the same scene, it is referred to as a ‘continuity error.’
extra: Continuity is what prevents a coffee cup from magically appearing and disappearing between cuts. Viewers may not consciously notice when it’s correct, but they’ll definitely spot mistakes—and those errors can pull an audience out of the story.

definition: Continuity reports are detailed records of each day’s shoot, including camera settings, screen direction, weather, props, and any possible deviations from the script. Continuity reports are a great way to ensure that everything—even the sound quality—is consistent from shot to shot.
extra: These reports act as a safety net for both the editor and director. If a scene needs to be reshot months later, the continuity report makes it possible to match details exactly, saving productions from jarring inconsistencies.

definition: Refers to the difference between light and shadow, or between maximum and minimum amounts of light, in a particular film image; it can be either high contrast(with a sharp delineation between the bright and dark areas) or its opposite low contrast.
extra: Directors use contrast to set mood—film noir relies heavily on high contrast, while romantic comedies often prefer softer, low-contrast visuals. It’s one of the most direct ways to influence how an image feels to the viewer.

definition: The expected elements in a type of film, without question, thought, or judgment.
extra: Genre conventions are like unspoken agreements with the audience. Horror fans expect a scare, and musicals usually deliver songs. Playing with conventions—either by embracing or subverting them—is part of what makes a film stand out.

definition: Refers to landmark legislation in the late 1930s designed to protect a child actor’s earnings by depositing some of the minor’s earnings in court-administered trust funds that the child receives when they reach the age of majority; named after the child actor Jackie Coogan.
extra: The law was born after Jackie Coogan’s parents spent most of his childhood earnings. Today, child actors still benefit from these protections, ensuring their work provides for their future rather than just enriching adults around them.

definition: A co-producer is someone who works alongside the producer to oversee and manage various aspects of the film production process. Key players in the producing process may be dubbed a co-producers when they are instrumental in either funding the production or providing other benefits like services or special equipment.
extra: Co-producers can vary widely in role—sometimes they’re hands-on with creative decisions, other times they contribute financing or resources. The title reflects significant involvement, even if responsibilities differ from project to project.

definition: A copyright is a type of intellectual property that gives its owner the exclusive right to copy, distribute, adapt, display, and perform a creative work, usually for a limited time. The creative work may be in a literary, artistic, educational, or musical form. Copyright is intended to protect the original expression of an idea in the form of a creative work, but not the idea itself. Copyright is subject to limitations based on public interest considerations, such as the ‘fair use’ doctrine in the United States, and known as ‘fair dealing’ in Canada. Copyright has become a very muddy territory in the process of filmmaking and it is always best to consult your production lawyer when you have a question who may also give approvals to the production team on what is fair use and/or cleared for use.
extra: In filmmaking, copyright is a minefield—songs, images, even a background TV clip can cause legal trouble if not cleared. That’s why productions often hire lawyers or clearance specialists to avoid lawsuits or distribution problems.

definition: Refers to the garments or clothing worn by actors/performers in a film.
extra: Costumes aren’t just clothing—they communicate character, time period, and even psychology. A torn jacket might show hardship, while an immaculate suit suggests wealth or vanity.

definition: Researches, designs, and selects the costumes to be appropriate to the film’s time period, the characters, their location, and their occupations.
extra: The best costume designers make choices that are invisible to the casual viewer. When costumes feel authentic, audiences stop noticing clothes and start believing the world on screen.

definition: A costume drama is a film set in a particular historical time period, often with elaborate costuming.
extra: Think of shows like Downton Abbey or films like Pride and Prejudice. Costumes are central not just for accuracy, but for immersing viewers in a bygone world.

definition: Costume supervisors work with the costume designer to ensure costumes or outfits are of the standard they require, ready and prepared in time for fittings, rehearsals, recordings or live shows. During filming, they supervise the continuity of outfits, the cleaning, maintenance and any repairs or adjustments.
extra: The supervisor keeps the wardrobe department running smoothly, making sure actors look consistent across multiple takes. Their job blends creativity with logistics.

definition: A Set Costumer is responsible for assembling the costume of the actor on set and making sure the Costume Designer’s vision is realized. Set Costumers will track clothing to ensure that they are loaded and unloaded safely and without causing damage or stains.
extra: Set costumers are the guardians of wardrobe continuity. They make sure an actor’s shirt isn’t suddenly buttoned differently between takes, and they handle emergencies like rips or stains mid-shoot.

definition: The process of making sure that every scene has a variety of shots to make sure that the editor has enough film to be able to cut the scene together.
extra: Coverage is what gives editors options. A scene may be shot wide, medium, and close-up so the final cut can control pacing, emotion, and focus more effectively.

definition: In modern filmmaking, a “cowboy shot” refers to a shot that frames a character from the head to the hip or mid-thigh. Because this angle is perfect for showcasing a gun holstered to a cowboy’s hip, it quickly became a staple in classic Western films—hence the name.
