extra: Even outside Westerns, cowboy shots are popular because they balance showing a character’s face and body language while still keeping weapons or tools visible in frame.

definition: Provides food and drinks to the crew on set, not to be confused with catering, which refers to the hot meals given to the crew.
extra: ‘Crafty’ is where crews grab snacks, coffee, and quick fuel during long shoots. Good craft services can lift morale and keep a set running smoothly.

definition: A camera shot taken from a large camera dolly or electronic device (an apparatus, such as a crane), resembling an extendable mechanical arm (or boom), that can raise the camera up in the air above the ground 20 feet or more; the crane allows the camera to fluidly move in virtually any direction (with vertical and horizontal movement), providing shifts in levels and angles; crane shots usually provide some kind of overhead view of a scene.
extra: Crane shots often add grandeur or scale, swooping over a battlefield or city street. They’re also used to smoothly transition from intimate to epic perspectives in a single move.

definition: Refers to superimposed screen titles or text intended to move across, up, down, or diagonally on the screen.
extra: One of the most famous examples is the opening crawl of Star Wars, which sets up the story before the first scene even begins.

definition: A Creative consultant is a credit that is given to people who have consulted on a film or television screenplay. Those given this credit in the television field work closely with an executive producer and head writer/showrunner. They are involved in the writing process (proposing and editing story outlines/scripts).
extra: This role often blurs the line between writer and advisor. Consultants may not pen dialogue themselves, but their feedback can shape story arcs or character development significantly.

definition: The person who developed a significant part of a TV show’s format, concept, characters, and pilot script. They have sequel rights to the material as well usually. Often, the creator is also the showrunner or a producer. Sometimes it is a writer of the series bible or writers’ guidelines.
extra: In television, the creator’s vision defines the DNA of the show. Even if they step back after the pilot, their influence carries through the entire series.

definition: The text appearing before or after a film detailing the cast, production crew, and technical personnel who worked on a movie. Each person listed receives credit for the position they filled in the making of the film or show.
extra: Opening credits set tone—think of James Bond sequences—while end credits honor the massive team effort behind every production.

definition: Refers to those involved in the technical production of a film who are not actual performers.
extra: The crew is the backbone of a production. From lighting technicians to grips, they handle the unseen labor that makes the actors’ performances possible.

definition: The cast and director leave the set so the lighting, set, dressing and camera departments can work. Stand-ins are used.
extra: This phrase signals that behind-the-scenes departments need uninterrupted time to prepare. Stand-ins ensure camera setups still match the actual actors.

definition: The period of highest tension just before the climax of a film (there can be more than one); the point at which events reach their highest level of tension.
extra: The crisis is where characters are tested most severely. It primes the audience for the climax, making the payoff emotionally satisfying.

definition: An individual who writes and/or publishes a review of a film from either an artistic or entertainment point of view.Film reviewsoften analyze and discuss a film’s details, its content and characters, a critique of the performances, camera work, directing, editing, production, and script; film critics are usually more philosophical and theoretical than film reviewers or commentators.
extra: Unlike casual reviewers, critics often place films in a broader artistic or cultural context. Their work can influence public perception and even box office success.

definition: The editing technique of alternating, interweaving, or interspersing one narrative action (scene, sequence, or event) with another – usually in different locations or places, thus combining the two; this editing method suggests parallel action (that takes place simultaneously); often used to dramatically build tension and suspense in chase scenes, or to compare two different scenes; also known as inter-cutting or parallel editing.
extra: Think of a bomb being defused while the villain closes in elsewhere. Cross-cutting builds suspense by making viewers juggle multiple threads at once.

definition: Refers to a fading technique that occurs in two stages: (1) fade to black, and then (2) fade to the next scene; a cross-fade always involves a black or blank screen, whereas a dissolve does not.
extra: Cross-fades often suggest a passage of time or a shift in tone, creating a softer, more reflective transition than a hard cut.

definition: A warning or courtesy said by anyone who must cross in front of a camera during set up. It alerts the camera operator.
extra: It’s a simple phrase, but essential to avoid ruining a take or causing accidents on set. Professional courtesy keeps the set running smoothly.

definition: A film or production that is made for one audience but may easily ‘cross-over’ to another unexpected audience; also refers to a film, actor, or production that appeals to different demographic groups or age groups and can move between two or more distinct franchises.
extra: Marvel movies are classic cross-overs, bringing characters from different storylines together. The term also applies when an indie film suddenly finds mainstream popularity.

definition: A shot or image of a large group of people (often extras) in a film; CGI is often used to film large crowd shots to avoid huge costs associated with hiring extras.
extra: Big stadium scenes or battles often combine a handful of extras with digital duplication. This keeps costs down while making the scene feel massive.

definition: A C-stand is a sturdy light stand that has three different legs that can be adjusted to accommodate steps, a long metal “arm,” and a round clamping head called a gobo.
extra: C-stands are workhorses on set. They hold lights, flags, or diffusers in place and are valued for their versatility. A grip can set one up in dozens of ways to shape the lighting environment.

definition: A Cucoloris is a type of flag with shapes cut into it that creates the look of tree branches, window shades, etc.
extra: Often called a 'cookie,' a Cucoloris adds texture to otherwise flat light. It’s a simple tool that can make a studio set look like natural sunlight filtering through leaves.

definition: A cue is the signal for an actor to start performing. Typically, a cue will be one actor’s last line of dialogue, signalling to the other person in the scene to start. However, a cue can also come from the director or from within the script.
extra: Cues keep the rhythm of a scene alive. In live performance, they’re crucial to timing, but even on film, hitting cues properly ensures dialogue flows naturally.

definition: A device (cards, scrolling screen, teleprompter, or other mechanism) with dialogue provided to help talent recite their lines; an electronic cue card is called a teleprompter.
extra: Cue cards are still common in live TV—think of late-night talk shows—where performers can’t stop and retake. Teleprompters modernize the same idea for smoother delivery.

definition: Usually a non-mainstream film that attracts a small but loyally-obsessed group of fans and remains popular and worshipped over many years. Cult films have limited but special appeal and often have unusual or subversive elements or subject matter; they are often replayed for repeat viewings and audience participation (and group identification) as midnight movies, not to be confused with B-films.
extra: Movies like The Rocky Horror Picture Show or Donnie Darko thrive as cult films. They may flop commercially but build passionate fan bases through midnight screenings and repeated viewings.

definition: An abrupt or sudden change or jump in camera angle, location, placement, or time from one shot to another; consists of a transition from one scene to another (a visual cut) or from one soundtrack to another (a sound cut); cutting refers to the selection, splicing and assembly by the film editor of the various shots or sequences for a reel of film, and the process of shortening a scene; also refers to the instructional word ‘cut’ said at the end of a take by the director to stop the action in front of the camera; cut to refers to the point at which one shot or scene is changed immediately to another. Also refers to a completely edited version of a film (e.g., rough cut).
extra: The word 'cut' is the most used term on set and in editing rooms. It can mean a command from the director, an editorial choice, or even the final version of a film.

definition: A brief shot that momentarily interrupts a continuously filmed action by briefly inserting another related action, object, or person (sometimesnotpart of the principal scene or main action), followed by a cutback to the original shot, often filmed from the POV of the character and used to break up a sequence and provide some visual relief, or to ease the transition from one shot to the next, or to provide additional information, or to hint at an impending change; reaction shots are usually cutaways; cross-cutting is a series of cutaways and cutbacks indicating concurrent action; a cutaway is different from an insert shot.
extra: Cutaways are often lifesavers in editing. They allow for smoother transitions, hide continuity errors, or provide important narrative details—like showing a character’s reaction during dialogue.

definition: A sub-genre of science fiction derived from combining the termscyberneticsandpunkand related to the digital or information technology society (referring to the proliferation of computers, the online world, cyberspace, and ‘hacking’); this sub-genre also incorporates classic film-noir characteristics into its style including alienation, dehumanization, the presence of counter-cultural anti-heroes, darkness, dystopia, and corruption.
extra: Films like Blade Runner and The Matrix are quintessential cyberpunk—mixing futuristic tech with gritty, dystopian societies. It’s as much about mood and philosophy as it is about technology.

definition: The curved, seamless, floor-to-ceiling backdrop or background used in studio sets.
extra: A cyc gives filmmakers a blank canvas—literally. It can be lit to appear like an endless sky, a wall of color, or just a neutral backdrop that disappears behind the action.

definition: The immediately processed, rough cuts, digital files or exposed film, without edits for the director, producer, or key crew to review to see how the film came out after the day’s (or the previous day’s) shooting; more commonly in the form of digital dailies; aka rushes used to determine whether there is a need to re-shoot.
extra: Reviewing dailies is often the first chance for a director to see how performances and visuals translate on camera. They guide whether adjustments or reshoots are necessary.

definition: A little-known movie that becomes a massive hit either financially or on the awards circuit.Moonlightwas the dark horse winner for the Best Picture Oscar overLa La Land.
extra: The term borrows from horse racing—an unexpected winner. Dark horse films often surprise critics and audiences alike, shifting awards seasons or box office trends.

definition: A technique for using shots filmed during the day to appear as moonlit night shots on the screen by using different lenses, filters, special lighting and underexposure.
extra: Day-for-night saves productions from the challenges of filming at night. Classic westerns and low-budget films leaned on this trick heavily.

definition: An actor or crew labour position who is in for one day only.
extra: Day players often fill small but essential roles—like a waiter with one line. They’re not part of the ongoing cast or crew but keep production moving.

definition: A comedic device in which a performer assumes an expressionless demeanour to deliver comedic lines or performances. Leslie Neilsen and Buster Keaton had famous deadpan deliveries.
extra: Deadpan comedy works by contrast—the humor lies in absurd lines delivered with total seriousness. It’s timeless, from silent film legends to modern sitcoms.

definition: A cinematography technique portraying great depth of field. Wide-angle lenses are used with small lens apertures to create a sharp focus in both distant and nearby planes within the same shot.
extra: Citizen Kane popularized deep focus shots, allowing viewers to see action in both the foreground and background simultaneously. It encourages audiences to scan the entire frame.

definition: A cinematic style in which several significant elements of an image are positioned at various points both near to and distant from the camera. This means that the characters in the shot have a large spatial scope, so that they sometimes even seem to disappear within the wide area. Deep space can be achieved by establishing a very long z-axis that opens the available stage. More often than not, deep space is combined with deep focus, which requires that elements placed along very different depth planes of the image (i.e. foreground, middle ground and background) be in focus at the same time. However, for deep staging, these objects do not necessarily have to be in focus. Staging in deep space is the opposite of staging in flat space.
extra: Deep staging gives directors visual complexity. By layering actors and props across space, the frame feels more dynamic and lifelike, as though the story world extends beyond the immediate action.

definition: Refers to a scene that was edited out of a film’s final cut for several possible reasons: the scene was poorly done, the scene was unnecessary, the film’s running time needed truncation, the film was avoiding an R or NC-17 rating, the film’s studio disapproved of it, etc.
extra: Deleted scenes often resurface as DVD extras or online bonuses. They can reveal subplots, alternate character beats, or just unnecessary material trimmed for pacing.

definition: The point in a film that immediately follows the climax when everything in the plot has been resolved. It’s typically the final scene in a movie and is also known as the resolution.
extra: The denouement provides closure, tying up loose ends and showing the aftermath. It’s the narrative cool-down after the emotional high of the climax.

definition: The depth of a shot’s focus in relation to the foreground, middle-ground and background. Shallow depth of field might keep only one of those planes in focus, while deep depth of field would keep all of them in focus.
extra: Depth of field shapes storytelling visually. A shallow focus can isolate a character’s emotions, while deep focus keeps multiple layers of action clear at once.

definition: Depth of Focus is directly related to depth of field. It refers to making an adjustment so that a camera shot keeps its deep focus throughout all of the various planes.
extra: This concept matters technically for camera operators. While depth of field describes what the audience sees, depth of focus concerns how precisely the lens and film or sensor must be aligned.

definition: Refers to colours of less luminosity and vividness. Desaturated colours have a reduced amount of their initial colour (hue) due to the addition of their complementary colour. Complementary colours are colours that face each other on the colour wheel. When mixed with each other, two complementaries reduce each other’s saturation towards grey; in other words, they desaturate each other.
extra: Desaturation is a favorite tool for war dramas or dystopian films—it drains the image of vibrancy, evoking bleakness, nostalgia, or realism.

definition: The process of working on fleshing out a script in hopes that it will be greenlit for production.
extra: Development is the stage where most projects stall. Writers, producers, and executives refine ideas endlessly before deciding if a film is worth financing.

definition: The resolution of a plot by what is basically a force from God. It usually refers to a clumsy, contrived, or illogical intervention that alleviates the tension through something other than a character’s actions. The bacteria inWar of the Worldscould be considered a deus ex machina, one of many cliches to avoid.
extra: Audiences often feel cheated by a deus ex machina. It resolves conflict without characters earning it, which is why writers are usually warned against using it.

definition: A person who helps train an actor in diction and/or using accents to suit the character an actor is playing.
extra: Dialect coaches are especially valuable when actors must portray real people or specific regions. A believable accent can make or break a performance’s credibility.

definition: Any spoken lines in a film by an actor, usually based upon a script, may be considered overlapping if two or more characters speak simultaneously.
extra: Dialogue carries plot, theme, and character. Writers use overlapping dialogue for realism, while sharp, stylized exchanges can define a director’s signature style.

definition: A sound editor who specializes in editing dialogue.
extra: Dialogue editors clean up performances—removing background noise, adjusting pacing, and ensuring conversations sound seamless even when pieced together from multiple takes.

definition: Means realistic or logically existing, such as the music that plays on a character’s radio in a scene; more generally, it refers to the narrative elements of a film (such as spoken dialogue, other sounds, and action) that appear in, are shown, or naturally originatewithinthe content of the film frame.
extra: If characters can hear it, it’s diegetic—like footsteps or a jukebox in a diner. Non-diegetic sound, like a dramatic score, exists only for the audience.

definition: A special effect camera filter or lens that softens the appearance of subjects and generates a kind of dreamy haze.
extra: Diffusers are often used in romantic or fantasy films to give the image a more ethereal quality. Classic Hollywood movies leaned heavily on this to flatter actors’ faces and hide imperfections.

definition: The softening or reduction of a light’s intensity. This is achieved through a translucent sheet made from silk or lace or through a diffuser before the light source to cut down on shadows.
extra: Cinematographers rely on diffusion to avoid harsh, unflattering shadows. For example, a bright key light can be softened with diffusion to make a close-up more natural and pleasing to the eye.

definition: A person who provides on-set quality control, image manipulation & colour correction, production continuity, troubleshooting and consultation to assist in fulfilling the requirements and vision of the cinematographer.
extra: The DIT has become indispensable in digital filmmaking. They ensure that what the director and cinematographer see on set matches what will be seen in post-production, protecting both creative intent and technical quality.

definition: In cinematographic terms, using light and dark lighting and composition to emphasize what is important within the frame.
extra: Great directors subtly guide where you look in a frame. A character stepping into a shaft of light or a foreground object blurring the rest of the image are both ways of directing the audience’s eye without them realizing it.

definition: The direction in which characters and objects move in the scene in relation to the frame. In describing screen direction.
extra: Maintaining screen direction is key for continuity—if a character moves left to right in one shot, cutting to them suddenly moving right to left can confuse viewers unless done deliberately for effect.

definition: The principal creative artist on a movie set. A director is usually (but not always) the driving artistic source behind the filming process and communicates to actors how they would like a particular scene played. A director’s duties might also include casting, script editing, shot selection, shot composition, and editing. Typically, a director has complete artistic control over all aspects of the movie, but it is not uncommon for the director to be bound by agreements with either a producer or a studio. In some large productions, a director will delegate less important scenes to a second unit.
extra: The director is often seen as the author of a film, though filmmaking is inherently collaborative. The balance of power between a director and producers or studios can define whether a film feels personal or commercial.

definition: The person responsible for the photographing or recording of a film, television production, music video or other live-action piece. The cinematographer is the head of the camera and lighting crew and would normally be responsible for making artistic and technical decisions related to the image and for selecting the camera, film stock, lenses, and filters. The study and practice of this field is referred to as cinematography.
extra: The DP shapes the visual identity of a film—everything from color palettes to camera movements. While the director drives story and performance, the DP translates that vision into images.

definition: A version of a movie a director is able to make without any studio interference. This is the version the director would like audiences to see. Arguably, the most famous director’s cut is that ofBlade Runner, which audiences and critics alike seemed to agree was superior to the theatrical version.
extra: Director’s cuts are often marketed as more authentic, though sometimes they’re used strategically to re-release a film. They can radically change a film’s tone or pacing, as with Blade Runner or Kingdom of Heaven.

definition: A labour organization representing the creative and economic rights of directors and members of the directorial team working in film, television, commercials, documentaries, news, sports and new media.
extra: The DGA is powerful in Hollywood labor relations, setting working conditions, credit standards, and pay protections for directors and their teams. Membership is almost essential for high-level work in the U.S.

definition: A national labour organization that represents over 6,000 key creative and logistical personnel in the screen-based industry covering all areas of direction, production design, accounting, production and editing.
extra: The DGC plays a role similar to the DGA but within Canada, ensuring fair labor practices and professional standards across Canadian productions. It also negotiates collective agreements for its members.

definition: The technique of recording sound simultaneously with the recording of the image.
extra: Direct sound helps preserve the authenticity of a performance—think of a live concert film where the audience’s energy is captured in real time. However, it can be tricky to control compared to studio dubbing.

definition: Refers to the making of an adapted, sanitized, ‘family-friendly’ version of a book or play by removing objectionable elements (such as crude language, sexuality, or violence) and modifying plot elements to make the tale more acceptable, entertaining, predictable and popular for mass consumption by audiences, as first exercised by the Disney studios in the 50s; now used as a derogatory term for how popular culture has been homogenized and cultural diversity minimized.
extra: While Disney’s approach opened stories to wider audiences, critics argue that it flattens cultural nuance. The term now often signals concern about the oversimplification of complex material for mass appeal.

definition: A transitional edit between two scenes, shots, or sequences in which the image of one shot is slowly replaced, blended, or superimposed with a different image. It’s usually done to suggest a passage of time.
extra: Dissolves were once a staple of classic cinema but are used more sparingly today. They carry a sense of elegance or nostalgia, often signaling memory or dream sequences.

definition: The organization responsible for coordinating the distribution of the finished movie to exhibitors, streamers, and other media versions of movies.
extra: Distributors determine how and where a film reaches its audience—through theaters, streaming platforms, or international markets. Their strategy can make or break a film’s financial success.

definition: A non-fiction narrative without actors. Typically, a documentary is a journalistic record of an event, person, or place.
extra: Documentaries can be strictly observational or highly stylized. From vérité-style political films to glossy nature features, they often blur the line between journalism and art.

definition: The filmmaker collective founded by Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg in 1995 established a clear set of rules and philosophy that rejected contrived camera work and special effects in lieu of “honest” and “truthful” storytelling. Some of the other rules included shooting on location and using hand-held cameras.
extra: Dogme 95 was as much a manifesto as a filmmaking style. Its restrictions aimed to strip away artifice, though ironically, those rules themselves became a kind of stylistic signature.

definition: The stereo-sound process for movies developed by Dolby Laboratories, Inc. to enhance sound quality. 35mm prints of films have dual optical soundtracks, while 70mm films have six magnetic tracks and multi-channel playback.
extra: Dolby Stereo was a game-changer in the 1970s, bringing immersive sound to blockbusters like Star Wars. It paved the way for the modern surround sound systems audiences expect today.

definition: A piece of equipment on wheels or a track that creates fluid camera movements. A dolly could be anything as low-tech as a wheelchair or as high-tech as a studio dolly using hydraulics. Usually, the camera operator and assistant ride on the dolly; the crew member who operates it is called a dolly grip.
extra: The dolly shot is a filmmaking classic. It can be used to follow characters smoothly through space or to create dramatic pushes into a scene, giving a sense of intimacy or grandeur.

definition: Builds and maintains all of the equipment on which cameras are mounted on a film set. They must work with a camera dolly, which holds the camera on a track, for moving or tracking shots.
extra: A dolly grip’s job requires precision and timing—the smoothness of a camera move can make the difference between a professional shot and one that feels jarring.

definition: A set of tracks upon which a camera can be moved.
extra: Dolly tracks allow for smooth, controlled motion. You’ll see them in scenes where the camera glides down a hallway or circles characters in conversation.

definition: An in-camera effect where you dolly towards or away from a subject while zooming in the opposite direction. This shot creates a sense of unease in the viewer, simulates a spatial warp, and can either shrink or extend distances based on the choice of direction.
extra: The dolly zoom is sometimes called the 'Vertigo effect' because Hitchcock used it to convey dizziness. It’s since become a visual shorthand for shock, realization, or disorientation.

definition: A list of scenes from the script that have already been filmed or a list of the contents of an exposed reel of film stock. An accurate dope sheet is the responsibility of the assistant cameraperson.
extra: The dope sheet helps keep track of production progress and prevents confusion during editing. Think of it as an early form of metadata management.

definition: An actor who stands in for another actor in certain scenes, some of which may involve dangerous circumstances or require special skills (e.g. a stunt double). Sometimes, body doubles are used in scenes that call for nudity or intimacy.
extra: Body doubles help protect stars while still giving the illusion of continuity. Audiences rarely realize when a double is used unless they’re looking closely.

definition: The process of exposing one frame twice so that elements of the two images are visible within the final product. It results in an effect similar to superimposition. It is commonly used to create a “ghostly” effect.
extra: Before digital effects, double exposure was a go-to trick for supernatural or dreamlike imagery. Even today, it’s sometimes used stylistically for its surreal quality.

definition: A dovetail plate, or a sliding plate, is the basis of most camera support systems used in feature film productions. It is a metal (usually aluminum) plate with a specific, finely machined profile upon which various accessories can be attached or supported.
extra: Though rarely noticed outside the camera department, dovetail plates are crucial for flexibility on set—allowing rapid switching between tripods, dollies, and stabilizers.

definition: Dramatic narrative and its representation on the screen.
extra: Dramaturgy is about how a story unfolds—its pacing, structure, and emotional rhythm. A well-crafted dramaturgy can make even a simple plot deeply compelling.

definition: A person who creates the renderings and construction plans for set construction.
extra: Set designers translate creative vision into technical drawings so that carpenters and builders can construct believable worlds, from a suburban kitchen to a futuristic cityscape.

definition: A dubis the process of inserting a new soundtrack into a movie or adding a new soundtrack of music, sound effects, or dialogue following production. A dub will match the lip movements and actions of the filmed shots to make it seem natural. This contrasts direct sound, where sound is recorded on the scene and synched with the shot.
extra: Dubbing is common for foreign films to reach new audiences, but it’s also used in domestic productions to fix dialogue or add lines later. Done well, it’s invisible; done poorly, it’s distracting.

definition: A shot with the camera tilted to one side, along the horizontal axis, producing a diagonal angle. It is typically done to create a sense of unease within the viewer.
extra: The Dutch angle is a favorite in thrillers and horror because it makes the audience subconsciously feel that something is wrong or off balance. Even in action films, it can suggest chaos or disorientation.

definition: Fire-retardant black duvetyne is commonly used for curtains, for scenery, and to control light spills. Many commercial lighting flags are made from duvetyne.
extra: If you’ve ever seen black fabric draped around a set to block stray light, that’s likely duvetyne. It’s practical, cheap, and safe—an unsung hero of production design and lighting control.

definition: A photographic technique meant to mask the projected image shape and size to any ratio that is seen as appropriate for the scene. An example of this would be the aspect ratio narrowing when an actor walks through a narrow passageway.
extra: Dynamic framing breaks the expectation of a fixed aspect ratio, using it instead as a storytelling tool. It’s become more popular in modern cinema to emphasize mood or environment in a subtle but powerful way.

definition: An imaginary, wretched, dehumanized, dismal, fearful, bad, oppressive place or landscape, often initiated by a major world crisis (post-war destruction) coupled with an oppressive government, crime, and unusual behaviour.
extra: Dystopian films often serve as cultural warnings, using exaggerated societies to reflect real-world anxieties. Think of classics like 1984 or The Hunger Games—their bleak worlds feel uncomfortably close to our own.

definition: A reference to a movie, person, or event that is intended to be too subtle to be noticed on the initial viewing.
extra: Easter eggs reward dedicated fans—whether it’s a hidden character cameo in a Marvel movie or a nod to a director’s earlier work, they create a layered experience that keeps viewers coming back.

definition: A camera rig system developed for handheld work. It suspends the camera from a centralized arm that is mounted to a waist belt for support.
extra: The Easy Rig gives camera operators the freedom of handheld shooting without the physical toll. It’s widely used in documentaries and long takes where mobility is crucial.

definition: Numerical markings printed along the edges of film stock at regular intervals, typically every foot or half-foot. These numbers serve as reference points for editors, colorists, and negative cutters to accurately identify and match specific frames during the post-production process, aiding in tasks like syncing sound, creating cuts, or ensuring continuity in visual effects.
extra: Edge numbers are a kind of invisible backbone for film editing. While audiences never see them, editors and lab technicians rely on them to keep everything perfectly aligned.

definition: The process (performed by a film editor) of selecting, assembling, arranging, collating, trimming, structuring, and splicing/joining together many separate camera takes (including the sound) of exposed footage (or daily rushes) into a complete, determined sequence or order of shots that follow the script. The choice of shots has a tremendous influence on the film’s final appearance.
extra: Editing is often called the 'invisible art' because when it’s done well, audiences don’t notice it—they just feel the story flow. Good editing can completely reshape performances and narrative rhythm.

definition: Short for Electric Fan. An E Fan is a powerful, electrically operated fan used on film sets to create wind effects. These fans can vary in size and strength, and they are often used to simulate natural wind, enhance the movement of fabrics or hair, or add dynamic elements to a scene. E Fans are an essential tool for special effects and atmospheric control in filmmaking.
extra: From gently rustling curtains to simulating a hurricane, E Fans are versatile tools. They also add subtle realism—wind in a character’s hair, for example, can make a shot feel alive.

definition: A lighting accessory used in the film industry to control and direct the spread of light from softboxes or large light fixtures. It consists of a grid-like structure that fits over the front of the light source, allowing light to pass through while limiting its spill and focusing it more precisely on a specific area or subject. This helps create a more controlled, softer light with reduced shadows and glare.
extra: Egg crates are like traffic lanes for light, keeping it from washing over areas unintentionally. They’re especially handy in tight sets where light control is crucial.

definition: The person or grip in charge of and familiar with the electrical equipment on the set.
extra: Electrics are indispensable on set, handling everything from power distribution to troubleshooting. Without them, even the most talented cinematographer wouldn’t have the tools to paint with light.

definition: Refers to a large, oversized door found in sound stages or studios, designed to accommodate the movement of big set pieces, equipment, or even vehicles in and out of the stage. The name comes from the door’s ability to allow even something as large as an elephant to pass through, making it essential for the logistics of setting up and striking large-scale productions.
extra: Elephant doors reflect the sheer scale of film production. They make it possible to roll in cars, massive props, or even entire sets without dismantling them.

definition: The shortening of the plot duration of a film achieved by deliberately omitting intervals or sections of the narrative story or action in the edit; an ellipsis is marked by an editing transition (a fade, dissolve, wipe, jump cut, or change of scene) to omit a period or gap of time from the film’s narrative.
extra: Elliptical cuts let filmmakers jump across time elegantly—like skipping a long journey and cutting straight to a character arriving. It keeps pacing tight without losing coherence.

definition: Credits appearing at the end of a film, aka end titles.
extra: End credits are more than a roll of names—they’re a recognition of the vast teams behind a film. In modern blockbusters, audiences stick around because they often hide post-credit scenes too.

definition: A French word meaning “terrible baby.” It refers to a young director who is brash or egotistical. This is often a director who is innovative but uses unorthodox techniques.
extra: The term can be both a compliment and a critique—such directors often disrupt tradition, bringing fresh perspectives but also ruffling feathers in the process.

definition: Refers to a 225 amp carbon arc Fresnel light, a powerful type of lighting fixture used in older film productions. These lights produce intense, daylight-balanced illumination by creating an electric arc between carbon electrodes. They were commonly used for large-scale exterior scenes or to simulate sunlight. The term “English brute” denotes a particular style or origin of these robust and heavy-duty lights, which have largely been replaced by modern HMI and LED technologies.
extra: The English Brute is a relic of an earlier era, when filmmaking required enormous, blazing lights to get the exposure we now achieve with efficient LEDs.

definition: Stands for “Enhanced Negative Density Reduction,” a Technicolor process used to increase the contrast of film negatives. This process enhances the visual impact of the film by reducing the density of midtones and shadows, resulting in a more pronounced and dynamic image. ENR is particularly used in color film production to achieve a richer, more vivid look by modifying the negative’s contrast characteristics.
extra: ENR was a tool for cinematographers who wanted more punch without relying solely on lighting. It gave films a gritty, high-contrast feel often associated with war or crime dramas.

definition: A film with a large cast without any true leading roles, and usually with multiple plotlines regarding the characters; it also literally means ‘the group of actors (and sometimes directors, designers, and crew) who are involved in a film.
extra: Ensemble films like Love Actually or Crash thrive on interconnected stories, giving equal weight to multiple characters instead of one central hero.

definition: A film with a large dramatic scope or requiring immense production.
extra: Epics are cinematic spectacles—think Lawrence of Arabia or Ben-Hur. They often span long time periods, grand landscapes, and huge casts, designed to overwhelm with scale.

definition: The short scene at the end of a movie that concludes the film. Often, the main characters will be older, reflecting on the events just witnessed.The Notebookends with such an epilogue.
extra: Epilogues provide closure, often showing characters years later or revealing the consequences of the story. They’re a way of saying, 'Here’s what it all meant in the long run.'

definition: A moment of sudden spiritual insight for the protagonist of a film, usually occurring just before or after the climax.
extra: Epiphanies shift the character’s worldview in an instant. In film, they’re powerful because they often set up the resolution—when the hero finally understands what truly matters.

definition: A long shot that shows the location from a distance. It is often an aerial shot, informing the audience of the time and locale of the setting. It helps orient the viewer so that they know where the next scene takes place.
extra: Establishing shots act as a compass for the viewer, letting them know where they are before diving into dialogue or action. They can be quick and subtle, or breathtaking wide shots.

definition: An electronic viewfinder attaches to your digital camera so that you can see the frame.
extra: Electronic viewfinders are invaluable outdoors, where LCD screens wash out in sunlight. They give camera operators a reliable way to judge exposure and framing on the spot.

definition: The individual/s responsible for overseeing a movie’s financing. The Executive Producer/s may also help arrange various elements of a film’s production, such as a writer and actors.
extra: An executive producer is often more of a business role than a creative one, though in some cases they shape the project significantly by attaching talent or securing funding.

definition: A term meaning a movie theatre owner.
extra: Exhibitors are the link between studios and audiences—they decide what actually makes it onto the big screen in local markets.

definition: Refers to a film, usually a low-budget or indie film not oriented toward profit-making, that challenges conventional filmmaking by using camera techniques, imagery, sound, editing, and/or acting in unusual or never-before-seen ways.
extra: Experimental films are playgrounds for new ideas. They might not find mainstream audiences, but their influence often trickles into commercial cinema in surprising ways.

definition: A sensational, often trashy B-film aimed at a particular audience and designed to succeed commercially and profitably by appealing to specific psychological traits or needs in that audience without any fuller analysis or exposition; often refers to films with extremely violent or sexual scenes; not necessarily a derogatory term.
extra: Exploitation films pushed boundaries in ways major studios wouldn’t, often leading to cult classics. Genres like grindhouse horror or blaxploitation emerged from this tradition.

definition: The conveyance of vital background information, either through actions or dialogue, to further the events of a story. It could also set up a movie’s story. It can include information about the main problem or what’s at stake for the characters. Writing exposition is particularly tricky when weaved into the script organically.
extra: Bad exposition feels clunky and obvious ('As you know, Bob…'), but when done well, it immerses the audience seamlessly in the world without them realizing they’re being told backstory.

definition: Refers to the measure of a film stock’s or digital sensor’s sensitivity to light, which is used to set the correct exposure settings during filming. It is closely related to ISO, but EI can be adjusted based on the specific lighting conditions or creative intent, allowing cinematographers to either underexpose or overexpose the film or sensor relative to its rated ISO for artistic effect.
extra: Changing EI gives cinematographers flexibility in tone—underexposing can make an image moodier, while overexposing can feel dreamy or washed out.

definition: The movie technique that involves reality distortion through sets, costumes, editing, and lighting. It’s meant to reflect the inner emotions of the characters or the filmmaker. It was popularized in Germany in the 1920s and ’30s, often characterized by dramatic lighting, grotesque shots and dark visual images.
extra: Expressionist films like The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari showed how cinema could visualize psychology, paving the way for stylized genres like film noir and modern horror.

definition: Used in a slug line as EXT., it indicates that the scene occurs outdoors.
extra: Slug lines that read 'EXT.' instantly tell the production team what’s needed—outdoor lighting, sound prep for wind or traffic, and sometimes permits for shooting on location.

definition: An actor who appears in a movie in a non-speaking, unnoticed role, such as part of a crowd or a patron in a restaurant. Extras generally do not receive a screen credit and are now called Background Performers.
extra: Background performers are essential for creating believable worlds. Imagine a busy café or a football stadium with only the main characters—without extras, scenes would feel strangely empty and artificial.

definition: A close-up shot that films the subject incredibly closely. In many cases, the outer portions of the subject will be cut out of the frame. Extreme close-ups are typically done on actors to showcase their eyes, mouth, or another singular part of the body.
extra: Extreme close-ups push the audience into intimate or unsettling territory. A close-up on an eye darting nervously, for example, can create suspense far more effectively than a wider shot.

definition: This may serve as an establishing shot and is taken from quite some distance. This can create a voyeuristic feel like someone is watching, spying, or observing.
extra: Extreme long shots are often used to situate characters in vast landscapes or overwhelming environments. They can make a character look small, vulnerable, or even lost in the world around them.

definition: A shot that portrays a subject’s view of another subject or object in the film, taken at the subject’s eye level.
extra: Eye level shots feel natural because they mirror how we normally see others. Directors often use them when they want the audience to feel like they’re on equal footing with the character.

definition: Anything within the sight of an actor. Where the actor will be looking during a scene.
extra: Managing eyelines is crucial for continuity. If one actor looks slightly off mark, it can ruin the illusion that two characters are sharing a gaze or reacting to the same object.

definition: An eyeline match is a cut in filmmaking between two shots that shows an illusion that the character, presented in the first shot, is looking at an object, presented in the second shot.
extra: This technique is subtle but powerful—it convinces viewers that two separate shots exist in the same space. Without eyeline matches, conversations and reactions would feel disconnected.

definition: A transitional tool that consists of a slow change in the intensity of a sound or image. A normally-lit scene will transition to black or vice versa. This also applies to sound and how it fades in and out of a scene.
extra: Fades are often used to signal the passage of time or the end of a chapter in a story. They’re less common in fast-paced modern editing but still appear in dramas or classical filmmaking.

definition: Refers to a light-hearted, gleeful, often fast-paced, crudely humorous, contrived and ‘over-the-top’ comedy that broadly satirizes, pokes fun, exaggerates, or gleefully presents an unlikely or improbable stock situation often characterized by slapstick, pratfalls, and other physical antics.
extra: Farce thrives on absurdity—think doors constantly slamming, mistaken identities, or elaborate physical gags. It’s exaggerated comedy that rarely slows down for realism.

definition: A movie editing technique consisting of multiple fast consecutive shots. These are known as staccato shots that only last for a brief duration of time, each to create a fast-paced effect.
extra: Fast-cutting is common in action sequences or music videos where energy and rhythm matter more than detail. Done well, it creates excitement; done poorly, it can feel disorienting.

definition: A camera device or effect to compress reality and highlight a scene or cause a dramatic effect, created by filming a scene with the film running at a rate less than the normal 24 frames per second and then projecting it back at standard speed, thereby creating the effect of moving faster than normal; generally used for comic effect.
extra: Fast motion can make a chase or routine task look ridiculous and playful. Silent film comedians like Charlie Chaplin often relied on this trick for physical gags.

definition: When the camera focuses or highlights a certain subject or action within a shot.
extra: When a director says to 'favour on' an actor, they’re instructing the camera to prioritize that person in framing—even if others are present. It’s a subtle way of steering audience attention.

definition: A term used to describe the performers who are placed in prominent positions in the background of the major action of a scene.
extra: Unlike regular extras, featured background performers may be visible enough for audiences to remember them. For example, a waiter who never speaks but is always near the leads can be 'featured background.'

definition: A “full-length” motion picture, one greater than 60 minutes in length, but usually about 90-120 minutes.
extra: The term 'feature' comes from when cinemas would screen shorts and newsreels alongside the 'featured' main attraction—the longer film that drew the audience in.

definition: A term often used before the 1970s to refer to a 20 to 45-minute film, usually a “making of” or “behind the scenes” mini-documentary or an extended trailer, which was usually displayed by theatre owners to “sell” a film for exhibition in their cinemas. In the 1990s and early 2000s, these featurettes were exclusively released on DVDs. Now, these special featurettes are largely released on YouTube as promotion for a film on its way to streaming platforms and VOD.
extra: Featurettes have shifted from being theater marketing tools to becoming bonus content for fans. Today, they serve as both promotion and world-building, often shared online before release.

definition: Usually, a light-hearted, upbeat comedy or romance that ends with an audience-pleasing conclusion. Sometimes, this term is used in a derogative manner.
extra: Feel-good films aim to leave viewers uplifted. While critics sometimes dismiss them as predictable, they remain popular because audiences enjoy reassurance and optimism on screen.

definition: A term used to describe a character in a movie, literally translated from French to “deadly lady.”
extra: The femme fatale archetype is central to film noir: mysterious, seductive women who often manipulate male characters to their downfall. Think of classic examples like Barbara Stanwyck in 'Double Indemnity.'

definition: Many elements within a film (the use of music, audio, sets, costuming, scripting, camera angles, framing, shot duration, a character’s actions, etc.) speak a ‘language,’ ‘grammar,’ or code that, when used by the filmmaker helps the viewer understand more about the plot and its characters.
extra: Audiences may not consciously analyze film conventions, but they instinctively recognize them. For example, ominous music signals danger long before it appears on screen.

definition: Refers to the measurement of the width of a film strip (in millimetres) used in a camera.
extra: Common gauges include 8mm, 16mm, 35mm, and 70mm. The gauge affects image resolution, cost, and even how portable the equipment is.

definition: A light-sensitive material that exists in a film’s emulsion or coating. It results in a fine-grained aesthetic, which requires more light to film, or a coarse aesthetic, which is preferable for low-light scenes.
extra: Film grain is sometimes simulated digitally to give modern productions a 'vintage' look. Directors may embrace grain for its texture and mood rather than trying to hide it.

definition: A collective term used to refer to a person(s) who have a significant degree of control over the creation of a film: directors, producers, screenwriters, DOPs, production designers, and editors.
extra: Not all filmmakers are directors—sometimes producers or cinematographers shape a film just as decisively. The term acknowledges the collaborative nature of cinema.

definition: A French word meaning “black film.” It was a popular genre in the 1940s with dark subject matter, downbeat tones, and low-key lighting. Often, the protagonist was an anti-hero or private detective. The Maltese Falcon is an example of a film noir.
extra: Film noir isn’t just about crime—it’s about moral ambiguity and atmosphere. Its influence continues today in neo-noir films like 'Blade Runner' or 'Drive.'

definition: A comprehensive (often chronological by year) listing of films featuring the work of actors, directors, or other crew members; it may also be a list of films for a specific genre or topic.
extra: Filmographies are often studied to trace a creator’s artistic growth. For instance, comparing early and late works of a director can reveal recurring themes or stylistic shifts.

definition: Refers to a film’s gauge or size and the film speed. It can also refer to the unused, unexposed film where photographic images will later be stored. The different types of film stock include tungsten and daylight.
extra: Choosing film stock was once a key creative decision—different stocks produced different color balances and sensitivities. Even in the digital era, directors emulate these looks.

definition: A particular story-telling approach, literally, to have one film within another; in some cases, the characters are aware of the ‘film-within-a-film,’ and break the fourth wall and enter into or interact with it, aka a subset film or picture within a picture.
extra: This device often comments on the nature of storytelling itself. Think of 'Singin’ in the Rain,' which features filmmaking within its plot, or 'Inception,' which layers realities like nested films.

definition: A plastic, glass, or gelatinous substance placed behind or before a camera lens. This changes the character and effect of the lighting within the frame of the film.
extra: Filters can soften harsh light, add color tones, or create stylized effects like starbursts. While many are now replicated digitally, cinematographers still use physical filters for precision.

definition: The last edited version of a film as it will be released.
extra: Having 'final cut' is often a privilege reserved for directors with significant creative control, as studios usually want the last say.

definition: Make-up, Hair and Wardrobe departments touch up the actors right before rolling the camera.
extra: This ensures continuity between takes and helps avoid visible flaws that might distract audiences.

definition: A member of the camera crew who adjusts the camera’s focus during filming.
extra: The focus puller’s role is critical in maintaining sharp images, especially in shots with shallow depth of field.

definition: Each person and camera goes back to where they started for the take.
extra: This resets the scene so it can be repeated consistently for multiple takes.

definition: A perspective in which the camera or viewpoint simulates the direct line of sight of a character or object...
extra: FPV makes the audience feel like they are inhabiting the character’s body, often creating intense immersion.

definition: Refers to the primary actors who appear in the scenes being shot...
extra: The term keeps set directions efficient and avoids confusion with stand-ins and doubles.

definition: An extreme type of lens that films subjects at super wide angles...
extra: This lens is often used for dreamlike, surreal, or comedic distortion effects.

definition: A film (usually humourous) in which the main character faces ‘culture shock’...
extra: The humor or drama comes from the clash between the character’s habits and the new world around them.

definition: A black, light-absorbing cloth (duvetyne) stretched on a metal frame and used to block out areas of light...
extra: Flags are key in shaping lighting setups, giving cinematographers control over shadows and highlights.

definition: A technique used in filmmaking where the natural order of the narrative is interrupted to show what happened in the past...
extra: Flashbacks often deepen character motivation or reveal hidden truths to the audience.

definition: The opposite of a flashback. It interrupts the natural order of the story to show what will happen in the future...
extra: Flash-forwards can create suspense by hinting at outcomes before the full context is revealed.

definition: A quick or brief shot (or image), sometimes as short as a single frame...
extra: Often used to create subliminal effects or a jarring psychological impact on viewers.

definition: A warning or courtesy given when using a flashing camera on set.
extra: This helps protect crew and cast from unexpected light bursts, especially those sensitive to strobe effects.

term: Flash in the Pan/ Fifteen Minutes of Fame
definition: Transitory, impermanent success or recognition...
extra: The phrase warns how quickly fame can fade in the entertainment industry.

definition: A section of a studio’s set consisting of a constructed wooden frame covered with materials...
extra: Flats are modular and reusable, forming the illusion of walls, doors, or entire rooms on set.

definition: A lamp that provides general diffuse lighting on a set.
extra: Flood lights fill shadows evenly, often serving as a base layer before adding more artistic lighting.

definition: A film that fails at the box office.
extra: Financial flops can still become cult classics if they gain a following later.

definition: The degree of distinctness or sharpness in an image...
extra: Focus choices guide the viewer’s eye to what matters most in the frame.

definition: An acting role that is used for personality comparison or contrast...
extra: The foil highlights traits in the main character that might not otherwise stand out.

definition: The art of recreating incidental sound effects (such as footsteps)...
extra: Foley makes films feel more natural and immersive by adding subtle, realistic sounds.

definition: An individual who works during the editing and post-production phase...
extra: They often perform sounds live while watching the footage to sync perfectly.

definition: A sound mixer who works with a Foley Artist to record sound effects.
extra: The Foley Mixer balances the levels and ensures the effects blend seamlessly with dialogue and music.

definition: A shot with framing that shifts to follow and keeps a moving figure or subject onscreen.
extra: This technique helps the audience stay connected to the character’s movement and perspective.

definition: Refers to a cinematic work that comes after, regardless of whether it is a sequel or a prequel.
extra: Studios often greenlight follow-ups if the original film is commercially successful.

definition: Any sequence, portion, or length of the film, either shot or soon-to-be shot...
extra: The term comes from the days when film was literally measured in feet.

definition: A visual technique that creates the illusion that objects or characters are larger, smaller, closer, or farther away...
extra: Classic films like 'The Lord of the Rings' used this technique extensively for hobbit and giant scale tricks.

definition: The opposite of a background. Any action or object closest to the camera.
extra: Foreground elements can frame the shot and add depth by layering the image.

definition: A practical effect technique where a scaled-down model or miniature is placed close to the camera to blend seamlessly with a full-scale background or live-action scene. This technique creates the illusion that the miniature is part of the larger set or environment, allowing filmmakers to depict large structures, landscapes, or other elements without building them at full scale.
extra: Foreground miniatures were used before CGI to save money and achieve realism. For instance, filmmakers could place a small model of a castle or spaceship in the foreground while actors performed behind it, making it appear much larger on screen.

definition: A feature-length motion picture with a predominantly non-English language dialogue track.
extra: Foreign films often introduce audiences to different cultural perspectives and storytelling traditions. For example, French New Wave or Japanese samurai films shaped global cinema even though they weren’t made in English.

definition: A literary device that is utilized to give a hint or indication of a future event in the story. It can be a very effective tool for developing curiosity, suspense, and even narrative harmony at the end of a film or novel.
extra: Foreshadowing can be as subtle as a symbolic prop or as overt as dialogue hinting at what’s to come. Hitchcock was a master of it, often planting visual or audio cues that only made sense later.

definition: The size or aspect ratio of a film frame.
extra: The format has huge artistic and technical consequences. For instance, a 4:3 aspect ratio feels intimate and boxy, while widescreen formats like 2.35:1 create a more epic, cinematic look.

definition: A phrase often used in special trade advertisements that studios pay for to promote “Oscar-worthy” films (and their actors and filmmakers) to create Oscar buzz for Academy Award nominations, especially for borderline films and/or lesser-known indie efforts and lesser-known performers that would probably be overlooked without the additional publicity.
extra: FYC campaigns are essentially political advertising for awards season. Studios spend millions targeting Academy members with screenings, ads, and gift packages to keep their films in voters’ minds.

definition: Refers to a trailer with four dressing rooms or small living quarters for cast members. Each room is usually equipped with basic amenities and is used on set to provide actors with private space for relaxing, getting ready, or changing costumes between takes.
extra: The term is part of on-set slang. Larger productions may use double-bangers, triple-bangers, or four-bangers depending on how many actors need their own spaces.

definition: The illusory, imaginary plane through which the audience is able to watch the film. It is possible for characters or the narrative to break the fourth wall, letting the audience know they are, indeed, watching a movie.
extra: When Deadpool or Ferris Bueller talks directly to the camera, that’s breaking the fourth wall. It disrupts immersion but can make the audience feel complicit in the story.

definition: A frame is a single image. It is the smallest compositional unit you can have in a film’s structure. A series of frames will be shown rapidly to make up the moving picture.
extra: Film runs at 24 frames per second in most cinemas, which tricks the eye into perceiving continuous motion. Each frame is essentially a still photograph.

definition: A measure of how many individual frames or images are displayed in one second of video or film. The FPS rate affects the smoothness and quality of the motion on screen. Common FPS rates include 24 FPS for most films, 30 FPS for television, and higher rates like 60 FPS or more for certain video games and high-definition content, which provide a smoother visual experience.
extra: Higher frame rates can feel hyper-real, sometimes called the 'soap opera effect,' while traditional 24 FPS has a cinematic quality audiences are accustomed to.

definition: Refers to the way a shot is composed and the manner in which subjects and objects are surrounded (‘framed’) by the boundaries or perimeter of the film image or by the use of a rectangle or enclosing shape (such as a shadow, mirror, door or hallway) within the film image. Camera angles such as low-angle and high-angle shots contribute to the framing; reframing refers to short panning or tilting movements of the camera to adjust to the character’s movements and keep them onscreen, centred, and in the frame.
extra: Good framing directs the audience’s attention. Directors like Wes Anderson are famous for symmetrical, meticulously composed frames that add to the storytelling.

definition: A term used in the film and television industry to describe a workday that begins on Friday and extends into the early hours of Saturday. This usually happens when there is a night shoot, or a production schedule runs late, leading to a shift that spans across two calendar days, often resulting in long, grueling hours for the crew.
extra: Crew members dread 'Fraturdays' because they wreck rest schedules and make turnaround times difficult. It’s a side effect of tight shooting calendars.

definition: An optical printing effect in which a single frame image is identically repeated, reprinted or replicated over several frames; when projected, a freeze frame gives the illusion of a still photograph in which the action has ceased; often used at the end of a film to indicate death or ambiguity, and to provide an iconic lasting image.
extra: The famous ending of 'The 400 Blows' freezes on the protagonist’s face, leaving his fate unresolved but etched in memory.

definition: A hard-lensed light that comes in different sizes. Each size of fresnel has a different nickname.
extra: Fresnels are common on sets because they can produce a focused beam or be 'spotted' and 'flooded' for different lighting needs.

definition: A film process developed in the 1950s in which actors and foreground objects were filmed before a projection screen, with a previously filmed background projected onto it.
extra: Front projection was used in classics like '2001: A Space Odyssey' to combine live action with large-scale scenic backdrops.

definition: The scale measurement of the size of the opening of the iris (the opening that lets light in) on a lens; common f-stops are 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 5.6, 8, 11, 16, and 22; the smaller the number, the larger the opening, and the more light that is allowed.
extra: F-stops directly affect depth of field. A lower f-stop (like f/1.4) creates a shallow focus look, great for isolating subjects.

definition: The head electrician in the film crew on a movie set. This individual is responsible for the design and final execution of the production’s lighting on the set.
extra: The gaffer works closely with the director of photography to translate the lighting plan into practical setups. It’s a leadership role on set.

definition: A strong fabric-backed tape that is easily removed when no longer needed. Used for all kinds of things on set.
extra: Gaffer tape is so ubiquitous on sets that it’s jokingly called 'the film industry’s duct tape.' It leaves no residue, making it perfect for cables and quick fixes.

definition: These are comedy films that are often non-sensical and literally filled with multiple gags and are designed to produce laughter in any way possible, often with comic or spoof references to other films.
extra: Movies like 'Airplane!' or 'Scary Movie' are classic gag-based comedies, prioritizing laughs over story coherence.

definition: Refers to the measurement of the width of a film strip (in millimetres) used in a camera.
extra: Common gauges include 8mm, 16mm, 35mm, and 70mm. Larger gauges usually mean higher image quality but greater expense.

definition: A mechanism inside a camera or projector that holds the film steady as it passes by the lens. “Checking the gate” is a phrase used when someone on the camera crew makes sure no dust or particles obstruct the exposure of the film.
extra: If dirt or hair gets stuck in the gate, it can ruin an entire take. That’s why 'gate check' is called after every important shot.

definition: A shot showing a character staring at something or someone that is typically outside of the frame offscreen. Gaze shots are often used in combination with a following point-of-view shot, which has the effect of putting the viewer into the position of a character for a short moment.
extra: The Kuleshov effect often depends on gaze shots — the audience interprets emotion based on what the character is shown to be looking at.

definition: A material sheet that is heat resistant and translucent and intended to be placed in front of a light source to either alter its colour, quantity or quality of light.
extra: Lighting gels are essential for color correction and creative effects. For example, a blue gel can simulate moonlight, while orange gels can match indoor tungsten lights.

definition: These are wire or metal frames that hold the gel in place so that it does not touch the hot surface of the globe or the lens.
extra: Without gel holders, gels would melt or burn against hot lights. They’re simple but crucial tools for safe lighting setups.

definition: The widespread distribution and simultaneous exhibition of a movie. This contrasts with a limited release, where a movie only plays at select theatres for its initial run.
extra: Big studio films almost always go to general release, while indie films often test in limited release before expanding nationwide.

definition: A mechanical engine which produces electricity from fuel. Frequently used for location shooting, either due to the unavailability or insufficient quantities of electricity locally available.
extra: Generators are indispensable on outdoor or remote shoots where plugging into a power grid isn’t possible. They often power lights, cameras, and base camp trailers.

definition: A French word meaning “type” or “kind.” It refers to a specific film class, such as science fiction or musical. All films in a given genre share common, distinctive thematic or artistic elements.
extra: Genre helps audiences know what to expect. At the same time, many great films play with or subvert genre conventions to surprise viewers.

definition: This is a remote head that can be operated in handheld mode or mounted to a dolly or crane. It stabilizes the image, keeps the perfect horizon and enables the camera to move in ways never really achieved before. The most common Gimbals are the MoVi Pro and the Ronin 2.
extra: Gimbals revolutionized handheld cinematography by replacing bulky steadicams in some situations, allowing smoother movement at lower cost.

definition: An Anton/Bauer proprietary mount that enables the battery to be mounted to the camera with three mounting posts. This is the industry standard in the United States.
extra: Gold mounts are valued for durability and secure connection, especially on heavy rigs. In Europe, however, the competing V-Mount standard is more common.

definition: A literary or film style characterized by dark and dreary influences, such as ghouls, the supernatural, the grotesque, deathly forces, and the mysterious. Settings include old mansions, castles, and a threatened heroine. Often used in reference to horror films with these characteristics to increase the film’s prestige.
extra: Gothic cinema often blends horror and romance, creating a moody atmosphere. Think of classic films like Hitchcock’s 'Rebecca' or modern ones like Guillermo del Toro’s 'Crimson Peak,' where the setting itself feels like a character.

definition: Refers to a brief extension of the workday beyond the scheduled meal break, typically lasting 10 to 15 minutes which everyone must agree to before the call is made. This period is granted to allow the crew to finish a shot or scene before breaking for a meal without incurring a meal penalty. While “grace” is intended as a short-term solution to avoid disrupting production, it should be used sparingly, as it can impact crew morale and working conditions.
extra: Grace is essentially a courtesy period that avoids penalties, but if abused, it can create tension. It’s one of those small but telling details about how a set respects its crew.

definition: A term used when a film has received the go-ahead to go into production. This contrasts with a red light, where a film remains stuck on a shelf, not to enter production.
extra: Getting the greenlight is a huge milestone in filmmaking. It usually means financing is secured and the project is officially moving forward, though many films still face hurdles after this stage.

definition: A crew member who procures, places, and maintains any vegetation on a set.
extra: The greensman ensures plants look natural and consistent across takes—whether it’s a lush jungle or a simple potted plant in a living room. It’s a small role with a big impact on realism.

definition: A Grindhouse was originally a burlesque theatre, often in a red-light district, showing exploitation and B-films. They became popular in the 1960s and ’70s, and Grindhouse films today are those that carry on that aesthetic.
extra: Grindhouse cinema is known for being raw, low-budget, and sensational. Quentin Tarantino and Robert Rodriguez famously revived the term with their 2007 double-feature homage, 'Grindhouse.'

definition: A crew member who sets up dolly tracks, moving props, camera cranes, and other pieces of equipment. The key grip is the head grip, which coordinates all of the duties with the other grips in the crew. The head grip receives direction from the gaffer.
extra: Grips are the backbone of the technical crew. While often invisible to audiences, their work makes smooth camera movements and complex shots possible.

definition: A grip tool. A clamp is a brace, band, or clasp used for strengthening or holding things together. These are often called spring clips. They come in 4 sizes, #.5, #1, #2 and #3. They are an essential tool for everything a grip has to do.
extra: Grip clips are like the duct tape of film sets: simple, cheap, and used everywhere. They might hold a gel to a light, secure fabric, or temporarily fix a set piece.

definition: A special effects process whereby actors work in front of an evenly-lit, monochromatic (usually blue or green) background, screen, or backdrop. The background is then replaced in post-production by chroma-keying or optical printer, allowing other footage or computer-generated images (CGI) to form the background image.
extra: Green-screens are the backbone of modern VFX, from superhero movies to weather reports. Green is used because it contrasts strongly with skin tones and clothing, making it easier to key out.

definition: The total box office take. The total amount of money a movie brings in during its theatrical release. It does not include earnings from DVD/Blu-Ray sales, or VOD rentals.
extra: Gross is the number most often reported in headlines, but it doesn’t reflect a film’s actual profitability. Studios care more about net profit after marketing and distribution cuts.

definition: A term originally coined by Federico Fellini to describe the bizarre-looking or deformed background characters in his films; grotesque is a live-action caricature with exaggerated features, but not necessarily to be viewed as frightening or sinister.
extra: The grotesque often toes the line between humor and discomfort. It exaggerates reality in a way that can feel unsettling but also fascinating, giving texture to a film’s world.

definition: A low-budget film made without acquiring filmmaking permits and often using non-SAG actors. Escape From Tomorrow is a guerrilla film shot without permission in Disneyland.
extra: Guerrilla filmmaking thrives on risk-taking—shooting quickly, cheaply, and often illegally. It’s scrappy, but sometimes produces unique, raw storytelling you couldn’t get with traditional production.

definition: An escapist film that engenders low expectations that the public enjoys despite or, more likely, because of its flaws are often quite personal film choices that are sometimes embarrassing to admit. Universally-loved ‘guilty pleasure’ films become cult films.
extra: Guilty pleasures often reveal more about viewers than the films themselves. For example, some people secretly love cheesy action flicks or melodramatic romances precisely because they’re over the top.

definition: A person responsible for maintaining actors’ hairstyles during filming.
extra: Hairstylists ensure continuity—hair has to match across shots, sometimes over months of shooting. They also collaborate closely with makeup and costume to create a character’s look.

definition: A shot is captured through a handheld camera deliberately designed to look wobbly, shaky, or unstable. It’s often used in documentary films or cinéma vérité works.
extra: Handheld shots add immediacy and realism, often making the audience feel ‘inside’ the scene. Think of Paul Greengrass’s Bourne films or found-footage horror like 'The Blair Witch Project.'

definition: The term “hard” refers to the quality of the light. A hard light quality creates harsh borders (as if drawn with a ruler) between lit and shady areas. Overall, it produces a bright illumination and thus reveals many details.
extra: Hard light is often used for dramatic effect—film noir shadows, interrogation scenes, or to highlight texture and grit. It’s unforgiving compared to soft light.

definition: Slang term for a normal indoor theatre.
extra: Before the drive-in era, ‘hardtop’ differentiated traditional movie theatres from outdoor screenings. The term’s mostly historical now.

definition: The Hays Code is a series of censorship restrictions imposed in the 1920s and enforced until the late 1960s. The code stated what could and couldn’t be shown in films, such as nakedness, methods of crime, illegal drug use, alleged sexual perversion, and other taboo subjects at the time. Named after Will Hays, chairman of the MPPDA, the organization in charge of regulating censorship in Hollywood.
extra: The Hays Code shaped Hollywood storytelling for decades, forcing filmmakers into inventive symbolism and subtext. It collapsed in the late ’60s, paving the way for the MPAA rating system.

definition: A shot is where the action comes directly to the camera. It works to increase the audience’s feeling of participating in the film. It works particularly well for 3D movies.
extra: Head-on shots can be startling because they break the ‘observer’ illusion, making viewers feel directly addressed or threatened.

definition: The room between the top of the frame and the top of the subject.
extra: Too much or too little headroom can feel awkward. Cinematographers use this subtly to affect audience perception—for instance, crowding a character against the top edge can make them feel trapped.

definition: A helicopter shot is a moving shot, often used as an establishing shot taken from a bird’s eye view. It is generally taken from a helicopter, allowing it to weave through a landscape.
extra: While drones now do most of the work once reserved for helicopters, the term ‘helicopter shot’ still gets used. Classic example: the opening shot of 'The Shining.'

definition: Another word to refer to the director of a film. For example, “The film was helmed by —.”
extra: A slightly old-fashioned but still common trade term. It emphasizes the director’s control, like a captain steering a ship.

definition: Refers to the major protagonists in a film with whom the audience identifies and sympathizes. Character traits often include being young, virtuous, handsome, or pretty.
extra: Modern cinema often subverts the traditional ‘hero/heroine’ archetype—think of flawed protagonists like Tony Montana or Furiosa.

definition: This is a cut that is intended to be imperceptible. At the end of the first shot, the camera moves closer or zooms in on a plain, typically dark-coloured object that fills the whole frame, thus providing the chance to implement an unobtrusive cut. The following shot shows the camera zooming out or moving away from the previous or another similarly-coloured object. Instead of using camera movement or zoom, this kind of cut can also be affected by a moving subject or object that temporarily covers the whole frame. In a sense, a hidden cut is a special form of a fade-out, fade-in transition in which the fading is simply part of the shot.
extra: Hidden cuts are famous in films like 'Birdman' or '1917,' which simulate being one continuous shot. They preserve immersion while allowing practical filming breaks.

definition: A shot in which the subject or scene is filmed from above, and the camera points down on the action, often to make the subject(s) small, weak and vulnerable.
extra: The opposite of a low-angle shot, which makes subjects powerful. High angles are often used to show vulnerability, as in horror films when prey is stalked.
