definition: Refers to the saleable or marketable elements of a film. A high concept refers to the need for a film’s main premise to be expressed as a simple formula in just a few words that all can easily understand. This idea portrays a shallow, condescending attitude toward undiscriminating film audiences by Hollywood’s marketers and often results in having film content controlled by what appeals to the lowest common denominator market.
extra: High-concept films are easy to pitch, like ‘Die Hard on a bus’ ('Speed'). They’re considered commercially safe, but critics argue they sacrifice depth for simplicity.

definition: In photography and cinematography, the term “contrast” refers to the difference in brightness between the lit and shady areas of an image. In this respect, an image in high contrast has many alternating deep dark shadows and very brightly lit areas, giving an uneasy impression.
extra: High contrast is often used in horror and noir to evoke tension or unease, while low contrast is softer and more romantic.

definition: An image with a resolution with a minimum of 480 scan lines, with the average being 720 and 1080 scan lines.
extra: HD was once a revolution in home media, replacing standard definition. Now 4K and even 8K are pushing HD into being the baseline rather than the cutting edge.

definition: One of the main lighting styles used in filmmaking and often associated with the bright overall lighting of sitcoms and ballroom scenes. A small ratio between the key light and the fill light characterizes high-key lighting. Normally, it is used in combination with soft light to create a pleasant atmosphere, which produces low contrasts between lit and shady areas.
extra: High-key lighting is cheerful and flattering, common in comedies, musicals, and commercials. It minimizes shadows and feels polished.

definition: The “Hitchcock’s Rule” is a cinematographic principle which was coined by Alfred Hitchcock in his famous discussions with François Truffaut. The rule states that the size of an object in the frame should equal its importance in the story at that moment.
extra: Hitchcock’s Rule is why a close-up of a key in 'Notorious' is more powerful than any dialogue—it tells the audience exactly what matters.

definition: Hitting a mark is for actors moving to the correct position during rehearsals and while the camera rolls. Sometimes, a mark will be set with a physical piece of crossed tape on the floor to help the actor stand in the right spot.
extra: It sounds simple, but hitting marks precisely is essential—focus, lighting, and framing all depend on it. Missing a mark can ruin a shot.

definition: An HMI is a powerful hard light that can be used in place of sunlight. This is a daylight-balanced fixture. The French developed the Fresnel lens to project light for long distances. This lens delivers beautiful hard shadows; it delivers a very even spread while in flood and spot. This light gives great shafts of light, awesome for bounces and projecting through diffusion frames.
extra: HMIs are a staple on film sets when sunlight needs to be simulated or matched. They’re powerful but require ballasts and can be dangerous if mishandled.

definition: An abbreviation for “Head of Department”.
extra: Each key department—camera, sound, makeup, production design—has its own HOD, who oversees the crew and reports directly to the director or producers.

definition: Before the slate. The set is locked; the sound may be rolling, but there is a need for a short delay that does not require the set to be unlocked or the roll stopped.
extra: It’s a technical pause that keeps continuity intact while avoiding the time and hassle of fully cutting and resetting.

definition: The term for an actor used for an extra day.
extra: Hold overs cost production money, since contracts often require paying actors for additional time—even if they’re not filming much that day.

definition: A respectful tribute to something or someone. In film, this generally occurs when one movie is referenced in a different film. Many Star Wars films pay homage to classic samurai movies.
extra: Homage differs from parody—it’s sincere rather than mocking. Tarantino films are full of homages to exploitation cinema and kung fu classics.

definition: Usually a trailer or truck and trailer combination outfitted for and used as the dressing room for actors when on location shoots away from permanent soundstages. Big trucks containing washrooms, AD office, and small dressing rooms.
extra: Despite the name, it’s not glamorous. The term originated from old sanitation trucks but stuck as slang for mobile facilities on set.

definition: A straight line is drawn across one or two vanishing points that mark the height at which the camera is positioned. Depending on the camera angle, the horizon line moves up or down within the frame, which is why it can be used to help deduce the type of camera angle. If the horizon line slopes to one side, the camera is in a canted angle position. Changing positions of the horizon line and optical distortions, depending on different camera angles and heights.
extra: Painters and photographers have used horizon lines for centuries to control perspective. Filmmakers use them for balance, tension, or disorientation.

definition: A genre of storytelling intended to scare, shock, and thrill its audience. Horror can be interpreted in many different ways, but there is often a central villain, monster, or threat that is often a reflection of the fears being experienced by society at the time.
extra: Horror constantly evolves—vampires in one decade, slashers in another. The genre often mirrors cultural anxieties, from Cold War paranoia to modern tech fears.

definition: A location or studio used for filming – even if the camera isn’t rolling. You shouldn’t lounge around or touch anything on a hot set because it may disrupt continuity. A set that is not finished being used. Not to be touched.
extra: The rule is simple: if it’s a hot set, don’t touch anything. Even moving a chair an inch could ruin continuity for the next shot.

definition: A movie that combines elements of two distinct genre types. As a result, it can’t be defined by a single genre. Little Shop of Horrors is a hybrid of a horror film and a musical.
extra: Hybrids are commercially risky but creatively rich—think of 'Get Out' (horror + social thriller) or 'Shaun of the Dead' (horror + comedy).

definition: Refers to manufactured promotional buzz and excessive advertising/marketing for a film or project, including celebrity appearances, radio and TV spots or interviews, and other ploys.
extra: Studios rely heavily on hype to secure opening weekend box office. Sometimes it works ('The Phantom Menace'), sometimes it backfires when expectations aren’t met.

term: IATSE/International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees, Moving Picture Technicians, Artists and Allied Crafts
definition: IATSE is a union that represents professional entertainment industry workers. They include more than 168,000 workers in virtually all arts, media, and entertainment crafts, with a mission to improve all entertainment workers’ lives both inside and outside the workplace.
extra: IATSE plays a major role in labor negotiations in Hollywood. Their strikes or contract disputes can shut down film and TV production nationwide.

definition: The use of a famous icon or symbol. It is designed to analyze the themes and various styles present within a film. The rose in Beauty and the Beast has become an icon.
extra: Film scholars use iconography to decode genre—cowboy hats for westerns, crosses for religious horror, trench coats and fedoras for noir.

definition: Generally refers to the picture that is the result of the photographic process.
extra: ‘Image’ can mean the literal frame onscreen or the broader visual impression a film creates in audiences’ minds.

definition: A large-screen film format roughly 10 times larger than the traditional cinema format (35mm). It debuted in 1970, and initially, it was used to showcase nature films or short documentaries. It produces amazing high-definition sharpness on movies projected onto screens eight stories high.
extra: IMAX has become a selling point for blockbuster releases. Directors like Christopher Nolan shoot sequences specifically for IMAX cameras.

definition: An aspect of the mise en scène which describes a state of compositional unevenness or disproportion. Imbalance can be achieved in various forms, for example, via the asymmetrical presence of subjects/objects, colour, light, and form.
extra: Imbalance often conveys tension or unease, making the audience subconsciously feel that something is ‘off.’

definition: Refers to filming in the exact order required for the final product, thereby eliminating the post-production editing stage; a fast, albeit unprofessional way to produce a film, often employed by student or amateur filmmakers; requires advanced planning to tell the desired story in order.
extra: While rare in professional productions, in-camera editing can be a teaching tool for students to learn sequencing and planning.

definition: Small independent, low-budget companies, mini-majors, or entities for financing, producing, and distributing films working outside of the system of a major Hollywood studio. An indie may lose its independent status when it grows large and powerful. Also refers to a movie, director, distributor or producer not associated with or produced by a major Hollywood film studio; often with groundbreaking subject matter designed for sophisticated audiences, and not necessarily produced with commercial success as the goal, unlike mainstream films.
extra: Sundance and SXSW became major showcases for indie films. Indies often take risks in style and subject matter that studio films avoid.

definition: Another name for the film or entertainment industry; also referred to as the show business, show-biz, or Hollywood.
extra: Insiders casually say ‘the industry’ to mean Hollywood as a whole, from studios to unions to talent agencies.

definition: A young, teenage actress often in an important or lead role in a film; usually portrays an innocent, sometimes naive, and attractive character; also refers to an actress sometimes known as a starlet; the male counterpart is known as a juvenile.
extra: The ingénue trope has been critiqued for limiting young actresses to narrow roles. Many modern films intentionally subvert it.

definition: A word used when people sign a contract to work on a film. It is often phrased as someone “inked a deal.”
extra: Common in entertainment journalism; e.g., 'The actor inked a deal with Netflix.' Related terms: 'greenlit,' 'signed on.'

definition: A shot occurring in the middle of a larger shot, typically a close-up of another object or some otherwise minor detail. It draws the audience’s attention to the item, providing more information. It is filmed at a different focal length or angle from the rest of the scene.
extra: Common in thrillers to highlight weapons, keys, or text messages. Related to 'cutaway.'

definition: An inside joke is an obscure, generally show business-related joke that is only understood by a few in the audience. You have to understand the reference to get it. For example, the great white shark in Finding Nemo is named Bruce, the name of the mechanical shark used for Jaws.
extra: Often used by directors to pay homage to crew, actors, or other films. Related concept: 'Easter egg.'

definition: Usually refers to a series of shots consisting of two simultaneous events alternating to create suspense; intercutting can also consist of shots of two people involved in a telephone conversation.
extra: A common form of parallel editing. Example: suspense scenes where a victim is stalked while the police rush to help.

definition: Used in a slug line as ‘INT.’, indicates that the scene occurs indoors.
extra: Screenwriting format: 'INT. HOUSE – NIGHT.' The opposite is 'EXT.' for exterior.

definition: A brief, intervening film scene or sequence, not specifically tied to the plot, that appears within a film.
extra: Often musical or atmospheric, breaking narrative tension. Related to 'montage' or 'cutaway.'

definition: A break in the middle of a film, normally in a feature-length film of three hours or more (although rare in North America these days); originally, intermissions served as a ‘stretch-restroom’ opportunity, or provide time for the projectionist to change reels; they often were accompanied by a medley of the film’s score – or a song score for musicals.
extra: Still common in Indian cinema and older Hollywood epics (e.g., Lawrence of Arabia).

definition: The successor to the American Standards Association’s (ASA) system for rating the sensitivity of photographic film to light. ISO now defines the standardized scale used in both film and digital photography to measure the sensitivity of sensors, impacting exposure settings and image quality.
extra: Lower ISO = less sensitivity, cleaner images; higher ISO = more sensitivity, grain/noise. Related to 'ASA' and 'DIN' film speed ratings.

definition: A copy of the film made for the purpose of making a large number of prints.
extra: Used in film duplication workflows to protect the original camera negative. Related to 'interpositive.'

definition: A title card appearing intercut with a scene. Commonly used in silent films.
extra: Silent-era example: 'Meanwhile, back at the ranch…' Still occasionally used stylistically in modern films.

definition: A term for an entire film or a subset of shots that are all finished shooting; also denotes when a director has the take that they wanted.
extra: Industry slang still in use, though increasingly digital workflows make 'in the can' metaphorical.

definition: Refers to a person or object that moves into the picture frame without the camera moving; in live-action stage plays, this refers to a character entering the stage.
extra: Common blocking instruction: 'Step into frame.' Opposite is 'exit frame.'

definition: An opening in the lens that controls the amount of light passing through, similar to the aperture.
extra: Measured in f-stops. Larger opening = shallower depth of field. Related to 'aperture' and 'exposure.'

definition: An earlier cinematographic technique or wipe effect, in the form of an expanding or diminishing circle (known as iris-out or iris-in), in which a part of the screen is blacked out so that only a portion of the image can be seen by the viewer; usually the lens aperture is circular or oval shaped and is often expanded or contracted as the film rolls, often as a transition from one scene to the next; this particular type of camera movement is also known as iris wipe, or circle-in/circle-out, similar to the opening or closing of the human eye’s iris; also refers to the adjustable opening (or diaphragm) in the lens that allows light to pass through – the measurement for the iris opening is f-stop.
extra: Classic in silent films and cartoons (Looney Tunes’ 'That’s all folks!' ending). Rarely used today outside homage.

definition: ISO now defines the standardized scale used in both film and digital photography to measure the sensitivity of sensors, impacting exposure settings and image quality. Pronounced ISO.
extra: Often mispronounced as 'I-S-O' instead of 'Eye-So.' Same as photographic ISO rating.

definition: See L-cut (below); aka split edit.
extra: In a J-cut, audio leads the picture; in an L-cut, picture leads audio. Common in dialogue transitions.

definition: The arm of a mechanical crane.
extra: Provides smooth sweeping camera movements. Related to 'crane shot.'

definition: An instability is introduced when images sampled at one frame rate are converted to a different frame rate for viewing. This effect is most noticeable when frames are repeated or deleted in order to obtain slow motion or fast motion. See also motion artifact.
extra: Often visible when 24fps films are shown on 30fps TV. Related: 'motion interpolation' and 'soap opera effect.'

definition: In the film industry, a “juicer” is a slang term for an electrician who works on a film set, typically as part of the lighting department. Juicers are responsible for setting up, operating, and maintaining the electrical equipment used to power lights and other devices during production.
extra: Informal crew slang; overlaps with 'electric.' Not to be confused with bodybuilding term.

definition: A filmed musical (drama, animation, etc.) that uses pre-existing popular songs (usually from a variety of artistic sources) as its song score; the songs are often re-imagined with different song styles; aka karaoke musical.
extra: Examples: 'Mamma Mia!,' 'Moulin Rouge!,' 'Across the Universe.'

definition: A jump cut is an editing technique in film and video where two sequential shots of the same subject are taken from slightly different angles or positions, creating a jarring or abrupt transition. This gives the appearance of a sudden jump in time or space, often used to convey urgency, disorientation, or a passage of time.
extra: Popularized by French New Wave (e.g., Jean-Luc Godard’s 'Breathless'). Still used for energy in vlogs and YouTube edits.

definition: The role of a young, teenage male character; the female counterpart is known as an ingenue.
extra: Archaic Hollywood casting term; now less commonly used but historically important.

definition: The contiguous positions of two scenes, objects, characters, or images in a sequence to contrast and compare them. It can also establish a relationship between two disparate ideas.
extra: Example: cutting between a wedding and a funeral. Related concept: 'montage' and 'dialectical editing' (Eisenstein).

definition: The kelvin, symbol K, is a unit of measurement for temperature. The Kelvin scale is an absolute scale, which is defined such that 0 K is absolute zero, and a change of thermodynamic temperature T by 1 kelvin corresponds to a change of thermal energy. Colour temperature is a way to describe the light appearance provided by a light bulb. It is measured in degrees of Kelvin (K) on a scale from 1,000 to 10,000. Typically, Kelvin temperatures for commercial and residential lighting applications fall somewhere on a scale from 2000K to 6500K.
extra: Film lighting shorthand: 3200K = tungsten, 5600K = daylight. Mixed lighting often corrected with gels.

definition: A general adjective denoting importance. Heads of departments are referred to as a “Key” or “Keys” on a film crew.
extra: Examples: Key Grip, Key Makeup Artist. Indicates leadership within a department.

definition: The key grip works closely with the director of photography and the gaffer to sculpt the desired look of a film by diffusing and cutting the light. The key grip is also in charge of camera movement whether on a dolly, camera crane or mounted on the hood or bumper of a vehicle.
extra: Often confused with gaffer; key grip handles rigging & camera support, gaffer handles electrical lighting.

definition: The main or primary light on a subject, often angled and off-center (or from above) that selectively illuminates various prominent features of the image to produce depth, shadows, etc.; high-key lighting (with everything evenly and brightly lit, with a minimum of shadows) is termed realistic (and often used in musicals and comedies), while low-key lighting (with less illumination, more shadows, and many grayish, dark areas) is termed expressionistic (and often used in film noir); three-point lighting uses: (1) a fill (or filler) light – an auxiliary light to soften shadows and areas not covered by the key light, (2) a backlight behind to add depth to a subject, and (3) a bright key light.
extra: Central to three-point lighting. Key-to-fill ratio defines mood (high ratio = dramatic, low ratio = flat/comedic).

definition: A Kino Flo is a bank of fluorescent bulbs used for soft light.
extra: Favored for interview lighting and color accuracy. Often replaced today with LED panels.

definition: A Klieglight is a powerful type of carbon-arc lamp that creates an intense light. It is sometimes used in filmmaking, but it can also be used for promotional purposes at movie premieres.
extra: Named after the Kliegl Brothers. Iconic for old Hollywood searchlights outside premieres.

definition: A movie deemed revolutionary. This can either be due to its artistic merits or its technological prowess. Jaws was a landmark film because it introduced the concept of the modern blockbuster.
extra: Examples: Jaws (1975), Star Wars (1977), Avatar (2009).

definition: A certain kind of transition between two scenes. The first scene ends with a fade, while the beginning of the next scene comes onto the screen through a fade-in.
extra: Also called a cross-dissolve; often used to show the passage of time.

definition: A small microphone that is clipped or taped to an actor to record dialogue. It is generally wireless and omnidirectional, as well as small enough not to be seen in the shot.
extra: Commonly used in television, theater, and documentary filmmaking for discreet audio capture.

definition: It is an edit used in digital films that refers to a transitional edit in which the video and audio do not begin simultaneously. The audio may begin before or after the picture is cut.
extra: An L-cut lets audio continue after the video changes; a J-cut lets audio start before the video changes.

definition: A recurring, intentionally repeated theme or element in a movie. This motif can be a person, sound, action, or idea. It helps unify the film by reminding the audience of its earlier appearance.
extra: Common in film scores; e.g., Darth Vader’s ‘Imperial March’ theme in Star Wars.

definition: An optical glass placed in a camera through which light can pass through. The image is focused before it makes contact with the film stock. There are numerous types of lenses out there, including normal, telephoto, and wide-angle.
extra: Special lenses: fisheye (distortion), macro (close-ups), anamorphic (widescreen).

definition: The process of shrinking a film image to appear on a television screen with black spaces below and above the image. This emulates the widescreen format typically used on older, box-shaped TV screens.
extra: Opposite process is ‘pan and scan’, where widescreen films are cropped to fit 4:3 screens.

definition: A term used to describe a stock shot. It can also refer to a commonplace or unimaginative shot. A shot of the New York skyline would be a library shot for any movie set in New York.
extra: Used for budget savings; stock footage libraries provide pre-shot material.

definition: The illumination present within a scene. It also refers to the manipulation of said illumination by way of the cinematographer trying to alter shadows and brightness.
extra: Types: high-key (bright, even), low-key (shadowy, dramatic), motivated (appears to come from an on-screen source).

definition: The movie producer who works on location. They are responsible for the budget of a given film shoot and the daily operations. The line producer manages the everyday aspects involving film expenses and all the people on the crew.
extra: Often the person ensuring production stays on schedule and under budget.

definition: The process of synchronizing the movement of the mouth with the words on the soundtrack.
extra: Critical in dubbing, ADR, and musical performances.

definition: The places or properties used to film. A location can either be exterior or interior, and it can take place in a real location or on a studio lot.
extra: On-location shooting vs. studio soundstages; each offers advantages in realism and control.

definition: Referred to as a buzz track. It refers to the recording of background sound while the crew is on location. Acquiring ambient noises helps improve the movie’s sense of realism.
extra: Room tone is used in sound editing to smooth over dialogue cuts.

definition: Stop what you’re doing and be quiet; the camera is about to roll.
extra: A set command from the assistant director to control noise and movement.

definition: An area being cordoned off and controlled by crew members to prevent either unwanted sound or pedestrians from ruining the take.
extra: Part of set security and crowd control during filming.

definition: A 1-2 sentence summary of the movie focusing on the main character, the conflict and an emotional hook.
extra: Used in pitching; e.g., ‘A young farm boy discovers he’s a Jedi and must defeat an evil empire.’ (Star Wars)

definition: A camera view of a character or object from a vast distance away. This makes the subject appear small in the frame. You can also have a medium or extreme long shot.
extra: Also called a wide shot; often used to establish geography and context.

definition: The process in which an actor re-records dialogue during post-production. This helps match the dialogue with the actor’s lip movements on screen. It is also known as Automated Dialogue Replacement (or ADR).
extra: Common when original sound is noisy, unclear, or needs translation.

definition: When the subject is filmed from below. The camera tilts up to capture the character or action, making the subject seem larger than life or more formidable.
extra: Used to convey power, dominance, or intimidation.

definition: A movie term coined by Alfred Hitchcock for a plot element or device that drives the action or logic of the plot. It is extremely important for the characters, but it is often ignored once it serves its purpose. The sled in Citizen Kane is a MacGuffin.
extra: Other examples: the briefcase in Pulp Fiction, the Ark of the Covenant in Raiders of the Lost Ark.

definition: The optimal time of day for filming magical or romantic scenes with the soft and warm lighting conditions naturally present. Also known as Golden Hour, it is characterized by golden-orange hues and soft shadows, which take place 30 minutes around sunset and 30 minutes around sunrise.
extra: Favored by cinematographers for its flattering, natural look.

definition: The main crew of the film set.
extra: Often distinguished from the second unit, which films stunts, inserts, or establishing shots.

definition: Putting tape down where actors stop in the scene.
extra: Marking ensures consistency in performances and keeps actors in focus and properly lit. It's a small but essential part of maintaining continuity on set.

definition: The last shot of the last scene of the day.
extra: Crews often look forward to the martini shot since it signals wrap for the day. The name is said to come from the idea that the next shot after this one is taken in a martini glass.

definition: The act of blocking out or covering up part of the camera frame with darkness or opaqueness. Most masks will be black. A mask would be necessary when portraying a character looking through binoculars.
extra: Masks are a practical way of guiding audience perspective. They mimic a character’s point of view or create stylized effects without expensive post-production.

definition: A long take or continuous shot that shows the setting or main action of a whole scene. Many scenes will have one or two master shots, with the rest of the scene comprised of smaller, tighter angles. A wide shot that shows the whole scene.
extra: Directors often shoot a master first to ensure coverage of the full scene, giving editors flexibility when cutting between angles.

definition: A transitional technique for cutting between two unrelated shots that are deliberately linked or matched by a physical, aural, visual, or metaphorical parallelism.
extra: Match cuts are iconic in cinema—like the bone-to-spaceship transition in Kubrick’s *2001: A Space Odyssey*. They create visual or thematic continuity.

definition: The process of optically combining or compositing separate shots into one print. This is achieved through double exposure that masks off part of the frame area for one exposure and the opposite area for the other.
extra: Before digital effects, matte shots were vital for creating environments that didn’t exist in reality, like grand castles or alien planets.

definition: A conventional camera shot filmed from a medium-length distance. It typically captures the actor from the waist up, while a medium close-up is from the chest up.
extra: Medium shots are versatile, balancing context with character expression. They're among the most common shots in both film and television.

definition: A film with an expressive plot where the characters have intensely strong emotions. It was originally a drama accompanied by music and typically contains elements of hardship, illness, and pathos.
extra: Melodramas emphasize emotional extremes and moral conflicts, often appealing to audiences’ empathy. Classic Hollywood melodramas shaped family and romance storytelling.

definition: A figure of speech in which a word or phrase denoting one kind of object or idea is used in place of another to suggest a likeness or an analogy between them.
extra: Filmmakers use visual metaphors to enrich storytelling—for example, a caged bird symbolizing a trapped character.

definition: An acting style designed by Stanislavsky in the early 1900s. It refers to actors who draw on personal emotions and experiences to create a more realistic performance. Daniel Day-Lewis and Jared Leto often utilize method acting to create their performances- each with varying degrees of success.
extra: Method acting can lead to powerful performances but is sometimes criticized for extreme behavior. It has deeply influenced modern acting styles.

definition: A small-scale model photographed in a certain way to give off the illusion they are larger than what they actually are. This specific shot is known as a miniature shot.
extra: Miniatures were essential before CGI, creating believable spaceships, buildings, and landscapes. Many classics like *Star Wars* relied heavily on them.

definition: “Putting in the scene” in French refers to the composition and arrangement of visual elements within the film frame, including costume, set décor, lighting, and character positioning.
extra: Mise en scène shapes how audiences interpret a scene. Directors like Wes Anderson are known for meticulous control of every visual element.

definition: A process of combining different sounds, music, dialogue, and sound effects from all sources into a movie’s master soundtrack. This is part of the post-production process. A mixer ultimately blends together the soundtrack.
extra: Good sound mixing is often unnoticed, but it deeply affects immersion. Award categories like the Oscars highlight its importance.

definition: A fictional movie that has the style of a documentary but with irreverent humour that’s designed to mock the subject of features. Waiting for Guffman is a mockumentary.
extra: Mockumentaries blur fact and fiction. Popular in comedy, they’ve expanded to TV with shows like *The Office*.

definition: Any climactic moment, revelation, or image that gives the audience “their money’s worth,” even if it costs more money to create.
extra: The money shot is often heavily marketed in trailers—it’s the scene audiences will remember, whether it’s an explosion, kiss, or reveal.

definition: A French term meaning “assembling shots” or “putting together.” It’s a film technique for compiling a series of short shots that create a composite picture. The montage in Rocky of the titular character shows us how hard he’s worked to compete in the final match.
extra: Montages efficiently compress time and information, often showing progress or change. Training montages are a sports film staple.

definition: A universal abbreviation for “Mit Out Sound,” which means there will be no audio on a take. Shot without recording sound.
extra: The term supposedly originated from a German director whose broken English turned 'without sound' into 'mit out sound.'

definition: Refers to a recurrent thematic element in a film that is repeated in a significant way or pattern; examples of motifs – a symbol, stylistic device, image, object, word, spoken phrase, line, or sentence within a film that points to a theme.
extra: Motifs build cohesion. For example, repeated water imagery in *The Shape of Water* reinforces its themes of transformation and connection.

definition: Phrase said by 1st AD when going on to the next shot/set-up.
extra: This phrase keeps production efficient. It tells the crew they’ve captured enough for that shot and prevents unnecessary retakes.

definition: An acronym meaning “Motion Picture Association of America.” It is an organization that represents the interests of the primary motion picture studios, including film ratings.
extra: The MPAA ratings system—like PG-13 or R—has shaped what content is accessible to audiences and often sparks debates about censorship.

definition: An independent film movement that originated in the early 2000s. It’s often characterized by naturalistic acting that’s occasionally improvised. The plots generally focus on a group of people in their 20s or 30s dealing with terrible jobs or bad relationships.
extra: Mumblecore emphasizes authenticity over polish. Filmmakers like Greta Gerwig and the Duplass brothers helped define the movement.

definition: The telling of a story by providing supplemental information given to the audience by a voice offscreen. The narrator can either be a character in the movie or an omniscient presence.
extra: Narration can add depth, irony, or context. Think of Scorsese’s *Goodfellas*, where voiceover shapes the audience’s perspective.

definition: A structured series of events, linked by cause and effect, that provides the plot of a film; a film that tells a chronological or linear story (with a beginning, middle, and end), as opposed to non-narrative films, such as poetic or abstract films.
extra: Narrative films dominate mainstream cinema because audiences naturally respond to stories with a clear beginning, middle, and end. Even experimental filmmakers often play with narrative structure, bending or breaking it to challenge viewer expectations.

definition: A film term signifying a hyperform of realism. With naturalism, life is depicted in an unbiased, stoic way. On the Waterfront is a naturalistic movie.
extra: Naturalism goes beyond realism by stripping away theatricality or exaggeration. It tries to show life as it truly is, even if that makes it feel raw, bleak, or understated.

definition: An innovative movement in the late 1940s and ’50s with roots in Italy. It refers to movies made outside the studio system. They are shot in real locations, sometimes feature no professional actors, and often do not require a script.
extra: Italian Neo-Realism revolutionized cinema with films like Bicycle Thieves. It emphasized ordinary people and real-life struggles, shaping later movements like the French New Wave.

definition: Originally referred to as the “Big Three” (ABC, NBC and CBS), but now with additional competitors, including Fox, it is often called ‘Free-TV’.
extra: Network television set the standard for broadcasting in the U.S. for decades, shaping culture and viewing habits long before cable and streaming disrupted the landscape.

definition: Originally referred to a collective of non-traditional, innovative French filmmakers, such as Alain Resnais, Eric Rohmer, and Jean-Luc Godard. They espoused principles of auteur theory. French New Wave movies are characterized by non-linear storytelling, improvised direction, and jump cuts.
extra: The French New Wave changed how films were made, influencing directors worldwide. Techniques like handheld cameras, jump cuts, and breaking the fourth wall became hallmarks of modern cinema.

definition: A film movement that took place in the United States from roughly 1967 to 1976. The movement was led by a group of film students, such as George Lucas, Steven Spielberg, and Martin Scorsese, with a passion for filmmaking and the desire to challenge the stagnant status quo.
extra: New Hollywood produced some of the most iconic American films, from The Godfather to Jaws. It was a rare moment when studios gave creative freedom to young directors, reshaping Hollywood storytelling.

definition: A business that might be described as a “movie arcade.” Patrons would pay a nickel to watch short films on individual machines like a Kinetoscope or a Mutoscope. Not to be confused with the television network.
extra: Nickelodeons were the forerunners of modern cinemas, making movies accessible to everyday people. They played a crucial role in popularizing film as entertainment in the early 20th century.

definition: A type of film base that was highly flammable. It was comprised of cellulose nitrate and was commonly in use until the late 1940s. At that point, it was replaced with an acetate base.
extra: Nitrate film was beautiful for its luminous image quality, but dangerously unstable. Many early films have been lost because of nitrate’s tendency to decompose or catch fire.

definition: Refers to a performer who has completely learned his or her lines. At this point, there is no need for the performer to hold a script because everything has been memorized.
extra: Going 'off book' is a major step in rehearsals. It allows actors to focus on movement, chemistry, and emotion rather than being tied to the page.

definition: Off-screen/Off-camera.
extra: These abbreviations in a script indicate that dialogue or action is happening outside the camera’s frame, a common technique for building tension or context without showing everything directly.

definition: Refers to action or dialogue off the visible stage or beyond the boundaries of the camera’s field of vision or depicted frame.
extra: Directors often use off-screen action to expand the world of a film, suggesting events happening beyond what the audience sees, which can add suspense or humor.

definition: When the narrator knows everything going on. The narrator understands all of the thoughts, feelings, and events transpiring between the characters.
extra: This god-like perspective is rare in film but powerful. It allows the audience to see deeper connections and motivations that the characters themselves may not realize.

definition: An abridged version of the shooting schedule. Also known as a “one-liner,” scenes are listed and arranged in shooting order and broken up by shooting days. This is the most commonly distributed schedule as it only contains the essential scene information.
extra: The one-liner is a practical tool on set, ensuring everyone—from crew to cast—knows the daily plan without being bogged down by excessive details.

definition: A phrase used when changing set-ups or moving to a different location.
extra: This phrase keeps production efficient. It signals to the crew that focus shifts quickly, minimizing downtime between shots.

definition: Positioning of the cast.
extra: Hitting your mark is crucial for camera focus, framing, and lighting. Even the best performance won’t work if the actor isn’t where the camera needs them to be.

definition: A technique when a camera’s frame rate exceeds 24 frames per second. As a result, the image on the screen appears to be in slow motion. This is a common technique for shooting miniatures.
extra: Overcranking adds weight and drama to a moment, whether it’s an explosion in an action film or a slow-motion replay in sports coverage.

definition: An adjective describing a shot with more light than recommended, resulting in a washed-out, blinding effect. It is typically used for dream or flashback sequences.
extra: Cinematographers sometimes use overexposure deliberately to create surreal, hazy, or memory-like visuals.

definition: When the camera is placed over the actors. It tends to be set at about a 90-degree angle from where the performers are located. It is also known as a bird’s eye view shot.
extra: This shot gives a god-like perspective, often making characters seem small, vulnerable, or trapped within their environment.

definition: A medium camera angle commonly used in dialogue scenes. The camera records the action and dialogue from behind the actors’ shoulders. The two individuals are then linked to each other, and the audience understands their positions.
extra: Over-the-shoulder shots are a staple of film grammar. They create intimacy and spatial continuity, making conversations feel natural.

definition: The opening credits or pre-credits in a film. This is often a musical selection that helps set up the theme and mood for the rest of the movie.
extra: Overtures were more common in older films, especially epics. They allowed the audience to settle in while music prepared them emotionally for the story.

definition: The tempo or speed of the dramatic action in a movie. The pacing can be enhanced by the speed of the dialogue, the soundtrack, and the style of editing used.
extra: A fast pace builds excitement, while slower pacing gives audiences time to reflect. Masterful pacing balances energy with emotional depth.

definition: An abbreviation for a panorama shot, referring to the rotation, scan, or horizontal movement of the camera in one direction. In film criticism, pan means to express a negative opinion of a movie.
extra: In cinematography, pans can reveal new information or follow action smoothly. In reviews, however, a 'pan' means quite the opposite—a harsh critique.

definition: A technique for avoiding letterboxing of a widescreen movie. Instead, it focuses on elements of the picture that are more relevant to the plot and adjusted accordingly. The picture will then mechanically pan to the side to show whatever is missing.
extra: Pan and scan was common on VHS and TV broadcasts, but many cinephiles hated it because it cropped directors’ original compositions.

definition: A statement, proposition, or situation that seems illogical, absurd or self-contradictory but which, upon further scrutiny, may be logical or true — or at least contain an element of truth.
extra: Paradoxes often drive science fiction plots—time travel, for instance, is full of them. They intrigue audiences because they challenge logic while hinting at deeper meaning.

definition: A term for screenplay directions, shown in parentheses, to express how the actor should deliver his or her lines. A parenthetical may read (angrily) or (calmly) before the dialogue.
extra: Parentheticals guide performance, but overuse can frustrate actors who prefer to interpret lines themselves.

definition: The optical phenomenon where the illusion of motion is created because the brain interprets multiple still images as one. When multiple images appear in fast enough succession, the brain blends them into a single, persistent, moving image.
extra: This principle is the foundation of all cinema. Without persistence of vision, film would just be a series of still pictures instead of moving stories.

definition: Reshooting part of the scene, not starting at the beginning.
extra: Pick-ups are common in production and usually save time. Instead of redoing an entire scene, filmmakers just capture the missing piece.

definition: Any vehicle that is on screen in a movie.
extra: Picture vehicles can be background cars in traffic or iconic stars themselves—like the Batmobile or James Bond’s Aston Martin.

definition: A standalone episode of a television series that is used to sell a show to a television network or other distributor. A pilot is created to be a testing ground to gauge whether a series will be successful.
extra: Pilots are essentially test cases. They often differ in tone, cast, or budget from the series that follows, since studios use them to judge whether a concept has legs before committing to a full season.

definition: Refers to a film project currently in the system that is under development. It is scheduled for a future release. Some synonyms include “in process,” “in the queue,” or “in the works.”
extra: Studios and production companies often juggle dozens of projects in the pipeline. It’s a way to track which films are moving toward production and which are stalled in development hell.

definition: A technique where the illusion of continuous movement in three-dimensional subjects, typically people, is broken up and made to look jerky or uneven. This is achieved by only printing selected frames from the continuously-exposed negative. This technique is commonly used in stop-motion animation.
extra: Pixilation gives a surreal, puppet-like quality to live actors. It’s been used by experimental filmmakers and animators to blur the line between real life and stop-motion animation.

definition: A shot taken from the perspective of one character to show what the scene would look like through his or her eyes. It is generally coupled with a reaction shot to establish the point of view.
extra: POV shots place the audience directly into a character’s shoes. Horror films use them to create dread, while dramas use them for intimacy or empathy.

definition: An epilogue or throwaway scene that occurs during or after the end credits. It can help generate buzz for an additional scene. Iron Man ends with a post-credits scene of Nick Fury informing Tony Stark about the Avengers Initiative.
extra: These sequences have become staples of blockbuster franchises, especially superhero films, where they tease future installments and keep fans talking long after the film ends.

definition: A description of all art that rebukes more modernist themes. Postmodern films work to subvert expectations of classic narratives and film structure.
extra: Postmodern cinema often plays with irony, pastiche, and self-awareness—think of films like Pulp Fiction that deliberately disrupt linear storytelling and genre conventions.

definition: Point of view.
extra: While shorthand for ‘point of view,’ in filmmaking it almost always implies a visual perspective—how a scene is framed to match what a character sees or experiences.

definition: A concept devised by the philosopher to ruminate on the nature of belief versus knowledge.
extra: Filmmakers sometimes reference Plato’s Allegory of the Cave to explore themes of perception and reality—The Matrix is perhaps the most famous modern example.

definition: The time period between 1930 and 1934 before the Hays Code was enforced in Hollywood. For 30 years afterward, promiscuity, adultery, and other themes were prohibited. However, pre-code films had no such restrictions.
extra: Pre-Code films are fascinating for their frankness—they feature themes and depictions that would vanish from Hollywood until the 1960s.

definition: The planning stage of a production after a movie has been greenlighted. This occurs before principal photography begins. Pre-production usually involves script treatment, scheduling, casting, production design, and financial planning.
extra: Pre-production is where most of the heavy lifting happens. A well-organized pre-production can save a film from costly mistakes later on.

definition: A later film in a franchise that presents events and/or characters that are set chronologically before the time of the original movie. It is the opposite of a sequel.
extra: Prequels can deepen mythology, but they risk undermining mystery if over-explained. Examples include the Star Wars prequel trilogy and The Hobbit films.

definition: A showing of a movie before it is released to the public. Studios will often pre-screen movies so that they can receive feedback from audiences to know what to alter before it is officially released.
extra: Pre-screenings can shape the final cut of a film. Audience reactions sometimes lead to major edits—or in extreme cases, entirely new endings.

definition: The main shooting dates of a film with the lead actors present creating the film. This is outside of second-unit photography, reshoots, or VFX shots.
extra: Principal photography is the heart of production—the period when most of the material audiences eventually see is captured.

definition: A way to describe the main characters in a movie. It is usually those who have dialogue. The principals are different from the protagonists and have greater roles than extras.
extra: In casting terms, ‘principals’ are the actors whose performances carry the story, even if they aren’t the lead or protagonist.

definition: A chief of a film’s production. The producer is in charge of raising funds, acquiring a story, hiring key personnel, finalizing the script, and arranging for distribution. The producer often serves as the liaison between the filmmakers and the financiers.
extra: Producers are often the unsung power behind films. While directors get creative credit, producers shape whether a project gets made at all.

definition: A movie’s overall visual look and design. Gives the viewer a sense of the time period, the plot location, and the character’s actions and feelings.
extra: Production design grounds a film in its world—whether it’s the gritty realism of a war movie or the fantastical landscapes of a science fiction epic.

definition: The individual responsible for the overall aesthetic of the story.
extra: Production designers oversee sets, costumes, and props to create a consistent visual language. They collaborate closely with directors and cinematographers.

definition: Refers to the overall quality of a movie. This value is based on criteria like set design and costumes. It is not based on criteria like the directing, acting, and script.
extra: When people say a film ‘looks expensive,’ they’re talking about production value. Even low-budget films can achieve high production value with creative design.

definition: Typically a brief scene, preface, or speech preceding the main plot of the movie. It often provides information that will help the audience better understand the plot and is the opposite of an epilogue.
extra: Prologues can set the tone and context before the story begins—Shakespearean in origin, they remain common in fantasy and epic films.

definition: A character who pushes a story forward. They are the central force of the story.
extra: The protagonist isn’t always the ‘hero.’ Antiheroes and morally complex leads still serve the same role: driving the narrative.

definition: A camera shot where the camera physically moves away from the subject. It helps provide the full context of the scene. It is the opposite of a push in.
extra: A pull back widens perspective, often revealing new information or emphasizing a character’s smallness in a larger world.

definition: A camera shot where the camera physically moves toward the subject. It provides a closer look to see more details. It is the opposite of a pull back.
extra: Push-ins create intimacy or intensity. They can heighten drama, focus on a key object, or signal a character’s realization.

definition: Refers to an ad research rating that gauges how easily a celebrity is recognized — and how well the celebrity is liked. This system is no longer as widely used.
extra: Think of it as an early measure of 'star power.' Q Scores helped advertisers decide whether a celebrity could sell products or attract audiences, but in today’s social media era, metrics like follower counts and engagement have largely replaced it.

definition: A quarter of a year; three months. Used by production accountants and publicity departments for financial issues.
extra: Studios often divide budgets, marketing pushes, and release schedules into quarters. For example, a summer blockbuster would fall into the third quarter of the year.

definition: A fixed price paid or charged for your goods or services.
extra: In film and TV, 'rate' often refers to crew wages or rental fees for equipment. Unions and guilds frequently set minimum rates, but experienced professionals can negotiate higher ones.

definition: A slang word for reconnaissance, meaning an inspection or exploration of an area to gather information. (Mostly used in the European Film/TV industry)
extra: A recce is essentially a location scout—directors, cinematographers, and designers walk through a set or filming location to anticipate challenges, such as lighting or sound issues.

definition: Play out the scene without rolling cameras.
extra: Rehearsals allow actors and crew to refine timing, blocking, and emotional beats. They can be informal table reads or full run-throughs with cameras marking shots.

definition: Start of the process that leads to recording the scene.
extra: You'll usually hear 'Roll sound!' followed by 'Rolling!' from the sound department, and then 'Action!' from the director. It’s part of the standard set protocol.

definition: The ambient noise of the set, lights, fans, rain, traffic, etc.
extra: Capturing room tone helps sound editors fill gaps between dialogue cuts so the audio track sounds natural and seamless, rather than jumpy or artificial.

definition: After you’ve recorded an ideal take, you might record an additional take for safety in case the ideal take is later discovered to be unusable.
extra: Safety shots are like insurance. Even if everyone thinks they’ve nailed it, a backup protects against unforeseen technical glitches, like a boom mic dip or camera wobble.

definition: Stand-Ins
extra: Second team members stand in for principal actors during rehearsals or technical setups, allowing the crew to adjust lighting and camera angles without tiring the stars.

definition: A smaller or “skeleton” crew of filmmakers who film any shots without the main actors; this can include aerial shots, scenery, or crowd shots.
extra: Second units are often responsible for action sequences or wide establishing shots. Big productions like superhero films sometimes have multiple second units running simultaneously.

definition: A small portion of a script that only contains the pages that will be filmed that specific day, plus the call sheet.
extra: Actors often carry sides on set so they only have to focus on that day’s dialogue and blocking rather than the entire script.

definition: Sound departments call this out once they are recording so the crew knows.
extra: The phrase comes from the days of film when camera operators had to wait until the film reel was running at full speed before starting a take.

definition: A small device that replicates a bullet wound, usually by squishing a capsule of fake blood.
extra: Squibs are staples of action films—they create the illusion of gunshot impacts without actual danger. Modern productions sometimes enhance or replace them with digital effects.

definition: A mount that is worn by the camera operator that allows for the camera movement to be separate from the operator’s movement, meaning a smooth shot can be created even while the operator is running and the camera movement is not held to the limitations of a dolly or tripod. It is important to know when a Steadicam is being used on set because, most of the time, that means that most of the set will be shown. Body rig used to stabilize the camera while it is in a virtual hand-held position.
extra: The Steadicam revolutionized filmmaking in the 1970s—think of the smooth, floating shots in 'Rocky' or 'The Shining.' It gave directors a new middle ground between static tripods and shaky handheld footage.

definition: A short sentence or clever phrase that memorably summarizes the film to a general audience. It’s supposed to tease what the film will be about. In Alien, the tagline is “In space, no one can hear you scream.”
extra: A great tagline can become as iconic as the movie itself—'Just when you thought it was safe to go back in the water' (Jaws 2) still lingers in pop culture.

definition: A single continuously-recorded performance, shot or version of a scene with a particular camera setup; often, multiple takes are made of the same shot during filming before the director approves the shot; in box-office terms, take also refers to the money a film’s release has made.
extra: Some directors, like Stanley Kubrick, were notorious for requiring dozens of takes until performances matched their vision. The word 'take' also carries a dual meaning when discussing box office 'takes.'

definition: A term applied to the actors as a group on a film set.
extra: While 'talent' technically applies to actors, in industry jargon it can sometimes extend to directors or key on-screen personalities, depending on context.

definition: The common term used for films with sound beginning in 1927. The advent of talkies marked the dawning of the era of sound films, as opposed to silent films.
extra: The first talkie, 'The Jazz Singer,' revolutionized cinema. While audiences were thrilled, many silent-era stars saw their careers fade if their voices didn’t suit sound pictures.

definition: A medium shot of people conversing; used as a criticism – denoting an uninteresting image.
extra: The phrase suggests static, unimaginative filming—like watching a news broadcast. Filmmakers often avoid 'talking heads' by adding movement or visual variety to dialogue scenes.

definition: A slang term meaning “pick,” “select,” “name,” or “appoint.”
extra: In casting or crew hiring, being 'tapped' means you’ve been chosen for a role or job without necessarily going through the usual audition or interview process.

definition: An excessively sentimental or emotional film, usually with suffering female protagonists, tragic circumstances, manipulative scenes, and dramatic musical scoring, aka melodramas, sometimes derogatorily referred to as a ‘chick flick’.
extra: Classic Hollywood melodramas like 'Imitation of Life' or 'Terms of Endearment' fit this label. While sometimes dismissed, tearjerkers remain audience favorites because of their emotional pull.

definition: A short trailer that is generally released many months before a movie is actually released to give a brief peek at what the movie will be like and to build audience anticipation. Teaser trailers are usually much shorter than the final trailer, which reveals more of the film’s storyline.
extra: Modern studios rely heavily on teaser trailers, sometimes dropping them a year before release. Marvel films, for example, often use teasers to build hype long before audiences see real plot details.

definition: A person with expertise in a particular field who provides advice for the production.
extra: For example, a military advisor might ensure authenticity in a war film, or a medical consultant could guide hospital scenes. They help keep details believable.

definition: The best-known colour film process. These films were highly saturated with vivid colours and a three-colour dye transfer system. It is also known as a three-strip colour.
extra: Technicolour gave classics like 'The Wizard of Oz' and 'Gone With the Wind' their unforgettable vibrancy. Its lush look is still imitated today with digital grading.

definition: Refers to a feature-length motion picture made for television, also known as a made-for-TV movie.
extra: Telefilms were especially popular from the 1960s through the 1990s. Today, they live on in the form of Hallmark movies and streaming originals.

definition: A camera lens with an incredibly long focal length and a narrow-angle of view. The purpose of this lens is to condense and compress depth within a space. It brings faraway objects closer to the viewer without moving the camera.
extra: Telephoto lenses are great for sports or wildlife filming. In dramas, they create a 'flattened' look where background and foreground appear closer together, adding visual tension.

definition: A feature-length movie funded by a TV network, intended to be premiered on television.
extra: These were once a staple of network programming, often tackling topical social issues. They now have spiritual successors in streaming originals.

definition: A standalone episode of a television series that is used to sell a show to a television network or other distributor. A pilot is created to be a testing ground to gauge whether a series will be successful.
extra: Not all pilots ever air—many are produced just to pitch to networks. Some shows, like 'Game of Thrones,' even reshot or heavily reworked their pilots before audiences saw them.

definition: A television production of a singular event (such as an awards show or concert) instead of a regularly scheduled series.
extra: Examples: The Oscars telecast, Super Bowl halftime shows, or charity concerts. Typically a one-off event, not part of an ongoing series.

definition: A brief advertisement or public service announcement between TV programs.
extra: Usually 15, 30, or 60 seconds long. Synonymous with TV commercial. Can be used for both marketing (e.g., film promotion) and public awareness campaigns.

definition: An industry term meaning a film that is expected to serve as primary support for a studio, to be a top-grossing blockbuster (usually during the summer season), to compensate for a studio’s other flops; usually the film is the start of, or an installment in, a franchise.
extra: Examples: Marvel’s Avengers films, Disney’s Star Wars installments. Named ‘tentpole’ because such films hold up the studio’s financial year.

definition: The central characteristic, idea, concern or motif in a film. A theme is the inferred stance taken on the central topic or message of a story.
extra: Examples: Love conquers all, corruption of power, survival against odds. Distinct from ‘plot’ (what happens) and ‘tone’ (how it feels).

definition: A medium shot consisting of three individuals in the frame. This contrasts to a “single” or “two shot.”
extra: Often used in dialogue scenes where dynamics between three characters are important. Balances framing differently than singles or two shots.

definition: A subdivision of Lucasfilm, Ltd dedicated to improving picture and sound for the cinema and the home. THX is a suite of high-fidelity audiovisual reproduction standards for movie theatres, screening rooms, home theatres, computer speakers, video game consoles, car audio systems, and video games.
extra: Famous for its ‘Deep Note’ audio logo. Developed by George Lucas’s company to standardize audio-visual presentation quality in theaters.

definition: Refers to any commercial venture connected to a film.
extra: Examples: Merchandise, novelizations, video games, fast-food promotions. Tie-ins extend a film’s marketing beyond the screen.

definition: A cinematographic term that relates to a close-up shot of the subject. A director often says “tight on” when they want an extreme close-up or tight framing on the subject.
extra: Used for emphasis or emotional intensity. Synonymous with ‘close-up’ but often implies even closer framing.

definition: When a camera tilts down or up along a vertical axis. It is often used to suggest a sense of imbalance or to emphasize a character’s menace or power.
extra: Contrasts with pan (horizontal movement). Example: tilting up from a villain’s feet to face height to emphasize intimidation.

definition: Electronic guide track added to film, video or audio material to provide a time reference for editing and synchronization.
extra: Displayed as HH:MM:SS:FF (hours, minutes, seconds, frames). Used by editors to precisely align footage and sound.

definition: A technique where frames are shot much slower than a normal rate (e.g., 24 frames per minute instead of per second). This allows the action to progress much faster than in reality. This is typical for nature documentaries to capture clouds moving or plants growing.
extra: Examples: construction projects, sunsets, city traffic. Often confused with ‘slow motion’ which is the opposite effect.

definition: A tint uses colour to make film stock appear in a different shading to attain a desired mood. The method behind this is generally done by hand, and it was often used in black-and-white movies before the widespread use of filming in colour.
extra: Common in silent films—blue tint for night scenes, red tint for fire or passion. Predecessor to full-color processes like Technicolor.

definition: The lead part in a movie or other production for an actor that is named after the title of the film.
extra: Examples: Hamlet in *Hamlet*, Forrest in *Forrest Gump*. Indicates the actor plays the character after whom the story is named.

definition: The words that appear on the film screen and convey information; categories of titles include credit titles, main titles, end titles, insert titles, and subtitles. Title design refers to the artistic manner in which the title of a film is displayed on the screen.
extra: Examples: Saul Bass’s iconic designs (e.g., *Psycho*, *Vertigo*). Title sequences often set tone or style for the film.

definition: The person who designs how a film’s title appears on the screen. The manner in which the title of a movie is displayed on the screen is widely considered an art form. Saul Bass is considered a master title designer.
extra: Notable modern title designers: Kyle Cooper (*Se7en*). Often collaborate with directors to establish a film’s visual identity.

definition: The mood or atmosphere of a film scene, often revealed by the director in how a film is directed and expressed to the audience.
extra: Examples: dark, comedic, hopeful, suspenseful. Tone shapes audience interpretation alongside theme and style.

definition: To star or to be billed above the title of a film. The topliner is the star of a particular film.
extra: Example: ‘Tom Cruise in Top Gun: Maverick’—Cruise is the topliner. Indicates leading billing and prominence in marketing.

definition: Literally meaning “forceful turn” in French. It usually refers to a lead actor’s performance that was incredibly skillful, brilliant, notable, masterful, reflecting a very high standard, and perfectly displaying the actor’s ability.
extra: Examples: Daniel Day-Lewis in *There Will Be Blood*, Meryl Streep in *Sophie’s Choice*. Not just good, but career-defining.

definition: A single component or channel of a soundtrack.
extra: Examples: dialogue track, music track, effects track. Tracks are mixed together in post-production for final audio.

definition: A smooth shot in which the camera moves alongside (‘tracking within’) or follows the subject through space, usually with the camera mounted on a dolly (on a dolly track); often seen as a side-to-side motion (relative to the scene or the action); also known as following shot; sometimes used interchangeably with dolly shot, pull back shot (pull-out, push-out, widen-out or push-back), trackback (moving away) or track in (or push-in) (moving forward), or zoom shot.
extra: Famous examples: the Copacabana entrance in *Goodfellas*, trench run in *1917*. Creates immersion and fluid movement.

definition: Refers to a personal touch or embellishment by an actor, director, writer, producer, or head of department within a film that becomes their signature or calling card.
extra: Examples: Tarantino’s trunk shots, Hitchcock cameos, Wes Anderson’s symmetry. Distinguishes an artist’s style.

definition: Refers to the professional magazines and publications that report the daily or weekly entertainment news of the entertainment industry.
extra: Examples: *Variety*, *The Hollywood Reporter*, *Deadline*. Known as ‘the trades’ in Hollywood jargon.

definition: A short publicity film, preview, or advertisement composed of short excerpts and scenes from a forthcoming film or coming attraction, usually two to three minutes long, often presented at the showing of another film.
extra: Called ‘trailer’ because they originally trailed (followed) the feature. Now one of the biggest marketing tools for films.

definition: Someone who conditions animals to perform various behaviours on cue.
extra: Example: Dog trainers for *Marley & Me*, horse trainers for Westerns. Must ensure animal safety and humane treatment.

definition: One of several ways of moving from (or joining together) one shot or scene to the next one, including such transitional effects or shots as a cut, fade, dissolve, and wipe; a transition focus between two scenes means the current scene goes out of focus and the next scene comes into focus.
extra: Examples: Star Wars’ iconic wipe transitions, classic fades to black. Editing tools to control pacing and tone.

definition: The person responsible for managing drivers and coordinating the transportation of a production’s cast, crew, and equipment from the various locations and sets used for filming.
extra: Critical on location-heavy shoots. Coordinates vans, trucks, trailers, and talent vehicles. Works closely with production management.

definition: A shot in which foreground action is superimposed on a separately filmed background by optical printing or digital compositing.
extra: Predecessor of modern green screen. Used in classics like *Mary Poppins*. Now largely done with digital compositing.

definition: A film made for the purpose of showing scenes from foreign, unfamiliar, or alluring places.
extra: Popular in early cinema, often shown before main features. Modern versions exist as documentaries or YouTube travel vlogs.

definition: A detailed literary summary or presentation of a film’s story (and each major scene), with action and characters described in prose form, and sometimes including bits of dialogue; often used to market and/or sell a film project or script; usually it is an abridged script longer than a synopsis (a brief summation of a film); a completed treatment is the late stage in the development of a screenplay after several story conferences have incorporated changes into the script.
extra: Treatments are essential in the development pipeline because they allow producers and studios to evaluate a story’s viability before a full screenplay is written.

definition: A group of three films that together compose a larger narrative and are related in subject or theme.
extra: Trilogies often allow for expansive storytelling — from The Godfather Trilogy to The Lord of the Rings — where each film both stands alone and builds into a larger arc.

definition: Refers to talent who can sing, dance and act skillfully equally well on a consistent basis; usually applicable to performers in the musicals genre; it also could refer to a person who can act, direct, and write.
extra: In Broadway and Hollywood musicals, being a triple threat is the gold standard — think Gene Kelly or Hugh Jackman, who seamlessly shift between acting, singing, and dancing.

definition: When a film is “in turnaround” in the film industry, it means that a studio has decided to halt its development or production, allowing the project to be shopped to other studios or producers. This status indicates that the original studio is no longer pursuing the project, often due to budget concerns, creative differences, or market considerations.
extra: Many iconic films nearly died in turnaround; Forrest Gump, for example, was passed on before finding its eventual studio home.

definition: Also refers to the time between the wrap of talent or crew and the start of the next shoot day. For example, “the union requires 12-hour turnaround.”
extra: This labor-related turnaround ensures rest and safety; breaking turnaround rules can incur penalties under union regulations.

definition: Shooting the reverse angle.
extra: This is especially common in dialogue-heavy scenes, where the camera switches perspective to show the other character’s reaction.

definition: A film that is marketed as having a surprise ending that shouldn’t be revealed (as a spoiler) to those who haven’t seen the picture.
extra: Audiences remember twist endings in films like The Sixth Sense or The Usual Suspects, where the reveal redefines everything seen before.

definition: Refers to a film with only two characters.
extra: These intimate stories — such as My Dinner with Andre — often rely heavily on dialogue and performance rather than spectacle.

definition: A medium or close-up camera shot of two people (often in dialogue with each other), often framed from the chest up, often used to contrast the two characters.
extra: Two shots are staples of romantic comedies and buddy films, visually emphasizing the dynamic between characters.

definition: When an actor is commonly (but unfairly) identified, associated with, or ‘stereotyped’ by a particular character role; casting against type is the reverse of typecasting.
extra: For instance, Bela Lugosi was forever linked with Dracula; some actors embrace typecasting, while others fight against it.

definition: A ¾-inch magnetic tape, which would originally be found on a professional cassette tape format. In recent years, it has been supplanted by new digital formats. It was a competing yet inferior tape format to both beta and VHS.
extra: U-matic tapes were heavily used in TV production and education during the 1970s–80s before digital took over.

definition: A ‘supporting’ role for a major (sometimes minor) star that is officially credited (usually in the end credits), but no mention (or billing) is made in the film’s advertisements or the opening credits.
extra: These roles can surprise audiences, such as major actors showing up in a cameo without advance marketing.

definition: A role that a major (or minor) star plays that is not credited in the credits or in the film’s poster.
extra: Brad Pitt’s cameo in Deadpool 2 as the Vanisher is a famous modern uncredited role.

definition: Refers to an understated, neutral and muted acting performance.
extra: This approach can be powerful when subtlety is needed — Ryan Gosling is often noted for his underacting style.

definition: The process of slowing down a camera’s frame rate. This is achieved by shooting at a slower speed than the usual 24 frames per second. This results in the captured images appearing in fast motion.
extra: Classic silent comedies by Chaplin and Keaton often used undercranking to create exaggerated, sped-up action.

definition: When an image is photographed with less light than what would be considered proper exposure. This results in a dimly lit, indistinct image that lacks contrast and is the opposite of an overexposed shot.
extra: Underexposure can be a mistake, but filmmakers sometimes use it intentionally to create mood or mystery.

definition: A low-budget, non-commercial film, usually independently made, without the traditional sources of funding or distribution.
extra: The 1960s saw a rise in underground cinema with figures like Andy Warhol and Kenneth Anger leading experimental works.

definition: An organization that represents the best interests of a certain segment of professionals in the motion picture industry. There are unions for writers, actors, directors, and most film crews. Unions negotiate contracts, pursue rights, and receive recognition. Therefore, there are rules and regulations when working with unions.
extra: Examples include SAG-AFTRA for actors, DGA for directors, and IATSE for crew — each with strict guidelines for productions.

definition: A unit production manager (UPM) is a member of a film production crew who plays an administrative role in the production process. The UPM reports to the line producer on the film, who oversees production and helps decide costs related to the daily production. As a UPM, you execute the line producer’s plans.
extra: UPMs are crucial for keeping productions on schedule and budget; they’re the logistical backbone of film sets.

definition: Member of the publicity department who works on location during the production of a movie. Duties include setting up press visits and electronic press kit interviews. In addition, the unit publicist assembles the biographical materials and notes about the making of the movie that are later turned into the movie press kit. Unit publicists are itinerant — they move from production to production and are on the production payroll.
extra: They often shape the public image of a film long before release, ensuring the right buzz is created during shooting.

definition: A character whose perspective we follow in the story but lacks a certain degree of credibility. These narrators may lack all the information necessary to translate the story to the audience adequately, or they have a clear bias.
extra: Classics like Fight Club and The Usual Suspects use unreliable narrators to keep audiences guessing.

definition: Refers to an imaginary, ideal (or mythical), perfect state or place (especially in its laws, government, social and moral conditions), often with magical healing and restorative properties.
extra: Cinematic utopias often serve as either aspirational or ironic backdrops — think Pleasantville or Tomorrowland.

definition: Parallel lines in a picture which are not parallel to the visual plane of the picture appear to converge in one or more vanishing points inside or outside the borders of the image. It is useful to analyze a motion still image regarding its vanishing points because they can help to determine the height of the camera and the camera angle. If a motion still has only one vanishing point, it is possible to draw a horizontal line across it and get the so-called “horizon line,” which marks the camera’s height when the frame is taken. If there is more than one vanishing point, it is necessary to find two opposite vanishing points, which are mostly located offscreen, and draw a line from one vanishing point to the other to get the horizon line.
extra: Understanding vanishing points is vital in cinematography and set design, especially when creating perspective-heavy shots.

definition: A femme fatale character with a bad reputation, usually seductive and scheming in nature or behaviour.
extra: The archetype traces back to silent cinema, where actresses like Theda Bara embodied the 'vamp' persona.

definition: A Variac (short for “variable AC”) is a type of electrical transformer that can be used to adjust the voltage output of an AC power source. It is commonly used in industrial and commercial applications where a variable voltage is needed for testing or for controlling the speed of motors. Variac is the trademark name of a variable autotransformer. This instrument limits the voltage that goes to tungsten lights and dims them. They come in 1K, 2K & 5K versions.
extra: In film sets, Variacs were invaluable before digital dimming tech, allowing precise control over practical lighting.

definition: A variety entertainment show from the stage featuring a series of short acts – songs, dancing, acrobatics, comedy skits, and animal acts. It was highly popular in America from the late 1880s to the 1920s, when it became overtaken by sound films and radio; most of the early film, radio and TV comedians found their start on the vaudeville circuit.
extra: Stars like Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton, and the Marx Brothers honed their craft in vaudeville before moving into film.

definition: A common household appliance for recording and/or playing prerecorded video tapes. See VHS, NTSC and PAL.
extra: The rise of the VCR in the 1980s reshaped film consumption, sparking the home video revolution and rental boom.

definition: Directional forces that lead our eyes from one point to another in a picture or a shot. Basically, there are three main different types of vectors: Index vectors are the most obvious type, as they take the form of something in the shot that is clearly pointing somewhere, such as a one-way sign. Motion vectors are created by elements in the shot that are moving in a certain direction, such as a bus driving left to right across the shot. Graphic vectors take the form of aspects in a scene with a directional element, such as skyscrapers in a city or a sidewalk cutting through the shot.
extra: Understanding vectors is key in cinematography and editing, as they guide viewer attention across the frame.
