definition: A camera technique achieved by tracking backwards while simultaneously zooming toward the subject, or vice versa. This keeps the subject at the center of the image while the surroundings stretch or contract behind them. Also known as a dolly zoom, this effect was named after Hitchcock’s prominent use in Vertigo.
extra: Spielberg famously used this in Jaws when Brody realizes a shark attack is happening on the beach.

definition: A video is a film or television programme recorded digitally (or, in the past, on tape) for people to watch on a television set.
extra: Today 'video' is used broadly, covering everything from streaming content to social media clips.

definition: Camera Assistants take the images generated by the film or digital cameras and display them live on video monitors so the director and other crew members can see exactly what’s being shot and can also see footage being played back for review.
extra: Video assist became industry standard after Jerry Lewis pioneered its use in the 1960s for reviewing takes.

definition: Tent/area where the monitors are set up for the director/s, producer/s, and script supervisor.
extra: On set, this is the nerve center for creative decision-making during a shoot.

definition: A person who works in the video medium — recording moving images and sound onto linear analog or digital tape, non-linear digital disc, or any other digital recording media, such as memory cards.
extra: Unlike cinematographers, videographers are often associated with events, news, or smaller-scale productions.

definition: A popular format for VCR systems worldwide in the 1990s.
extra: The VHS vs. Betamax format war ended with VHS dominance, cementing it as the home video standard for decades.

definition: Usually a type of action film in which the protagonist takes the law into his/her own hands as a self-appointed doer of justice, revenge, and payback.
extra: Examples include Death Wish and Taxi Driver, where societal failures push individuals toward violent justice.

definition: A scene in a movie that can stand on its own. For example, the orgasm scene in When Harry Met Sally is often viewed and referenced on its own, separated from the rest of the film. A vignette can also refer to a masking device, often with soft edges.
extra: Filmmakers like Richard Linklater often structure films around a series of vignettes rather than a single plotline.

definition: Anything added to a movie that was not in the original shot under the subcategory of special effects. They can either be achieved through CGI or through special techniques, such as rear projection and double exposures.
extra: VFX today includes everything from Marvel’s CGI-heavy blockbusters to subtle digital touch-ups.

definition: The person that prepares the miniature models, creature puppets, or whatever the camera subject is, to perform whatever the object is supposed to do during the shot. Riggers create digital skeletons for 3D computer-generated (CG) characters. These skeletons, or rigs, are like puppets that define the movements of a character or creature, such as how a big cat runs, how a person’s face and mouth move when they sing, or how someone raises an eyebrow.
extra: Rigging is critical for believable animation — Pixar films, for example, rely heavily on advanced rigging systems.

definition: The head of a production’s visual effects crew. VFX supervisors are in charge of the whole VFX project. They manage the VFX pipeline, including all of the VFX artists that work in this process. They have ultimate responsibility for all of the VFX elements produced for a project by their company or studio.
extra: They collaborate closely with the director and cinematographer to ensure VFX integrate seamlessly into live-action footage.

definition: Recorded dialogue that comes from off-screen or is unseen in the frame. It is often done to convey a character’s thoughts or from a narrator. In a script, a voice-over is abbreviated as “V.O.”
extra: Voice-over narration is a hallmark of noir films like Sunset Boulevard and modern works like Goodfellas.

definition: The unseen person who does the speaking necessary to create a voice-over.
extra: Voice-over artists are key in animation, advertising, and dubbing industries, often shaping character identity.

definition: Initial check when you first turn on your walkie talkie to make sure it’s working. Someone should reply with “Good Check” if they can hear you clearly.
extra: On film sets, reliable walkie use is critical for coordination between departments, especially on large locations.

definition: A minor role consisting of a single, brief appearance on the screen, usually not appearing in the credits and without dialogue; contrast with extras, bit parts, and non-speaking roles.
extra: Walk-ons are often opportunities for newcomers to get screen time. Unlike extras, they are usually more noticeable, even if the part doesn’t include lines.

definition: A walk-through is the first rehearsal done on a film’s set. It is necessary for the director to figure out camera positioning, sound, and lighting. This is done before the cameras start to roll.
extra: Walk-throughs are essential for avoiding mistakes once filming begins. It gives everyone—from actors to the camera crew—a chance to visualize the scene together.

definition: A murmur sound effect, used to establish a crowd of people on location.
extra: If you’ve ever heard extras mumbling 'walla walla' in the background, that’s where the term comes from. It helps create the illusion of a bustling environment without distracting dialogue.

definition: The general term used to talk about the costume department. It can also refer to an individual costume and all of the accessories associated with it.
extra: Wardrobe choices often carry symbolic meaning—what a character wears can instantly suggest status, personality, or transformation.

definition: The section of a production’s crew concerned with costumes. Individual job titles include costume designer, costumer, and costume supervisor.
extra: This team ensures continuity, repairs, and last-minute fixes. They’re crucial when shooting spans weeks or months and costumes must stay consistent.

definition: The head of the wardrobe department working under the Costume Designer. Also referred to as Costume Supervisor.
extra: They manage fittings, keep track of multiple costume changes, and solve logistical challenges like period-accurate clothing for large casts.

definition: A phrase spoken when someone is coming through or around set with an object that could potentially hit someone.
extra: On set, communication like this prevents injuries. It’s part of the safety culture where heavy or sharp equipment moves constantly.

definition: An oscilloscope used to measure and monitor video or audio levels.
extra: Colorists and cinematographers rely on waveform monitors to ensure accurate exposure and color—far more precise than just eyeballing a monitor.

definition: One who specialises in weapons, armours, and firearms.
extra: They not only supply weapons but also enforce strict safety protocols. Their expertise ensures both realism and protection on set.

definition: Wood wedges used for levelling and stabilizing.
extra: They may seem mundane, but wedges keep cameras steady, platforms level, and props secure. Small tools like this often save productions from costly mishaps.

definition: A movie often set in the “Wild West” of the late 19th-century United States, Western Canada, or Northern Mexico.
extra: The Western is one of Hollywood’s foundational genres, shaping the myth of the American frontier with themes of justice, lawlessness, and survival.

definition: A plywood dolly used as a dolly for smooth surfaces.
extra: This type of dolly is simple but effective—ideal for quick, smooth tracking shots without the complexity of advanced dolly rigs.

definition: An extremely fast pan, incorporating much motion blur. The term refers to the “whipping” action that the camera operator uses to move the camera.
extra: Whip pans are often used to convey urgency or to create clever transitions between scenes without cutting.

definition: A camera setting that establishes the true colour of white. This produces a baseline from which all other colours are measured. White may not appear “white” under all lighting conditions, so this helps correct it.
extra: Without proper white balance, footage can look too blue indoors or too orange in sunlight. It’s one of the most basic but critical camera settings.

definition: A random signal with a consistent amount of energy per hertz.
extra: In film sound design, white noise can fill silence, mask unwanted sound, or create atmosphere—often in unsettling horror sequences.

definition: A story or play about a murder in which the identity of the murderer is not revealed until the end. It often refers to a mystery or detective film. The lead character in a whodunit is a crime-solving detective, such as in the Sherlock Holmes series of films.
extra: Whodunits thrive on audience speculation. Clues, red herrings, and misdirection are their bread and butter, making them endlessly rewatchable.

definition: A shot (often abbreviated WS) taken with a lens that is able to take in a wider field or range of view than a regular lens. It exaggerates distance and depth, keeping all objects in focus. An extreme wide-angle lens giving a 180-degree view is called a ‘fish-eye’ lens.
extra: Wide-angle shots are great for landscapes or cramped interiors. They can also distort perspective for creative effect, making rooms seem larger or characters loom.

definition: A lens with a focal length smaller than that of a normal lens, they capture a wider shot of the scene. 16mm, 25mm, 35mm, and 50mm lenses can be considered wide.
extra: Wide lenses aren’t just for scenery—they’re often used in action films to emphasize dynamic movement and spatial relationships.

definition: A rectangular aspect ratio, wider than the standard 1:33:1 used before the 1950s. After that time, widescreen processes such as VistaVision and CinemaScope came into the mainstream and became the industry standard.
extra: Widescreen forever changed cinema, making films feel more immersive and giving directors a broader canvas for visual storytelling.

definition: Wild track, also known as wild sound and wild lines, is an audio recording intended to be synchronized with film or video but recorded separately. It is a non-sync sound, recorded without the camera running, usually recorded to supplement the sync takes.
extra: Directors often use wild lines to fix dialogue issues or add emphasis during editing. It’s a subtle but vital tool in post-production.

definition: A distinctive scream archived by Warner Brothers and used repeatedly on countless films including Star Wars and Kill Bill.
extra: The Wilhelm scream has become a running in-joke in Hollywood. Spotting it is almost a game for film buffs.

definition: An optical effect or transitional technique where one shot seems to be “wiped off” the screen by another shot that replaces it. It is also known as a flip-over or push-over.
extra: George Lucas famously used wipes in Star Wars to give the saga a pulpy, old-serial feel. It’s a bold alternative to the standard cut or dissolve.

definition: A term referring to the public discussion or buzz that a film can acquire, fueled by sneak previews and advance advertising; word of mouth is an important marketing element in a film’s success or failure.
extra: Studios spend millions on marketing, but nothing beats positive buzz. Word of mouth can turn a modest indie film into a cultural phenomenon.

definition: The name by which a movie is known while it is being made. This is sometimes different from the title with which it is released.
extra: Working titles are often placeholders to avoid leaks or to reflect a project in progress. Some even stick—like Star Wars, originally called The Star Wars.

definition: A positive duplicate of the original negative.
extra: Workprints let editors and directors shape the film without damaging the fragile original negative. Today, digital equivalents serve the same purpose.

definition: Any audio/video recording and editing system.
extra: Modern workstations combine hardware and software, allowing editors to handle massive amounts of footage with relative ease.

definition: A person or animal trainer responsible for the care and handling of all non-humans on set.
extra: Wranglers ensure animal safety and performance, but also compliance with legal standards—credits often include 'No animals were harmed.'

definition: To finish shooting, either for the day or the entire production.
extra: The word 'wrap' has become almost ceremonial. Cast and crew often celebrate 'wrap parties' as a marker of completing the project.

definition: A general term for someone who creates a written work, be it a novel, script, screenplay, or teleplay.
extra: In film, the writer lays the foundation. Even with improvisation or rewrites, the script is the blueprint for everything that follows.

definition: A light that was developed by Dick Hall for the film Blade Runner. Jordan Cronenweth’s inspiration for Blade Runner was moving lights that were tracked in every interior space. It has a flood and spot function that gives you a beautiful circle of light, but when you flood it out, it gives you a donut shape pattern because the globe is in the center of the parabolic mirror reflector.
extra: This light became iconic for Blade Runner’s futuristic atmosphere. Cinematographers value xenon lights for their intensity and unique beam patterns that help create surreal and dramatic visual worlds.

definition: The technique using an electrostatic process to copy or transfer an image, commonly found in office copiers and used in cartoon production.
extra: Disney popularized xerography in animation during the 1960s to streamline cel production. It gave films like 101 Dalmatians their scratchy, hand-drawn look.

definition: A small memory card format used in older digital cameras.
extra: These cards were once common in early digital still cameras but have largely been replaced by SD cards due to storage and speed limitations.

definition: A very bright, daylight balanced lamp.
extra: Xenon lamps are frequently used in film projectors and high-intensity searchlights because of their bright, white light that closely mimics daylight.

definition: A standard sound connector used in professional audio.
extra: XLR connectors are the workhorses of pro audio. They’re used on everything from microphones to mixing boards, prized for their durability and balanced signal transmission.

definition: An informal voluntary certificate for a pornographic film, indicating large amounts of explicit sex. Contrast with NC-17.
extra: The 'XXX' label isn’t an official rating like MPAA classifications; it emerged as a marketing shorthand for extreme adult content.

definition: A stereo-mic structure that uses two microphones placed and aimed in crossed directions which feed two channels for stereo pickup.
extra: This mic setup captures a natural stereo image without phase issues. It’s a go-to in recording live concerts or ambient sounds for film.

definition: Slang for a fabricated story.
extra: Calling something a 'yarn' often implies it’s entertaining, even if it’s not entirely true—like tall tales or embellished anecdotes in movies.

definition: A slang term, meaning a boring film.
extra: Critics or audiences might dismissively call a slow or poorly paced movie a 'yawner,' highlighting how subjective film reception can be.

definition: A colour space used in NTSC and PAL broadcast video systems.
extra: YUV separates brightness (Y) from color (U and V), which allowed early TV systems to remain compatible with black-and-white sets while introducing color.

definition: A method of cutting negative for blow-up. Also refers to a method of preparing A and B rolls for print.
extra: Zero cut techniques ensured seamless film printing before digital workflows. Editors used it to maintain continuity and precision in final prints.

definition: Refers to a very low-budget, independently-made, non-union, less than B-film grade movie, usually with a first-time director and actors. These films are often quickly made for the teen youth market and look amateurish but with campy appeal. They can include exploitative subject matter plus surfing films, motorcycle flicks, and cheap horror films. Z-films become prime candidates for cult film status.
extra: Z-movies, often ridiculed for their poor production values, sometimes achieve cult status precisely because of their flaws—think Ed Wood’s infamous Plan 9 from Outer Space.

definition: A variable focal length lens.
extra: Zoom lenses allow cinematographers flexibility without swapping glass, though some filmmakers prefer prime lenses for their sharpness and 'look.'

definition: A single shot taken with a lens that has a variable focal length, thereby permitting the cinematographer to change the distance between the camera and the object being filmed and rapidly move from a wide-angle shot to a telephoto shot in one continuous movement; this camera technique makes an object in the frame magnify and appear larger; the movement towards a subject to magnify it is known as zoom in or forward zoom, or reversed or decreased to reduce its size is known as zoom out/back or backward zoom.
extra: Zoom shots were especially popular in 1970s cinema. Directors sometimes use them to create a sense of unease, or to mimic a character’s sudden focus on something.

definition: An early movie process for creating animated projections.
extra: Eadweard Muybridge developed the zoopraxiscope in the 1870s, projecting sequential images of motion—essentially a stepping stone to modern cinema.

definition: A revolutionary special effects 3D process invented by cameraman Zorian Perisic, incorporating a camera system and a projector with synchronized zoom lenses to create the illusion of movement in depth.
extra: The Zoptic process was famously used for Superman’s flying sequences in the 1978 film, making audiences believe Christopher Reeve was truly soaring.

definition: Key lighting is the primary and usually strongest source of light in a scene or photo. It sets the overall mood and defines the subject’s main illumination. While it’s typically the first light set up on a shoot, it doesn’t always have to face the subject directly. Positioning the key light to the side or behind the subject can create moodier, more dramatic effects with shadows and depth. Avoid placing it near the camera axis, as this causes flat, uninteresting lighting that removes texture and depth.
extra: Use key lighting when you want to highlight a subject clearly and make it stand out within the scene. It’s the foundation of your lighting setup and shapes the viewer’s attention.

definition: Fill lighting is used to soften or eliminate the shadows created by the key light. It’s less intense and usually positioned opposite the key light. The purpose is to add dimension by controlling contrast without removing all shadow, preserving depth. Fill lights are often diffused or bounced to create soft, even illumination. Reflectors placed around three-quarters opposite the key light are commonly used to spread gentle light. Many scenes use just key and fill lights to achieve natural depth and balance.
extra: Use fill lighting to reduce harsh shadows and lower contrast, making details in shadowed areas visible. It helps reveal more of the scene and keeps the lighting balanced and natural-looking.

definition: Backlighting is the light positioned behind and slightly above the subject to separate it from the background, adding depth and a sense of three-dimensionality. It’s often the last light added in a classic three-point lighting setup. This light is usually diffused to cover more of the subject softly, lighting areas like the shoulders and the back of the neck rather than just the top of the head. When used alone, backlighting can create striking silhouettes by emphasizing shape over detail.
extra: Use backlighting to create a glowing rim or halo around your subject, accentuating outlines and making subjects pop off the background. It’s great for emphasizing form or creating dramatic silhouettes.

definition: Side lighting illuminates the subject from one side, parallel to the camera’s line of sight. It often creates strong contrasts between light and shadow, highlighting texture and contours. This lighting style is key to producing a dramatic or chiaroscuro effect—where areas of light and dark contrast sharply, revealing the three-dimensional form of subjects. When combined with a fill light, the fill is typically much weaker (around one-eighth the intensity) to preserve the dramatic shadows while softening the darkest areas just enough.
extra: Use side lighting to emphasize texture, detail, and depth. It enhances the spatial relationship in a scene, making subjects appear more sculpted and dynamic. It can also create an emotional tone of tension or mystery.

definition: Practical lighting refers to light sources that appear naturally in the scene, such as lamps, candles, televisions, or fireplaces. These are part of the set design and contribute to the lighting ambiance while also functioning as props actors interact with. Practical lights often emit a softer, dimmer light that might not be strong enough to illuminate a subject fully, so supplemental lights are often hidden nearby to boost the effect without spoiling realism. Adjustable dimmers are also used to control their intensity smoothly.
extra: Use practical lighting when the light source is part of the scene’s story or action, like a bedside lamp that characters can turn on or off. It adds authenticity and atmosphere, grounding the scene in reality.

definition: Bounce lighting involves redirecting a strong light source off a reflective surface—such as a white reflector, ceiling, or wall—to produce a larger, softer, and more diffused light area. This technique allows filmmakers to create gentle, even lighting without harsh spots, especially when softboxes or diffusers aren’t available. Bounced light mimics natural, ambient light and helps fill in shadows without introducing new direct sources.
extra: Use bounce lighting to soften and spread light evenly over a scene or subject. Bouncing light off a ceiling can create ambient illumination that looks natural and reduces harsh shadows.

definition: Soft lighting isn’t about direction but quality: it creates light that gently wraps around subjects, reducing harsh shadows and contrast. Cinematographers achieve soft lighting by diffusing strong lights with materials like softboxes, silk, or bounce surfaces. This technique enhances skin tones and textures subtly and can simulate gentle natural light conditions. It’s used aesthetically to beautify subjects or convey calm, gentle atmospheres.
extra: Soft lighting is flattering for people, minimizing wrinkles, blemishes, and harsh facial shadows. Use it to create pleasing, natural-looking images or to soften dramatic scenes.

definition: Hard lighting originates from a small or direct light source, such as the sun on a clear day or a focused spotlight. It produces strong, well-defined shadows and high contrast, emphasizing shapes, textures, and edges. While often seen as harsh or unflattering, hard light is an intentional stylistic choice that can highlight details, create striking silhouettes, and give scenes an intense, dramatic look.
extra: Use hard lighting to accentuate the contours, texture, and structure of your subject. It adds drama and visual interest by enhancing contrasts and creating bold shapes.

definition: High key lighting is a bright, evenly lit style with very few shadows and minimal contrast, often approaching overexposure. It uses multiple light sources balanced at similar intensities to flood the scene with light. This style originated in classic Hollywood and remains popular for its clean, cheerful, and upbeat look, frequently used in comedies, commercials, and musicals.
extra: Use high key lighting to create a lighthearted, dreamy, or positive mood. It works well for scenes needing a sense of clarity, openness, or fantasy.

definition: Low key lighting is the opposite of high key: it emphasizes shadows, darkness, and contrast by using minimal lighting—often just a strong key light with little or no fill light. This approach produces moody, mysterious, or suspenseful atmospheres, making it perfect for genres like film noir, horror, and thrillers where shadow and ambiguity drive emotional impact.
extra: Use low key lighting for dramatic, tense, or mysterious scenes. It’s effective at conveying moodiness, danger, or intimacy by sculpting the scene with shadow.

definition: Motivated lighting is designed to mimic natural or existing light sources within the scene—like sunlight streaming through a window, moonlight, or street lamps—helping blend artificial lighting seamlessly with the environment. It often supports practical lights by enhancing or adjusting their intensity and coverage without breaking realism. Techniques include using filters, gels, and diffusers to simulate specific light qualities, colors, and shadow patterns associated with these sources.
extra: Use motivated lighting to replicate or enhance the look of real-world light sources naturally. Filters, gels, and modifiers help create authentic light colors and shadows, preserving the scene’s visual logic.

definition: Ambient lighting refers to the natural or available light already present in the shooting environment, such as sunlight, moonlight, or streetlights. While artificial lights often supplement it for control, ambient lighting forms the base illumination in a scene. Outdoor shoots frequently rely on ambient light during golden hours (early morning or late afternoon) for soft, flattering conditions. Because ambient light changes with weather and time, careful planning is needed to maintain consistency.
extra: Use ambient lighting when you want natural, broad illumination without emphasizing a specific style. It evenly lights environments and is versatile for many situations, but requires flexibility for changing conditions.

definition: A static camera movement means the camera remains completely still, usually mounted on a tripod or fixed support, allowing everything within the frame—actors, props, and background elements—to move freely. This creates a deliberate frame where the viewer’s focus is guided purely by what happens within that locked shot.
extra: Examples: In The Wolf of Wall Street, static shots capture spontaneous and improvised dialogue scenes, emphasizing actor performances and natural interactions. This technique is excellent for highlighting subtle facial expressions, nuanced acting, and carefully composed visuals. By not moving the camera, directors create an intimate and focused atmosphere where tension and emotion can build quietly without distraction, making it ideal for dramatic, intimate, or conversational scenes.

definition: A pan involves rotating the camera horizontally from left to right or vice versa, sweeping across the scene. It’s commonly used to follow moving subjects, explore a location, or reveal key narrative details gradually, directing the audience’s gaze along a natural path.
extra: Examples: In La La Land, whip pans — extremely fast horizontal sweeps — energize the dynamic between Sebastian and Mia, injecting momentum and excitement into their interactions. Pans work like a storyteller’s tool, guiding the viewer’s eyes fluidly across the frame to reveal new information or track a character’s movement, helping maintain spatial awareness and narrative flow in a visually engaging way.

definition: A tilt is the vertical counterpart to the pan, where the camera moves up or down while fixed on its axis. This motion often serves to establish scale by revealing towering structures, characters, or dramatic environments, or to disclose something important that was previously hidden.
extra: Examples: Spielberg’s famous tilt in Jurassic Park dramatically reveals the enormous dinosaurs, emphasizing their size and inspiring awe. Tilts are especially effective in action and thriller genres to create feelings of discovery, power, or vulnerability. They can also mimic a character’s gaze, enhancing immersion by letting viewers share that perspective of looking up or down.

definition: A dolly shot is achieved by mounting the camera on a wheeled platform or track system, enabling smooth, controlled movement in any direction. This movement can follow characters closely, retreat to reveal the broader scene, or move laterally to track action, immersing the audience in the narrative flow.
extra: Examples: Stanley Kubrick’s use of the dolly in The Shining includes a slow pull-out shot that gradually reveals Jack’s isolation and mental unraveling, enhancing the film’s psychological tension. Dollies allow precise and fluid movements that can be both subtle or dramatic, drawing viewers deeper into the story’s world. When combined with a zoom lens, the dolly zoom effect emerges — a visually unsettling technique that warps depth perception to portray dizziness, shock, or altered states of mind.

definition: The push-in is a movement where the camera physically moves closer to the subject, tightening the frame to increase emotional intensity, build suspense, or reveal internal conflicts and subtle reactions that might otherwise go unnoticed.
extra: Examples: In The Assassination of Jesse James, the push-in shot on Robert Ford intensifies the emotional weight and draws the audience directly into his troubled mindset. This technique is carefully planned to make viewers feel like they are moving closer to the character’s emotional core, heightening intimacy and tension, and often marking moments of realization or dramatic change.

definition: Pulling out is the opposite of a push-in, where the camera moves away from the subject, widening the frame to show more of the environment or to highlight a character’s isolation, vulnerability, or insignificance within the larger world.
extra: Examples: Kubrick’s pull-out in The Shining visually separates Jack from his surroundings, emphasizing his loneliness and detachment. Pull-outs create emotional distance and broaden the narrative context, helping the audience see a bigger picture or understand a character’s relationship to their environment, often enhancing feelings of solitude or exposure.

definition: Zooming changes the camera lens’s focal length to magnify or shrink the subject within the frame without physically moving the camera. This optical effect alters the size of the subject but does not change the spatial relationship between objects, which can create an unnatural or disorienting sensation.
extra: Examples: Stanley Kubrick’s use of zoom in Full Metal Jacket often unsettles viewers, reminding them of the artificiality of film and intensifying psychological unease. Zooms are widely used in horror and thriller genres to build discomfort or highlight critical moments, especially when paired with camera movement to create complex visual effects like the dolly zoom.

definition: Also known as the vertigo zoom, this iconic shot combines simultaneous dolly movement (the camera physically moving closer or farther) and zooming in the opposite direction. This creates a striking distortion of perspective, warping the background while keeping the subject the same size, producing a dizzying, surreal effect.
extra: Examples: Alfred Hitchcock’s Vertigo popularized this technique to visually represent dizziness and psychological disorientation. Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings used it to create supernatural effects, conveying shock and altered reality. The dolly zoom is a powerful storytelling tool to visually express intense emotional or mental shifts.

definition: The roll involves rotating the entire camera along its lens axis, tilting the horizon line and creating a sideways tilt of the image. This disorienting move often signals instability, confusion, or dreamlike, chaotic states within the story.
extra: Examples: The throne scene in Black Panther uses a roll to subtly convey unease and tension in Wakanda’s political atmosphere. Rolls are used sparingly due to their strong visual impact but can effectively evoke dizziness, disorder, or a shift from reality, amplifying the emotional or psychological tension in a scene.

definition: A tracking shot moves the camera fluidly through a scene, following characters or action seamlessly. This technique keeps the viewer immersed by maintaining continuous motion and spatial connection without cuts, often requiring precise choreography of actors and camera operators.
extra: Examples: Long, uninterrupted tracking shots are used in dramas and action sequences to build tension and immerse the audience in the environment. These shots help maintain narrative momentum and emotional engagement, as the camera glides naturally with the characters, allowing the scene to unfold in real time.

definition: An arc shot circles the camera around a subject in a smooth curved path, adding a sense of energy, movement, and dynamism to a scene. It can reveal different angles of a character or setting, intensifying emotions or disorientation.
extra: Examples: In The Dark Knight, the arc shot circles around the Joker, increasing his unpredictability and chaotic energy. Arc shots can produce dizziness or confusion in viewers, often used to heighten emotional tension, create a feeling of being surrounded or trapped, or simply energize the visual storytelling.

definition: Boom movements raise or lower the camera vertically using equipment like cranes or jibs, allowing dramatic high or low shots. This vertical movement can reveal entire landscapes, emphasize scale, or follow characters from above or below, adding grandeur and spatial awareness.
extra: Examples: Epic establishing shots in large-scale productions often use boom movements to introduce vast settings or reveal hidden parts of the scene. This movement helps filmmakers add drama and spectacle, making locations feel more immersive and powerful, and guiding audience focus from ground level to towering heights or vice versa.

definition: A handheld shot is filmed with the camera held directly by the operator, resulting in natural shakiness and unsteady movement. This raw, immediate style adds realism, urgency, or intimacy, often used to put the viewer in the middle of chaotic or emotionally intense scenes.
extra: Examples: The Big Short uses handheld shots combined with zooms to create a documentary-style authenticity. Handheld cameras convey energy and chaos, making them perfect for war movies, thrillers, or vérité-style films that want to feel spontaneous and immersive, capturing moments as if seen through human eyes.

definition: A Steadicam shot uses a specialized stabilizing rig worn by the camera operator to produce smooth, fluid movement even while walking or running. It eliminates the shakiness of handheld shots but preserves mobility and flexibility to move freely through complex spaces.
extra: Examples: Steadicam is widely used in dramas and thrillers for long takes, POV shots, or intricate tracking shots through tight environments. This technology allows filmmakers to combine the intimacy and immediacy of handheld with the polished, professional look of stabilized footage, enhancing storytelling with graceful camera flow.

defination: A close-up shot is when your subject covers most of the frame. You can achieve this by being physically close to the subject or by using atelephoto lensfrom afar. When close-up shots are used to depict a person, a close-up shot helps you to show the expressions and emotions of the character. It’s also a very intimate shot. Instead, if the subject is an object or an action – then it’s used to direct the viewer’s attention. For example, if two people are arguing and one is holding a knife behind his back – you might want to do a close-up shot at the hand with the knife.
extra: Use close-up shots to show important details, emotions, or expressions. They work well when you want the audience to focus closely on a character's feelings or a key object.

defination: A medium shot is still centered on the main subject, but it shows more of the context. It generally refers to all shots that frame a person from the waist up, although something tighter across the torso is still OK. With a medium shot, not only are you showing the context but also the body language – you can also include more characters. They are also a great way to transition between close-ups and wider shots.
extra: Use medium shots when you want to show a character's body language or interactions with others, while still keeping some background visible.

defination: Long shots – also known as wide shots or establishing shots  – show your entire subject and leave enough space around it. If you want to show a new location where your subject arrived or introduce a new ambient while keeping a strong presence of the subject – this is the way to go. The long shot also shows the full length of the subject, so can be useful in exaggerating scale when comparing the subject to the objects surrounding it.
extra: Use long shots to show the full scene or environment around a character. It's helpful to introduce new locations or show how a character fits into their surroundings.

defination: An extreme close-up is exactly what the name suggests – it’s taking the close-up shot to the extreme by closing in on a detail of the subject. With these shots, you can emphasize a reaction or an expression on the character – for example, a tear. It’s not necessarily used with characters – it can be an object too—for example, an extreme close-up of a watch to show how the time is passing.
extra: Use extreme close-ups to highlight very small but important details, like a tear or an object that has meaning to the story.

defination: An extreme long shot is a very wide camera shot that leaves your subject so far away that it almost gets lost within the scene. You can use this to show your character feeling isolated or vulnerable in a vast space.
extra: Use extreme long shots to show vast landscapes or to make a character seem small and alone in a large environment.

defination: Originally called cowboy shot because it depicts the subject from the mid-thigh, this allowed for the cowboy guns to be on the frame to capture the quickdraw. You may still call it a cowboy shot, but you might also find it an American shot. This type of shot is close enough to the subject that you can still see emotions and expressions – but you can also show part of the scene, especially what they are doing with their hands.
extra: Use cowboy shots when you want to show a character’s upper body and hands, especially in action scenes or to highlight gestures.

defination: This is one of the most common camera shot framing types when there’s a conversation happening in the scene – usually between two characters. The camera is placed behind the character who is listening – so you can see part of the head and the shoulder. Then, in focus, you see the person who is speaking. It literally shows how you would see if you were peaking over the shoulder of the character. Usually, this shot alternates continuously as the conversation goes on, creating a shot-reverse-shot sequence. This camera shot allows the viewer to understand who is involved in the conversation and still appreciate the non-verbal communication from the person who is talking. In some cases, the camera angle changes too, indicating a different relationship between the characters. For example, if you make a shot over the shoulder from a high angle, you show your character looking down at the other, making them look ‘smaller.’
extra: Use over-the-shoulder shots during conversations to show who is talking and listening, making dialogues more engaging and clear.

defination: With a zoom shot, the camera doesn’t move. You might see the character closer or further away, but it’s an effect due to the change offocal length. Although, there is an effect called the dolly-zoom, which is used to create an unusual visual perception, and it’s been used by Alfred Hitchcock, Martin Scorsese, Steven Spielberg, and other great directors.
extra: Use zoom shots when you want to change the focus on a subject quickly without moving the camera. It can highlight emotions or surprise.

defination: The master shot is the most important and is often the first on the shot list. It should cover an entire action or an entire scene. However, they play a different role in modern films than they used to – before, the whole shooting revolved around the master shot. Now, multiple camera shots, camera angles, and camera movements make films more dynamic.
extra: Use master shots to capture the full scene or action from start to finish, helping viewers understand the overall layout.

defination: POV stands for point of view. So, POV shots show things from the perspective of a particular character. It’s an effective technique to pull the viewer into the action by giving them a first-person angle of view. Many films in history have successfully used this technique. You can see some famous examples in the above video reel. Typically, a POV shot comes after a medium shot or a close-up where you see the character looking at something – then you jump right into their perspective with a POV to see what they were looking at.
extra: Use POV shots to let the audience see what the character sees, making the experience more personal and immersive.

defination: Typically, an establishing shot is a wide shot or an extra wide angle shot. This is because they’re used to establish a time and a place where your story is happening. Establishing shots can have different camera shot sizes depending on how much context you need to give to the viewer. If you want to signal that you’re in a specific city, an extreme wide shot from an aerial angle is often helpful. Other times, you simply need to show the outside of a building to indicate where the characters are.
extra: Use establishing shots at the start of a scene to show where and when the story is happening.

defination: This camera angle indicates that you’re looking up at the subject. How low? That depends on what you want to tell with this shot – but technically speaking, anything below the eye level of the subject is already a low-angle shot. When the camera is positioned almost at ground level, it’s also called aworm’s eye view. In general, you use this camera shot angle to show the subject big and powerful or because you want to include something tall behind your subject in the frame.
extra: Use low angle shots to make a character look strong, powerful, or dominant.

defination: For this camera angle, you need to be shooting at ground level – but unlike the low angle shot, the camera is not looking up. In this case, the camera is low on the ground because you want to show something that is happening down there.
extra: Use ground level shots to focus on actions or details happening close to the ground, giving a natural and immersive perspective.

defination: Continuing up the axis of the camera, you can do a knee-level shot. This camera angle is shot at the knee level of a character, and it’s often used to include another character’s entire body because it’s further away.
extra: Use knee level shots to show characters from a lower point of view while still capturing their full body, often useful for action or movement.

defination: Usually, a hip-level camera angle is used for a cowboy shot. This allows you to show the character from the mid-thigh widow distortion. In photography, a hip-level shot is also common when street photographers capture candid snapshots preventing people from noticing them.
extra: Use hip level shots when you want to capture a natural, casual view of a character or scene, often showing body language.

defination: The shoulder-level shot is one of the most common camera shot angles – as the name indicates, it’s done by positioning the camera at the same height as the subject’s shoulders.
extra: Use shoulder level shots for neutral, everyday perspectives, especially during conversations or normal actions.

defination: At the top of the list, the eye-level shot is the most used of all camera angles. This is because it doesn’t have a particular effect or impact on the viewer – it offers a familiar perspective. Most of the story is told at this level because it’s neutral. This way, it’s immediately noticeable to the viewer when you want to create an effect and change the camera angle.
extra: Use eye level shots to show scenes naturally and neutrally, making viewers feel like they are watching from a normal human perspective.

defination: A high-angle shot is when you have the camera looking down at the subject – it doesn’t matter how high or low in the axis this is. In short, it’s the opposite of a low-angle shot. A high-angle shot is used to emphasize the character’s vulnerability or impotence.
extra: Use high angle shots to make a character look small, weak, or vulnerable.

defination: Abird’s-eye viewis a more extreme version of the high-angle shot – it’s also known as an overhead shot or crane shot. Usually, it’s paired up with a wide camera shot – this way, you can see down on the subject but include a good part of the context. You’ll frquently see an overhead shot on Youtube when the subject is talking about a product being reviewed.
extra: Use bird’s-eye view shots to show a scene from directly above, giving a clear overview or making subjects look small and part of a bigger space.

defination: The highest camera angle is the aerial view. This was often called the helicopter shot because the camera operator was usually in a helicopter to capture this view. Nowadays, you can find an aerial shot more often becausedroneshave made it more affordable for all filmmakers and photographers. Even amateur videographers can get stunning aerial footage – something inconceivable before commercial drones.
extra: Use aerial shots to capture large outdoor scenes, landscapes, or big events from high above for a grand or dramatic effect.

defination: This is one of the most peculiar types of camera angles because it’s a point of view that’s completely unnatural. It doesn’t matter how high or low the camera is, nor the shot types – a dutch camera angle is characterized by a tilted horizon. To achieve this, you need to rotate the camera on its axis. Because it’s not the way we’re used to seeing things, it makes the viewer feel disoriented or uneasy. TheDutch angleis also known as the German angle because it was often used in German expressionist films. You might also call it canted or oblique angle.
extra: Use Dutch angles to create a sense of tension, unease, or confusion in a scene.

definition: Continuity editing is the process of arranging and reordering shots to create a seamless and logical flow of story. It preserves spatial and temporal consistency so that the audience experiences the illusion of uninterrupted time and space. By following rules such as the 180-degree axis, match on action, and consistent screen direction, continuity editing ensures clarity and immersion in narrative storytelling.
extra: This is the invisible backbone of most Hollywood films. When done well, the audience doesn’t notice it at all—they simply feel oriented in the scene. It’s what makes a conversation cut back and forth between two people without the geography becoming confusing.

definition: Cross-cutting is a technique that alternates between two or more sequences happening simultaneously in different locations, often converging toward a climax. It not only shows parallel action but can also link storylines thematically, creating tension or emotional contrast.
extra: Think of D.W. Griffith’s *Intolerance*, where multiple storylines across centuries were cross-cut, or the iconic bomb-defusal countdown scenes. Editors use rhythm and pacing here like a conductor guiding an orchestra.

definition: A cutaway is an inserted shot that momentarily shifts attention from the main action to a secondary detail, character reaction, or related image. It provides breathing space, adds context, and can smooth out otherwise jarring edits.
extra: Cutaways are the editor’s safety net. They cover continuity problems, add humor (like a dog’s reaction in a comedy), or subtly redirect audience focus without breaking the narrative thread.

definition: A fade is a transition where the image gradually dissolves into or out of a solid color, most often black. Traditionally used to mark the passage of time, shifts in narrative tone, or the end of a sequence, fades remain one of cinema’s oldest yet most evocative tools.
extra: Even though some modern filmmakers avoid fades in favor of quicker cuts, they can still create a sense of finality or emotional resonance. A slow fade to black, for instance, can feel like an exhale at the end of a dramatic scene.

definition: J and L cuts are split-editing techniques where the audio and visuals transition at different times. A J cut introduces audio from the next scene before the current image ends, while an L cut carries over audio from the previous scene after the image has already shifted. This staggering of sound and image makes scene transitions feel natural and continuous.
extra: If continuity editing is about keeping the audience grounded, J and L cuts are about making the film breathe. They’re especially common in dialogue scenes, where you hear a response before you see the speaker, mimicking how conversations unfold in real life.

definition: A jump cut is an abrupt shift in a single shot that skips forward in time, creating a visible 'jump' in the subject’s position or action. While traditionally seen as a mistake in classical editing, it became a deliberate stylistic tool in modern cinema to disrupt smooth continuity and energize the rhythm of a sequence.
extra: Jean-Luc Godard’s *Breathless* famously embraced jump cuts to break convention. Today, YouTube creators use them constantly to speed up dialogue and keep attention from drifting.

definition: A match cut links two shots through visual, spatial, or thematic similarity, creating a smooth yet meaningful transition. It emphasizes continuity not just of time and space but of ideas, often bridging two seemingly unrelated moments into a poetic or symbolic connection.
extra: The most famous match cut is Kubrick’s bone-to-spaceship transition in *2001: A Space Odyssey*. Done well, it can be witty, shocking, or lyrical—one of the editor’s most elegant storytelling tricks.

definition: Montage is an editing approach that compresses time, events, or information by combining a rapid sequence of shots into a cohesive whole. It often relies on rhythm, music, and juxtaposition to deliver emotional or intellectual impact greater than the sum of its parts.
extra: From Eisenstein’s political montages to Rocky’s training sequences, montage has shaped both avant-garde cinema and pop culture. It’s shorthand for growth, change, or overwhelming experience.

definition: Shot/reverse shot alternates between two opposing camera angles, usually in dialogue, to show one character and then the other. When paired with consistent eyelines and the 180-degree rule, it gives the impression of a continuous space and natural conversation.
extra: This technique is so common that most audiences never question it. Breaking the 180-degree rule here, though, can disorient viewers—a tactic some directors use intentionally to unsettle a scene.
